Young leaves are eaten boiled in several changes of water or raw in moderation; mature plants are too bitter, while thoroughly dried seeds are also edible.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves are boiled in several water changes or eaten raw moderately; mature leaves become too bitter. Thoroughly dried seeds are also edible.

stories.summary: Climbing perennial native to South Africa, originally recorded on moist forest edges in the Drakensberg Mountains. It has glossy, lobed, ivy-like leaves and scented yellow pompom-like flowers without obvious petals. It spreads readily from small stem, runner or underground-stem fragments and is invasive in several regions.
An annual herb native to Eurasia. Its single upright stem is covered with short curly hairs and bears deeply lobed leaves, topped by a broad cluster of many small yellow flower heads.

Annual flowering herb native to the Palaearctic. Its small yellow flower heads usually lack ray florets, with the disc florets mostly hidden by black-tipped bracts. It thrives in disturbed ground and reseeds from downy seeds that become sticky when wet.
stories.edibilityNote: Reported as poisonous to humans; chronic exposure to its pyrrolizidine alkaloids can cause irreversible liver damage.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to Eurasia and North Africa, small-flowered catchfly has branching stems covered in long, curling hairs and shorter glandular hairs. Its white, pink or two-coloured flowers have a hairy, veined outer cup that becomes inflated when fruit forms.
An annual herb native to central and southern Mexico and Guatemala. Its edible mottled seeds absorb abundant liquid when soaked, developing the gelatinous coating characteristic of chia drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: The edible seeds are cultivated and commonly used as food in parts of the Americas and elsewhere.

stories.summary: A mustard-family plant once indigenous to North Africa and southern Europe, hedge mustard is now established worldwide. Its tall, upright stems bear tiny yellow flowers and fruits pressed close and parallel to the stem. Cultivated European forms provide bitter, cabbage-like leaves eaten raw or cooked, while the seeds are made into mustard paste.
stories.edibilityNote: Cultivated leaves are eaten raw or cooked; seeds make mustard paste. The plant is also eaten with yogurt in parts of the Levant.

stories.summary: Annual or biennial herb native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia. It has spiny bluish-green leaves, yellow dandelion-like flowers and milky sap when cut.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are eaten as a palatable, nutritious vegetable.

stories.summary: An annual to biennial mustard native to Eurasia, Brassica rapa includes cultivated forms such as turnips, bok choy and napa cabbage. Wild and weedy forms typically have a slender taproot and leafy rosette, while turnip forms develop a swollen storage root; most flowers have four yellow petals followed by narrow seed pods. Cultivated varieties are eaten as roots or leafy vegetables, with young leaves eaten raw and older leaves typically cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: Cultivated roots and leafy vegetables are eaten; young leaves may be raw, older leaves are typically cooked, and raw seeds may irritate some people.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to Europe and western Asia, with a hollow upright stem and wind- or water-carried seeds. Young leaves are less bitter and can be eaten raw; leaves are also cooked, and steaming reduces the bitterness of older leaves.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw when young or cooked; steaming reduces older leaves’ bitterness. Young roots are also edible and used as a coffee substitute.

stories.summary: An annual flowering plant native to Eurasia and now naturalized worldwide. Its sprawling stems bear a single line of hairs that switches sides at the nodes, along with small white flowers. Its leaves are eaten as a vegetable, often raw in salads, though some varieties or similar species may be too fibrous.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten, often raw in salads; some varieties or similar species may be too fibrous, and use is not advised during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

stories.summary: Annual flowering herb native to parts of Europe, especially the Mediterranean Basin. It has a hairy stem, dense clusters of unequal white flowers tinged pink or red, and small greenish or pinkish fruits covered in long prickles.

A mat-forming perennial, or rarely annual, native to Europe, Greenland, the Himalayas and Japan. Its hairy, tear-shaped opposite leaves form star-like patterns, and its stems spread along the ground and root where they touch it.
Flowering plant native to Europe, lesser hop trefoil has three leaflets and small yellow flowers. It is generally accepted as the main plant representing the traditional Irish shamrock.

Annual flowering herb native to most of Europe except the British Isles, northern Asia, and northern and northwestern Africa. Its rounded, coarsely toothed leaves bear stinging hairs, and it is reputed to sting more strongly than the common nettle.

A sprawling annual legume of uncertain native origin; its centre of diversity is thought to be the Fertile Crescent, though molecular confirmation is lacking. Its compound leaves end in branched tendrils, and its pea-like flowers are usually bright pink-purple.
stories.edibilityNote: Human dietary use is documented at early Neolithic sites; the seeds contain anti-nutritional compounds that limit modern cultivation.

stories.summary: An evergreen trailing perennial native to the Mediterranean region, greater periwinkle roots along its stems to form dense ground cover. It has glossy dark-green leaves and solitary violet-purple flowers from early spring to autumn.

Annual climbing herb native to southern Europe, North Africa and nearby islands. Dense stem hairs can give it a silvery-white appearance, while one-sided flower clusters bear dark reddish-purple blooms.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds and forage have been reported to poison humans.

stories.summary: Bushy shrub or spreading tree native to south-eastern Australia. It has bluish-grey or silvery leaves and spherical heads of yellow flowers. Its leaves are sometimes used in Indian chutney, while Ngunnawal and Wiradjuri people traditionally made flour from the seeds.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are sometimes used in Indian chutney; Ngunnawal and Wiradjuri people traditionally made flour from the seeds.

stories.summary: A tree native to south-eastern Australia, blackwood has dark grey-black, deeply fissured, scaly bark on older trunks. It bears densely packed pale yellow to nearly white flowers, followed by curved, twisted or coiled seed pods. Indigenous Australians harvest and eat the seeds as bush food.
stories.edibilityNote: Indigenous Australians harvest and consume the seeds as a common bush food.

stories.summary: A large shrub or small tree native primarily to California and southwestern Oregon, it often has several trunks and a broad, rounded crown. It leafs out very early, but inland plants commonly shed their leaves by late summer while coastal plants retain them longer. Native groups occasionally ate its poisonous seeds only after boiling and leaching them for several days, then grinding them into meal.
stories.edibilityNote: Native groups occasionally ate seeds or nut meats after boiling and leaching toxins for several days, then grinding them into flour or meal.

stories.summary: A shrub native to western California and northwestern Baja California, California sagebrush has aromatic, silvery-gray foliage with finely divided leaves. Its flowers are small and inconspicuous, while its rounded form branches from the base.

A deciduous, often multi-stemmed shrub found across most of North America. Its nut sits inside a beak-like husk whose tiny filaments can irritate skin. Indigenous peoples ate and commonly traded the nuts, which have the same uses as other hazelnuts.
stories.edibilityNote: The nuts were eaten and commonly traded among Indigenous groups and are used like other hazelnuts.

stories.summary: A woody shrub native to south-central China. Its dull green oval leaves have fuzzy white undersides, and its white flowers are followed by red-orange fruits dispersed mainly by birds. Introduced elsewhere as an ornamental, it has become invasive in California and Oregon and a troublesome weed in Hawaii.
Tall evergreen tree endemic to southeastern Australia. It has mostly smooth bark, whitish waxy juvenile leaves, glossy green adult leaves, and white flowers followed by woody fruit.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are used as a herbal tea.

stories.summary: A woody perennial shrub native to Mediterranean Europe, northwest Africa, the Azores and the Canary Islands, French broom has yellow flowers and hairy pods that burst open to scatter seeds. It can produce abundant seed, regrow after cutting or burning, and become invasive where introduced.

An evergreen conifer native to California’s Central Coast and Mexico’s Guadalupe and Cedros islands. Its bright-green needles usually grow in clusters of three, although var. binata has pairs. Its cones may remain closed until forest-fire heat opens them and releases the seeds.

Perennial herb native throughout the Americas, Africa and western Asia. Its blue flowers have two large blue petals and a smaller white petal; each flower lasts only one day, though buds may open several days apart.
stories.edibilityNote: Documented as a wild edible consumed by many groups across its range, and commonly eaten in Brazil.

stories.summary: Deciduous tree native to eastern North America. It can live for several hundred years and develop a high, spreading, umbrella-like canopy, but Dutch elm disease has devastated its populations since the 1920s.

A deciduous tree native to eastern North America, the American tuliptree is the tallest tree of the region’s temperate deciduous forest. Its glossy, four-lobed leaves have a squared-off tip and turn bright yellow in autumn, while its upright greenish-yellow flowers resemble tulips and bear an orange band.

An annual plant native to regions of the Americas, common ragweed emerges in late spring and reproduces by seed. Its wind-borne pollen is highly allergenic, while its numerous oil-rich seeds are eaten by songbirds and upland game birds.

Conifer tree endemic to New Caledonia. It has a slender, spire-like crown and rough, resinous bark that peels in papery strips. A 2017 study found that cultivated trees tend to lean south in the Northern Hemisphere and north in the Southern Hemisphere while growing upright at the Equator.

A deciduous tree native to Indomalaya and Australasia, chinaberry has fragrant pale-purple or lilac flowers and yellow fruit that can remain through winter. Its fruit is poisonous to humans when eaten in large quantities.
stories.edibilityNote: Berries were historically used for homemade whiskey in the southern United States, but leaves and fruits must not be eaten; fruit can poison humans in large quantities.

stories.summary: A tree native to the Caribbean, notably Puerto Rico and the Lesser Antilles. It bears showy, tubular pink flowers in spring and summer, followed by splitting pods that release many thin, winged seeds. It is cultivated as an ornamental street and shade tree and for timber.

A large coniferous tree native to western North America, California incense-cedar develops orange-brown bark that becomes grey, fissured and peeling with age. Its flattened sprays of bright green foliage release a shoe-polish-like aroma when crushed.
stories.edibilityNote: Indigenous people of California used the foliage as a flavouring.

stories.summary: Flowering shrub native to the mountains of Nepal, China and Taiwan. It has a low, spreading habit with flat, symmetrical sprays of glossy deciduous leaves, followed by pink to white summer flowers.
A small evergreen flowering shrub native to the western and central Mediterranean. Its dense aromatic grey-green foliage is topped in summer by masses of yellow, button-like flower heads.

A perennial climbing plant native to West Asia, Europe and North America, common hops sends up shoots in spring and dies back to a cold-hardy rhizome in autumn. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants, and the female cone-shaped flowers are used to flavor and preserve beer.
stories.edibilityNote: The female flower cones are used to flavor, bitter and preserve beer.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to temperate North Africa, Europe and parts of western Asia, it has slender green leaves and spikes carrying numerous pink, spurred flowers. Its traditional medicinal use in Europe dates from the late Middle Ages, but clinical evidence for human effectiveness remains limited or inconclusive.

A desert gymnosperm endemic to the Namib Desert between Angola and Namibia. It grows from a thick trunk and produces only two continuously growing leaves; individuals are believed to live for more than 1,000 years and perhaps 2,000.

An evergreen tree or shrub native to western and southern Europe and northwest Africa, European holly has glossy green leaves that are often sharply prickled. Its bright red or yellow fruits occur only on female plants and require nearby male plants for fertilisation.
stories.edibilityNote: The berries are generally regarded as toxic to humans.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native to China. It bears white flowers in late summer, and its flowers and leaves are sometimes prepared as herbal tea, including by families in Laoshan Village, Shandong Province.
stories.edibilityNote: Flowers and leaves are sometimes used for herbal tea by families in Laoshan Village, Shandong Province, China.

stories.summary: An herbaceous biennial or short-lived perennial native to western Europe and North Africa. It forms a woolly leaf rosette before producing a tall stem of hanging, spotted tubular flowers. Its leaves, flowers and seeds are poisonous to humans and can be fatal if eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, flowers and seeds are poisonous to humans and can be fatal if eaten.

stories.summary: A coniferous tree native to eastern Canada and the north-central and northeastern United States, northern white-cedar has fan-like branches, flat sprays of scale-like leaves and peeling red-brown bark. Some cliff-growing specimens are exceptionally old but remain small and stunted.
stories.edibilityNote: Ojibwa reportedly made soup from soft-twig inner bark; twigs were also brewed as tea. Prolonged internal use or use during pregnancy may be harmful.

stories.summary: A low annual flowering plant native to Europe, it has naturalized elsewhere and is considered a weed in some places. Common on disturbed or open ground, it produces numerous small yellow flower heads from June to December in the Northern Hemisphere.

Shrub native to China, with white flowers, orange-to-red round fruits and sharp-spined branches. Its bitter, astringent fruits are inedible to humans, and its leaves, fruits and seeds contain hydrogen cyanide.
stories.edibilityNote: The bitter, astringent fruits are inedible; leaves, fruits and seeds contain hydrogen cyanide.

stories.summary: A biennial wildflower native to southeastern Europe, Mediterranean Turkey and North Africa, purple salsify has grasslike leaves, milky stems and purple flower heads. Its root and young shoots are eaten after boiling, while fresh leaves may be eaten raw or cooked; after flowering, the root becomes stringy and inedible.
stories.edibilityNote: Root and young shoots are eaten after boiling; fresh leaves may be raw or cooked. After flowering, the root becomes stringy and inedible.

stories.summary: A usually annual, occasionally biennial herb native to southern and central Europe and western Asia, it has yellow flower heads that open early in the morning and often close by late afternoon. Its later seed head resembles a dandelion's but is distinctly larger.
stories.edibilityNote: Edibility reports conflict, and the cited books were later found not to discuss this species.

stories.summary: A large deciduous tree native to much of Europe, especially humid climates. Young trees and clipped hedges often retain their dead leaves until spring. Its nuts are eaten, although large quantities are slightly toxic; historically they were pressed for cooking oil or soaked before being ground into flour.
stories.edibilityNote: Nuts are eaten but are slightly toxic in large quantities; they were used for cooking oil or soaked to remove tannins before making flour.

stories.summary: An evergreen fir tree native to eastern and central Canada and the northeastern United States. It has a narrow conical crown, resin-blistered young bark and upright dark-purple cones that turn brown and break apart to release winged seeds in September.
stories.edibilityNote: Humans eat the needles directly or in tea; the Innu also grate and eat the inner bark.

stories.summary: An annual or short-lived perennial flowering plant of cultivated, probably hybrid origin. Its nearly circular leaves shed rain as rolling droplets, while its yellow, orange or red flowers are mildly scented. All above-ground parts are edible; the peppery flowers are used in salads and stir-fries, and unripe seed pods are pickled.
stories.edibilityNote: All above-ground parts are edible; flowers are eaten in salads or stir-fries, and unripe seed pods are pickled as a caper substitute.

stories.summary: A succulent perennial herb native across Europe, North Africa, and northern and western Asia, where it grows beside brooks and ditches. Its spreading, often reddish branches carry paired leaves and small four-petalled flowers that are bright blue or pink.
stories.edibilityNote: It may historically have been eaten as a winter salad and was used in ineffective traditional scurvy remedies.

stories.summary: Annual herb considered native to North Africa and temperate Eurasia, though its precise origin is uncertain. Its vivid red, four-petalled flowers usually have black basal spots, last only one day, and can reappear from a long-lived seed bank after soil disturbance. The black seeds are edible alone or in bread, although most culinary poppy seed comes from another species.
stories.edibilityNote: Black seeds are eaten alone or in bread; most poppy seed harvested for cooking comes from Papaver somniferum.

stories.summary: A large shrub or small tree native to western and central Europe, Midland hawthorn has a dense crown and shallowly lobed leaves. Its flowers usually have several styles, producing slightly oval fruits with several seeds.

A flowering shrub native broadly to Europe, northwestern Africa and southwestern Asia, though its exact native range is unclear. Its spreading branches bear sharp spines and bell-shaped flowers. The edible berries vary from green to red, purple, yellow or white and are used in desserts and preserves.
stories.edibilityNote: The cultivated edible berries are used in foods including desserts and preserves.

stories.summary: A perennial fruiting plant native to Europe and northern Asia, red raspberry grows new canes from a long-lived root system. First-year canes usually lack flowers, while second-year canes produce side shoots and flowers. Its edible red fruits are sweet but tart, ripen in summer or early autumn, and leave a hollow centre when picked.
stories.edibilityNote: The edible fruit is sweet but tart; wild fruits are aromatic, and the species is an important food crop.

stories.summary: A shrub native to Europe and Western Asia, common hazel has rounded nuts and produces its flowers before the leaves in early spring. The seed kernel is edible raw or roasted, or ground into a paste.
stories.edibilityNote: The seed kernel is eaten raw or roasted, or ground into paste; its bitter brown skin is sometimes removed before cooking.

stories.summary: A herbaceous biennial, rarely perennial, native in its wild forms to parts of Europe, North Africa, Macaronesia and Western Asia. Cultivated groups include sugar beet, beetroot and chard, with fleshy roots or edible leaves and midribs; roots may be red, white or yellow.
stories.edibilityNote: Cultivated forms provide table sugar, beetroot, and edible chard or spinach-beet leaves and midribs, eaten cooked in several ways.

stories.summary: Deciduous tree native to central and eastern North America, mostly in riverside habitats. Its grey-black bark is deeply furrowed into diamond-like patterns, while its round fruits contain exceptionally hard, corrugated nuts. The kernels are edible, and spring sap can be drunk or concentrated into syrup or sugar.
stories.edibilityNote: The kernels are eaten in many dishes; spring sap may be drunk or concentrated into syrup or sugar.

stories.summary: A biennial or perennial plant whose wild form is considered native only to the coasts of France, Great Britain and Spain. It forms a stout rosette of thick, fleshy grey-green leaves before producing branched clusters of four-petalled yellow flowers. Cultivars such as cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale and Brussels sprouts are important human food crops.
stories.edibilityNote: Numerous cultivars are eaten as vegetables, including their leaves, stems, buds and flower clusters.

stories.summary: A floating freshwater plant native throughout most of Africa, Asia, Europe and North America, it has one to four small leaves and a single root hanging in the water. It mainly multiplies by division and can form carpets over still pools; in temperate regions it produces dense resting organs that sink for winter.

Herbaceous perennial native to Eurasia, specifically the Balkans, Anatolia and the Caucasus. Feverfew has pungently scented, light yellowish-green leaves and conspicuous daisy-like flowers with white outer florets and yellow centres. It spreads rapidly by seed and may become invasive outside its native range.
A hairless perennial herb native to Eurasia, it grows best near water and bears very pale violet-pink flowers that are rarely white. The plant is edible and has a peppery taste resembling watercress.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is edible and has a peppery, watercress-like taste.

stories.summary: A grey-leaved perennial herb native to Europe, northern Africa, and southwestern and central Asia, white horehound has crinkled, downy leaves and clusters of white flowers high on the stem. Its extract flavors bittersweet hard candies, while the plant is also used in horehound beer, herbal tea and cocktails.
stories.edibilityNote: Its extract is used in sugar-based hard candies; the plant also flavors beer, herbal tea and cocktails.

stories.summary: A heteroblastic tree endemic to New Zealand, lancewood has a long juvenile stage with a slender, ridged trunk and rigid, downward-pointing toothed leaves. As it matures, it branches into a rounded crown and develops shorter, wider leaves.
A large perennial carnivorous sundew native to south-eastern Australia and New Zealand. It is distinctive among sundews for its narrow leaves, which fork into branching pairs.

Flowering shrub or tree native to southeastern Australia and New Zealand. Its heavily branched stems carry small, evergreen, aromatic leaves whose colour varies by cultivar. Flowers are usually white or pink, though some cultivars have red or violet blooms.
stories.edibilityNote: It is cultivated as a source for mānuka honey; no directly edible plant part is identified.

stories.summary: An evergreen shrub native to southern Peru, Bolivia and northern Argentina, Fuchsia boliviana bears large drooping clusters of scarlet flowers in late summer and autumn. Small red-purple edible fruits follow the flowers; a white-flowering form has a white tube and scarlet petals.
stories.edibilityNote: The small red-purple fruit borne after flowering is edible.

stories.summary: Aromatic evergreen tree or large shrub native to the Mediterranean region. Its smooth green leaves are used for seasoning; whole leaves are typically removed before serving, while ground leaves can be safely eaten, and dried berries and pressed leaf oil are also used as spices.
stories.edibilityNote: Whole leaves usually season food and are removed; ground leaves are eaten safely, while dried berries and pressed leaf oil are spices.

stories.summary: Fast-growing deciduous maple tree native to the eastern and central United States and southeastern Canada. Deeply lobed leaves flash their downy silver undersides in light breezes, while its unusually heavy winged fruits mature in early summer and may travel by water.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Americans used sap from wild trees to make sugar and in bread.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native to eastern and central Europe and western Asia, it has a broad, rounded crown. Its five-lobed leaves release milky sap when broken and usually turn yellow in autumn, while its paired winged fruits spread almost flat.

A spreading sumac native to North America, from southern Canada through much of the United States to northeastern Mexico. Its compound leaves turn scarlet in autumn, and upright clusters of edible crimson berries persist through winter.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Americans ate young sprouts as salad; the sour fruit was chewed or made into a lemonade-like drink.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to the eastern and central United States and the far south of eastern and central Canada. It often forms a dense, multi-stemmed crown by suckering, and its smaller-than-cultivated-filbert nuts can be eaten raw.
stories.edibilityNote: The nuts are edible raw but smaller than commonly cultivated filberts; they can also be pressed for culinary oil.

stories.summary: A small deciduous tree native to eastern North America and northern Mexico, it has four showy white, pink or red bracts surrounding clusters of tiny flowers. Its leaves turn rich red-brown in autumn.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is poisonous to humans, and the red berries are explicitly described as inedible.

stories.summary: A long-lived oak native to eastern and central North America. Some specimens have been documented at more than 450 years old. Its acorns can be eaten by humans, though bitter ones may need their tannins leached.
stories.edibilityNote: Acorns can be eaten by humans; bitter ones may need their tannins leached.

stories.summary: Medium-sized tree native to North America, especially eastern and central Canada and the United States. Its shallowly lobed leaves have pale, bluish undersides, and its acorns germinate soon after falling rather than remaining dormant.

A large deciduous oak tree native to central and eastern North America, bur oak has deeply ridged grey bark and exceptionally large acorns with broad, often fringed cups. Its acorns can be eaten raw or boiled.
stories.edibilityNote: The acorns can be eaten raw or boiled.

stories.summary: Deciduous tree primarily distributed across the central and eastern United States. Its glossy, deeply lobed leaves usually turn bright scarlet in autumn, while its acorn kernels are very bitter.

Medium-sized deciduous tree native to the eastern and central United States and extreme southern Ontario, Canada. Its mature crown has upward-pointing upper branches, horizontal middle branches and drooping lower branches. Leaves are cut by extremely deep U-shaped gaps, with pale orange-brown tufts beneath at vein junctions; juvenile trees often retain dead leaves through winter.
stories.edibilityNote: Acorns are described as very bitter and unpalatable unless traditionally processed; explicit human food use is not documented.

stories.summary: A large oak tree native to eastern and central North America. It can withstand seasonal flooding, and its bristle-tipped, lobed leaves develop relatively late brown-to-red autumn colour that varies by region.

A large deciduous tree native to eastern North America. Mature trees have shaggy bark, while young trees have smooth bark, and their nut crops are erratic. The hard-shelled nuts are edible and were historically an important Indigenous food.
stories.edibilityNote: The nuts were an important Indigenous staple and remain edible; the bark is also used to flavor maple-style syrup.

stories.summary: A flowering plant of unstated native origin, it is introduced in mainland Portugal. It bears many thorns, so protected contact is advised, and its wood is used for flooring, cargo-vehicle bodies and solid furniture.

A deciduous tree native to eastern and central North America, red mulberry has rough, sandpaper-like upper leaf surfaces and soft-haired undersides. Its blackberry-like fruit ripens from pale green to red or dark purple. The sweet berries are eaten raw, used in pastries or preserves, and fermented into wine; Powhatan people also ate them, sometimes boiled.
stories.edibilityNote: Sweet berries are eaten raw, cooked in pastries or preserves, and fermented into wine; Powhatan people historically ate them, sometimes boiled.

stories.summary: Medium-sized deciduous tree native to eastern North America and Mexico. Older bark resembles alligator hide, while the glossy foliage turns purple and then vivid scarlet in autumn. It can live for more than 650 years.

A fast-growing ash tree native to eastern and central North America, white ash usually has compound leaves with seven leaflets and pale undersides. Its C-shaped leaf scars help distinguish it from green ash, while its foliage often turns bright orange or red in autumn. Invasive emerald ash borers are devastating its North American population.

A deciduous tree native to eastern and central North America, with leaves usually divided into seven to nine leaflets. Its foliage turns golden yellow in autumn, and it commonly grows beside streams and on low-lying ground.

A small tree native to eastern North America from Ontario south to Texas and Florida, it develops a spreading, flattened crown as it matures. Its glossy green leaves turn gold to red in autumn, while its red fruit is edible and can be made into jelly or crushed for tea.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is edible and may be made into jelly or crushed to prepare tea.

stories.summary: A thorny bush or small tree native to most of the eastern United States and eastern Canada. Its pale grey bark stands out in winter, while its mature fruit varies from deep burgundy or scarlet to yellow, sometimes with a red cheek.
A North American crabapple that grows as a bushy shrub or small tree with twisted branches. Its fragrant fruits can remain hanging in clusters long after its leaves have fallen.

Deciduous shrub or small tree native to eastern North America. Its white flowers fade to pale pink and appear before the leaves in mid- to late spring; orange-red plums mature in late summer or early autumn. The juicy, sour fruit is eaten raw only when fully ripe or cooked, and Indigenous peoples historically dried it as a winter staple.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten raw when fully ripe or cooked in pies, preserves and jellies; Indigenous peoples historically stored it dried for winter.

stories.summary: A North American shrub or small tree occurring widely across Canada and parts of the United States, it commonly forms thickets. Its long-lived soil seed banks help it appear rapidly after disturbance, and it produces small red fruits with hard pits.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is edible and is used in canning, jams, jellies and preserves.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree or shrub from the New World, black cherry has white flower clusters followed by reddish-black fruit and yellow-to-red autumn leaves. Its smooth, banded young bark becomes deeply broken and nearly black with age.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit flesh is safe to eat; capuli fruit was eaten raw and made into jelly and drinks in pre-Columbian Mexico.

stories.summary: Shrub or small tree native to North America. It bears white flower clusters followed by red-to-black fruits. Only fully ripe fruit is edible and was part of Native American cuisine; unripe fruit is toxic and the stone is poisonous.
stories.edibilityNote: Fully ripe fruit is edible and traditionally part of Native American cuisine; unripe fruit is toxic and the stone poisonous. Also made into preserves and wine.

stories.summary: A fast-growing tree native to northern North America and far eastern Russia. Its sticky, resinous buds release a strong, sweet fragrance resembling balsam fir.

A deciduous willow tree native to Europe and western and Central Asia, white willow has an irregular, often leaning crown. Its leaves are notably pale, with fine, silky white hairs especially on their undersides.

Deciduous tree native to much of North America, black willow is the continent’s largest willow species. Older trees have deeply fissured, nearly black bark, while their slender shoots snap cleanly at the branch junction when sharply bent.

A shrub or small tree native to southern Europe, North Africa and parts of western Asia, purple willow has unusually opposite, narrow leaves. Its flexible, sometimes purple-tinged stems are widely used for basket making, and its upright catkins appear before the leaves in spring.
stories.edibilityNote: Eating the leaves can cause severe abdominal pain; consumption may also cause gastrointestinal bleeding and kidney damage.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native to eastern North America. Its leaves are often heart-shaped and noticeably unequal at the base, while its small, fragrant flowers hang in clusters. The foliage and flowers are edible, especially the more palatable tender young leaves.
stories.edibilityNote: The foliage and flowers are edible; tender young leaves are considered more palatable.

stories.summary: A large deciduous tree native to North America. Its cork-like bark has wart-like projections, its coarse leaves are distinctly asymmetrical, and its small fruits ripen from orange-red to dark purple and may remain for months.
stories.edibilityNote: Berries are edible without cooking; Omaha ate them casually, while Dakota and Pawnee pounded them for use with meat, fat, or parched corn.

stories.summary: An evergreen tree native to the Indian subcontinent. It begins growing on another tree and may eventually envelop it, while its descending aerial roots take hold in the ground and become supporting woody trunks, creating an exceptionally broad canopy.

A ground-growing orchid native to Central America and northern South America, the fire-star orchid produces long fleshy roots along most of its stem. Its showy red-orange flowers can appear throughout the year and have a tiny cross-shaped central lip.

An annual pulse native to the northeastern Mediterranean, white lupin occurs naturally from the Balkans to Sicily and Turkey. It has winter and spring forms. Its seeds are eaten as snacks, commonly after soaking or brining, and in parts of Greece after brief seawater soaking before being consumed raw.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten as snacks, usually soaked or brined; in parts of Greece they are briefly seawater-soaked and eaten raw.

stories.summary: A tropical banyan tree native from India through southern China, Japan and Southeast Asia to the western Pacific and Queensland. Numerous aerial roots descend from its branches and can develop into additional trunks, while its strong roots may lift paving in introduced urban settings.

A clump-forming succulent flowering plant native to desert regions from northeastern South Africa north to Malawi and Zambia. It has erect, four-angled green stems and large, star-shaped red-and-yellow flowers with wrinkled, silky, hairy surfaces and the smell of rotting flesh.

Small mustard-family annual, rarely biennial, native to Eurasia and Africa. It forms a basal leaf rosette, completes its life cycle in about six weeks and naturally self-pollinates. Its small genome and rapid growth make it a major model plant in biology and genetics.
stories.edibilityNote: Eaten in salads or cooked, though its use as a spring vegetable is uncommon.

stories.summary: A low-growing plant with no stated native origin, it is found across parts of Europe, western Asia and northwestern Africa. It has stiffly hairy leaves in a rosette and small heads of violet-blue flowers that bloom from May to September.

A fruiting vine native to China, it is the source of most commercial kiwifruit varieties. Depending on variety and breeding, its smooth, bronze-skinned fruit can have green, yellow or red-centred flesh and is described as sweet and aromatic.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten as kiwifruit; less-hairy yellow forms are described as suitable for eating without peeling.

stories.summary: An evergreen vine native to southern and western South America. Its heart-shaped, greenish-yellow flowers have intricate purplish-brown markings and a carrion-like smell that attracts fly pollinators; its winged seeds are dispersed by wind.

A slow-growing, long-lived evergreen conifer endemic to California’s coastal ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills. It has stiff, sharp needles and large nut-like seeds enclosed in fleshy coverings that turn dark green to purple in late autumn. In deep shade it may lean or develop several stems, and it can resprout slowly after fire or other disturbance.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds were reportedly highly valued as food by Indigenous Californians, but are inedible raw.

stories.summary: Small conifer native to the Pacific Northwest of North America, often becoming shrubby in less moist settings. It grows extremely slowly, commonly develops a hollow trunk, and bears bright red, berry-like cups around poisonous seeds; the juicy cup itself seems edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The juicy red cup around the seed seems edible, but the seed, leaves and bark are extremely poisonous and should not be consumed.

stories.summary: Evergreen shrub endemic to the Cape Provinces of South Africa. Its dense branches bear aromatic, needle-like leaves and pink, sometimes white, star-shaped flowers that may cover the shrub from May to October.

An erect, compact shrub native to South Africa, it branches densely from the base. Pink-tinged buds open into abundant small white flowers, and its aromatic leaves are traditionally used to remove odours and repel insects.

Shrub or tree endemic to the Temora-Cootamundra district of New South Wales. It has smooth bark, grey-green divided leaves and spherical heads of bright yellow flowers, followed by straight leathery pods.

Salt-tolerant flowering perennial endemic to Europe, growing wild along mainland European and British coasts. It forms spreading mounds with large fleshy leaves and abundant white flowers. Its blanched stems have been eaten as a vegetable in Britain since around the turn of the 18th century.
stories.edibilityNote: Blanched stems are eaten as a vegetable; wild emerging shoots were historically harvested in southern England during early spring.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to temperate South America, including southern Brazil and parts of Argentina and Uruguay. Its flowers are the only white ones in the petunia genus, and it is one parent of the commonly grown garden petunia.

A branching annual native to temperate North Africa, Europe and parts of western Asia, it has bristly stems and a slender taproot that does not swell like cultivated radish. Its flowers are usually white but may be yellow or purple. All tender parts are edible; the pods and washed outer root skin can also be eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Tender parts, including spicy leaves and flowers, are edible; seedpods and the washed outer skin of the root can also be eaten.

stories.summary: An annual plant native to the western Mediterranean from Portugal to Italy. It has hairy stems and bright yellow flowers arranged in spaced groups. Its yellow seeds, called lupin beans, were once a common Mediterranean food and are now mainly eaten pickled as snacks.
stories.edibilityNote: Yellow seeds, or lupin beans, were formerly common Mediterranean food and are now mainly eaten pickled as snacks.

stories.summary: A forage legume whose single-cut agricultural type originated in Europe and double-cut type in the Middle East. Its tannin-rich leaves are associated with reduced gut nematode reproduction in sheep and goats.

A low-growing annual native to most of Europe, Asia and North Africa, henbit dead-nettle has rounded leaves, with its stalkless upper leaves clasping the stems. Its pink-to-purple flowers appear very early, sometimes through winter in warmer regions. Young leaves and shoots, stems and flowers can be eaten raw or cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves and shoots, stems and flowers can be eaten raw or cooked.

stories.summary: Perennial herb native to the Pacific coast of the United States and Canada, where it grows close to the ocean. Its yellowish-green, divided leaves and tiny yellow flowers form low mats resembling yellow footsteps. It is vulnerable in Canada and critically imperilled in Washington.

A bulbous flowering plant native to southwestern Europe, northwestern Africa, Madeira and the Canary Islands, three-cornered garlic has triangular flower stalks and narrow leaves that smell strongly of onion when crushed. Every part, from bulb to flower, is edible fresh or cooked and can be used like spring onions or wild onions.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts, from bulbs to flowers, are eaten fresh or cooked and used similarly to spring onions or wild onions.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to western, central and northern Europe, it forms ground-hugging rosettes and readily colonises lawns despite mowing. Its white, often red-tipped flower heads close at night, open in the morning and follow the sun.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten raw or cooked; older leaves become more astringent. Flower buds and petals are eaten raw, and the plant is used as tea.

stories.summary: A perennial flowering plant native to Southern Africa, narrow-leaved ragwort has narrow, stalkless leaves and branched stems topped with yellow flower heads. It contains alkaloids that are poisonous to mammals.

A perennial vine native to Europe and Asia, and also reported native to northern Africa. It scrambles over other plants and bears purple star-shaped flowers followed by attractive red berries that are poisonous to humans.
stories.edibilityNote: The berries are poisonous to humans, and the entire plant is considered poisonous.

stories.summary: Annual plant of unspecified native origin, widespread around the Mediterranean, including North Africa, and in the Middle East.
A flowering plant native to Europe, Madeira and northwestern Africa, bird's foot clover can grow in salty conditions. It has been introduced to Australia and New Zealand.
Annual flowering plant native to the Caucasus and northern Iran. Its weak stems form dense groundcover, with tips often turning upright, while sky-blue flowers have dark stripes and white centres.

A perennial, ground-hugging flowering herb native throughout Europe, most of western and central Asia, and northwest Africa. It forms hairless green mats resembling moss, roots readily where stems touch the ground, and bears tiny white flowers whose petals may be absent.

A biennial or perennial flowering plant native to the Mediterranean region and western Europe, pale flax favours dry, sunny grasslands on calcareous or neutral soils. Its pale-blue flowers are streaked with darker colour, and fibre can be made from its long, narrow stems.
Creeping liverwort native to the Mediterranean region. It can form dense green mats and is easily recognized by crescent-shaped cups holding reproductive buds, which rain can dislodge.

Herbaceous perennial native to dry meadows and open woodland across Europe, with its native range extending to western Siberia and the Caucasus. Its flower heads form an open, star-like display rather than a brush-like tuft, with mostly violet-purple flowers and occasional white ones from June to October.

Creeping evergreen perennial native to Mediterranean Europe and North Africa, extending through the Middle East to Iran. It has shiny scalloped leaves and tubular late-summer flowers. Dietary supplements made from germander are highly toxic to the liver and have caused acute hepatitis, including at least one reported fatality by 1992.
stories.edibilityNote: Germander dietary supplements are highly liver-toxic and have caused acute hepatitis; at least one fatal liver failure was reported by 1992.

stories.summary: A shrub endemic to Tenerife’s Cañadas del Teide depression and nearby upper pine-forest scrub. Its grey stems and pale green-grey leaves are hairy, while pale pink flower heads become balls of whitish seeds as summer progresses.

A flowering plant native to Europe, temperate Asia and northern Africa, it bears white flowers and is common in meadows, open woods and fields. Around the Mediterranean, young shoots and tender leaves are eaten; young leaves may be raw before flowering, while older leaves are usually cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: Young shoots and tender leaves are eaten around the Mediterranean; young leaves may be raw before flowering, while older leaves are cooked.

stories.summary: A perennial flowering herb native to Europe, common comfrey grows in damp grassland and beside rivers and ditches. Its stems are bristly, while its tubular flowers are usually cream-yellow or pink-purple. Despite mild toxicity and potential liver harm, its leaves and shoots have been considered edible, even raw; stalks are said to be best gathered before flowering and blanched before steaming.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and shoots have been considered edible, even raw; stalks were reportedly gathered before flowering and blanched before steaming, despite toxicity and potential liver harm.

stories.summary: A low, trailing plant native to rocky habitats in southern Europe, ivy-leaved toadflax has small purple, snapdragon-like flowers. Its flower stalk seeks light until fertilisation, then turns away and pushes the developing seed capsule into dark crevices.
stories.edibilityNote: Sometimes eaten as a salad green in Southern Europe, although it has also been described as slightly toxic.

stories.summary: Annual or perennial herb native to Europe, Asia and North Africa. Its slender glandular stems carry slightly fleshy, threadlike leaves, sometimes with hard or spiny tips, and small pink flowers.

A biennial herb found through most of Europe and into the Maghreb and western Asia. Hairy, purple-spotted stems and swollen nodes help distinguish it; eating the poisonous plant can cause digestive inflammation, drowsiness, vertigo and cardiac weakness.
stories.edibilityNote: Eating the plant can cause digestive inflammation, drowsiness, vertigo and cardiac weakness; toxins occur mainly in its upper parts and fruits.

stories.summary: Perennial flowering plant native to Europe, northern and western Asia, and North Africa. It forms low, evergreen mats with fleshy leaves and bright yellow, star-shaped flowers, while its acrid leaf fluid can cause skin rashes.
stories.edibilityNote: Considered poisonous when consumed despite its reported peppery taste; consumption is discouraged.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to western, central and southern Europe, northwestern Africa, southwestern Western Asia and Siberia, salad burnet has fern-like toothed leaves and crimson spherical flower clusters. Its young leaves, which taste mildly of cucumber, are used in salads, sauces, drinks and flavourings; older leaves become bitter.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves are used in salads, dressings, sauces, drinks and flavourings; older leaves tend to become bitter.

stories.summary: An annual or short-lived perennial wildflower from Europe, wild pansy bears flowers that may be purple, blue, yellow or white. The plant, especially its flowers, is edible and described as low in toxicity.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant, especially its flowers, is edible and described as having low toxicity.

stories.summary: A low-growing herbaceous perennial native to Eurasia, white clover forms spreading mats as its creeping stems root at the nodes. Its leaves almost always have three leaflets, while the whitish flower heads may become tinged pink or cream as they age.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are survival food; raw plants are hard to digest, but boiling helps. Avoid flowers long after picking because cyanides may form.

stories.summary: Annual flowering plant native to Africa, Asia and Europe. It is hairy, with paired, coarsely toothed leaves and tiny pale blue to blue-violet flowers. Its fruit capsules are heart-shaped, and it flowers from April to October.

A perennial flowering plant native mostly to Eurasia and North America, although the typical variety has spread beyond its native range. Creeping stems root at the leaf joints to form low mats, while upright branches bear small white flowers marked with dark purple.
A herbaceous plant native across temperate Europe, Asia Minor and the Caucasus, common cornsalad is eaten raw, usually in salads or as an accompaniment, and is widely used in central European salads.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is eaten raw, generally in salads or as an accompaniment, and is widely used in central European salads.

stories.summary: Perennial flowering herb native to Europe and western Asia. Its lobed, blue-green leaves release yellow-orange latex when injured, and it bears four-petalled yellow flowers. The whole plant is toxic in moderate doses, and ingestion may damage the liver.
stories.edibilityNote: The whole plant is toxic in moderate doses; ingestion may cause liver toxicity.

stories.summary: Biennial or perennial flowering herb native to northern and central Europe, red campion has hairy, slightly sticky stems and leaves. Its deeply notched dark pink to red flowers appear from May to October, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Young leaves and flowers are edible, though cooking or blanching is recommended to remove their bitter aftertaste.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves and flowers are edible; cooking or blanching is recommended to remove the bitter aftertaste.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa, field pansy is introduced elsewhere as a weed of disturbed and cultivated ground. It has toothed leaves and usually white flowers, although the lower petal differs and the upper petals may be tinged purple.
A low, spreading shrub native to western and central Europe. It has fine leaves in groups of three and dry-textured, bell-shaped purple flowers, rarely white, appearing from mid- to late summer.
stories.edibilityNote: Bell heather is used as a source of heather honey.

stories.summary: A flowering perennial rush native to temperate Europe, extending to North Africa, the Caucasus and Scandinavia, it has brush-like flower clusters. It spreads through short runners and seed and commonly grows in native grasslands, lawns and fields.

A bulb-forming perennial native from Portugal and Morocco east to western China, wild tulip occurs across much of the Mediterranean, Black Sea region and Central Asia. It has narrow blue-grey leaves and scented yellow spring flowers, sometimes tinged red outside.

A deciduous tree native to Western Asia and central, eastern and southern Europe, including southern England. It often has a fluted, crooked trunk with smooth greenish-grey bark, and its strongly veined leaves have a distinctive corrugated texture.

Bulbous perennial native to most of Europe, Turkey, Iran and the Caucasus. Its late-spring flowers hang in clusters and have six white segments, each marked greenish near the tip. All Leucojum species are poisonous.
stories.edibilityNote: All species of Leucojum are poisonous.

stories.summary: A flowering shrub or small tree native to Europe and western Asia, and locally to northwest Africa, blackthorn has dark bark and dense, stiff, spiny branches. Its creamy-white flowers appear shortly before the leaves in early spring, followed by purple-black sloes that ripen in late autumn. The tart, astringent fruit is used in preserves and liqueurs and is more suitable fresh after autumn frost.
stories.edibilityNote: Sloes are used in preserves, pies and liqueurs; fresh fruit is tart and astringent unless picked after autumn frost.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial native across most of temperate Europe and western Asia, the cowslip is absent from some northern areas but reappears in northernmost Scotland and Scandinavia. It produces clusters of deep-yellow flowers in spring and frequently hybridizes with other primroses.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves were traditionally eaten as salad greens in Spain; historical English uses include flower-flavoured wine, sugared flowers, salads and boiled greens.

stories.summary: A perennial herb naturally distributed across Europe, non-tropical Asia, North Africa and Australia, it has a red-tinged stem base and fleshy, sour edible leaves. It is eaten cooked or in salads, but its oxalic acid content means moderation is advised, especially for people with kidney problems, rheumatism or gout.
stories.edibilityNote: The sour leaves are eaten cooked or in salads; moderation is advised, especially for people with kidney problems, rheumatism or gout.

stories.summary: Multistemmed willow shrub reported native to Europe, western Asia and the Himalayas, although its exact native range is uncertain; it is certainly native from central Europe east to western Asia. Its long, straight, flexible twigs are traditionally used for basketry, while its narrow leaves have silky grey-haired undersides.

A small spring-flowering annual native to Europe, western Asia and parts of North Africa south to Ethiopia. Its leafless flowering stems carry four deeply split white petals that can look like eight, making it easy to recognize.
Short-lived herbaceous perennial native to Europe, with hairy leaves and abundant spring flowers. Its buds begin pink, then open into flat, intensely sky-blue flowers with yellow centres.

An evergreen perennial native to mountainous Central and Southern Europe and Asia Minor. It has glossy leaves and drooping yellow-green spring flowers, often edged with purple; its foliage smells pungent when crushed. All parts are poisonous and can cause violent vomiting and delirium.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; eating the plant can cause violent vomiting and delirium.

stories.summary: Spreading herbaceous perennial native throughout Europe and temperate Asia. Its variable, sometimes spotted leaves accompany pink or purple flowers with helmet-shaped upper lips and whitish lower lips marked with purple dots.

An annual or biennial herb native to Europe, much of Asia, and parts of Africa, hairy bittercress commonly grows in damp, disturbed ground. Its ripe upright pods burst when touched, flinging seeds away. The leaves, flowers and seedpods are eaten raw or cooked and taste mildly peppery; the seeds can replace mustard.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, flowers and seedpods are eaten raw or cooked; leaves are used in salads, and seeds can substitute for mustard.

stories.summary: An aromatic, perennial evergreen creeper in the mint family, ground-ivy has no native origin specified in the supplied account and was spread worldwide by European settlers. Its square stems root where they touch the ground, forming dense mats, and release a distinctive smell when damaged.
stories.edibilityNote: It has long been eaten as salad greens; pre-bloom leaves can be cooked as a vegetable or made into tea.

stories.summary: A plum species growing as a large shrub or small tree, native to Southeast Europe and Western Asia. It is among the first European trees to flower in spring, often blooming before its leaves open. Its edible yellow or red fruits may be sweet enough to eat fresh or sour and better suited to jam.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits are edible; sweet varieties are eaten fresh, while sour ones are used for jam and in Georgian cuisine.

stories.summary: A biennial or perennial flowering plant native to temperate Europe, it has fleshy, heart- or kidney-shaped leaves forming a basal rosette. Historically, it was consumed in drinks and sandwiches for scurvy, and its leaves were brewed into ale.
stories.edibilityNote: Historically consumed in drinks and sandwiches for scurvy; its leaves were also brewed into scurvygrass ale.

stories.summary: An evergreen perennial native to parts of the Alps, Apennines and northern Dinaric Alps. It produces large, usually white flowers from midwinter to early spring, but all parts are considered toxic when consumed or contacted through damaged-tissue sap.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are considered toxic when consumed; damaged plant tissue also releases irritating sap.

stories.summary: A trailing evergreen subshrub native to central and southern Europe and southwestern Asia, lesser periwinkle roots along its stems to form broad colonies. It has glossy, leathery dark-green leaves and mainly spring-to-midsummer violet-purple flowers, although cultivated selections may be pale purple or white.

A small, hardy perennial flowering plant native to Eurasia, sweet violet spreads by above-ground shoots and forms a rosette of kidney-shaped leaves. Its scented flowers are usually dark violet or white. Both its leaves and flowers are edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves and flowers are edible.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub or small tree native to Europe and western and central Asia, goat willow has unusually broad leaves with grey, woolly undersides. Its silky silver catkins appear before new leaves in early spring; male catkins turn yellow and female ones pale green on separate plants.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to much of Europe, spindle has autumn leaves ranging from yellow-green to reddish-purple. In autumn, its red, purple or pink fruit splits open to reveal orange seeds; the fruit is poisonous if eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is poisonous; ingestion can cause liver and kidney damage or death, particularly in young children attracted by its bright colour.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Euonymus europaeus
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A perennial flowering plant native to western Europe, from Spain and Portugal east to Germany and north to England and Wales. It grows from a bulb and bears pale yellow flowers with a darker central trumpet. Its bulbs and leaves contain the poison lycorine and should never be eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Bulbs and leaves contain lycorine and should never be eaten.

stories.summary: Annual flowering herb native to Eurasia. Its square stems carry leaves that shade from green below to purple above, and unlike true nettles it cannot sting. Young tops and leaves are eaten in salads, stir-fries or sauces, while flowers can be crystallized with sugar and egg white.
stories.edibilityNote: Young tops and leaves are used in salads, stir-fries or sauces; flowers can be crystallized with sugar and egg white.

stories.summary: Flowering perennial native to the Caucasus. It has large, heart-shaped leaves, usually marked white or cream, and sprays of small blue flowers from mid-spring.

An annual herb probably native to Central America, jimsonweed has night-opening trumpet-shaped flowers and egg-shaped seed capsules that may be spiny. It is poisonous: all parts contain dangerous tropane alkaloids, and ingestion can cause delirium, hallucinations and potentially fatal poisoning.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts contain dangerous tropane alkaloids; ingestion can cause severe poisoning and carries a high risk of fatal overdose.

stories.summary: A tuberous perennial herb native around the Black Sea and in a separate Mediterranean population from Turkey’s Hatay Province through Lebanon to northern Israel. Its rounded or heart-shaped leaves vary from green to silver-patterned, and its squat pink, magenta or white flowers bloom from winter into spring.

A perennial flowering plant native to Bulgaria, Hungary, Albania and the former Yugoslavia. Among the first crocuses to bloom, it bears slender flowers ranging from pale silvery lilac to reddish purple, although one variant is white.

A perennial flowering herb native across Europe and Asia, white deadnettle generally grows in moist, fertile ground. Its softly hairy, nettle-like leaves do not sting, and it bears white flowers around the upper stem.
stories.edibilityNote: Young shoots and leaves can be cooked as a vegetable.

stories.summary: An evergreen climbing shrub native and endemic to Madeira, Madeiran ivy commonly grows on rocky slopes, soil and tree trunks, especially in laurel forest. Its aerial roots cling to trees, cliffs and walls, while its stems may be tinged red or purple and its round fruits turn black when ripe.

A clinging evergreen vine native to most of Europe and parts of western Asia, it climbs with strongly gripping aerial rootlets or spreads as groundcover. Creeping stems carry lobed leaves, while flowering stems have unlobed heart-shaped leaves; its berries are somewhat poisonous to humans.
stories.edibilityNote: The berries are somewhat poisonous to humans.

stories.summary: A variable climbing wild rose native to Europe, northwest Africa and western Asia, it has arching stems armed with hooked prickles. Its sweet-scented summer flowers range from white to deep pink and mature into red-orange hips in autumn.
stories.edibilityNote: Ripe autumn hips are eaten after avoiding their internal hairs or made into drinks and preserves; flowers and petals are also eaten.

stories.summary: A vigorous deciduous twining climber native to much of Europe, North Africa, Turkey and the Caucasus, it bears showy clusters of creamy white or yellowish tubular flowers. The flowers may be flushed pink or red and are far more strongly scented at night than during the day.

Annual honesty is an annual or biennial flowering plant native to southern Europe, from Spain to Romania. Its white, pink or violet flowers are followed by translucent, disc-shaped fruits whose silvery central membranes may persist through winter and are often used in dried arrangements.

A perennial herb native to temperate Eurasia, wood avens grows along shady woodland edges and hedgerows. Its fresh root smells like cloves, while its hairy fruits bear hooked burrs that catch on animal fur.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves can be cooked like spinach; roots are used to spice soups and flavour ale.

stories.summary: A deciduous perennial herb native to Europe and southwestern Asia. It has apricot-scented flower spikes, while its soft hairs and hooked fruits readily cling to animals and clothing.
A flowering plant native to most temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere, it has yellow flowers and pointed leaves with toothed, sometimes nearly hooked margins.

A spiny shrub native to Europe, it is especially common across much of the British Isles. Its broad, toothed leaflets grow in groups of three or five, and pink or magenta flowers produce nearly black fruit.
Annual poppy native to Europe, North Africa and southwestern Asia. It has showy pale-red flowers, elongated hairless seed capsules and white to yellowish latex released from damaged tissue.

A small, usually biennial herb considered native in North America, it also occurs widely across Europe and North Africa. Bruised or uprooted plants have a strong unpleasant smell, while ripe fruits are explosively ejected from the plant.

Perennial plant with no native origin specified, common across much of Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Turkmenistan. It flowers in summer and bears toxic fruit that has been used in traditional medicine.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is toxic.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to Europe, northern Africa and central Asia. Its early-summer flower clusters have a ring of large, sterile white flowers around smaller fertile ones, followed by bright red, single-seeded fruits.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit is edible only in small quantities and can be made into jelly; large amounts are mildly toxic and may cause vomiting or diarrhoea.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Viburnum opulus
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A robust herbaceous perennial native to Europe and Asia, including China, Japan, Kazakhstan, the Koreas, Mongolia, Siberia, Russia and Turkmenistan. It has aromatic, dark-green, deeply toothed leaves and small golden-yellow flowers in dense, flat-topped clusters in summer.
stories.edibilityNote: Used to add aroma and bitterness to vermouth and in sweet and savoury dishes.

stories.summary: A tall deciduous shrub native to Europe, northernmost Africa and western Asia. Unlike other buckthorns, it has no thorns; cut bark reveals a bright lemon-yellow inner layer, and its berries ripen from green through red to black.

A robust perennial herb native to Europe, northwestern Africa, parts of western and central Asia, and the Caucasus. It has reddish hairy stems, deeply lobed leaves and fluffy mauve flower heads that attract many insects.

A herbaceous perennial native to Europe and southwestern Asia, musk mallow has hairy stems and leaves that become deeply divided higher on the plant. Its five-petalled pink flowers bloom in summer and have a distinctive musky scent.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers can be added to salads, and seeds are described as edible, although the passage flags a citation as needed.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to Europe and northwestern Asia. It has square, hairy stems with swollen joints and small, snapdragon-like flowers patterned in purple, pink or white; it readily occupies disturbed ground and roadsides.

An annual or perennial flowering herb native to Europe and southwestern Asia. It has erect hairy stems with milky sap, toothed leaves, and loose clusters of pale yellow flowers. Its young leaves are edible in salads or cooked like spinach, though their fine hairs may make them preferable mixed with other vegetables.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves can be eaten in salads or cooked like spinach; their fine hairs may make mixing with other vegetables preferable.

stories.summary: A biennial flowering herb, rarely a short-lived perennial, native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its prickly stems and leaves carry lavender flower heads that open in bands and dry into persistent cones of hard, spine-tipped bracts.

Rhizomatous flowering perennial native to southern Africa. It has broad, arrow-shaped leaves and a large white sheath surrounding a fragrant yellow flower spike. Eating the raw plant may severely burn and swell the mouth and throat and cause stomach pain and diarrhoea.
stories.edibilityNote: The raw plant contains calcium oxalate and may cause severe mouth and throat irritation, stomach pain and diarrhoea.

stories.summary: Shrub or tree native to southeastern Europe and Turkey. Its branching twigs carry tiny linear leaves and dense flower spikes, with each small flower bearing four pink petals. Introduced populations are invasive in parts of western North America and elsewhere.
A flowering tree or shrub native to China and Korea. It tolerates moist, salty soils and has tiny scale-like leaves and dense clusters of fragrant flowers, usually pink but ranging from white to red.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to Europe and Asia, it has arching reddish stems and pale-green, feathery foliage. Upright plumes of small pink flowers cover new growth from late summer to early autumn.

A shrub or small tree endemic to the Canary Islands, it is believed to occur on every island except El Hierro. It is common at lower elevations, including shores and estuaries, and tolerates some salinity.

An evergreen flowering tree native across parts of Africa, the Middle East, and western and southern Asia, athel tamarisk grows along watercourses in arid areas. Its tiny leaves exude salt that forms a crystalline crust, while nectar from its blossoms produces distinctively flavoured honey.
stories.edibilityNote: Nectar from the blossoms produces high-quality honey described as having a unique taste.

stories.summary: A self-supporting tree with no stated native origin, it has simple leaves and can grow to about 6.3 metres.
Herbaceous perennial native to Southern Europe. Its scalloped leaves hold beads of water in wet weather, while dense clusters of chartreuse-yellow flowers rise above the foliage.

Annual or perennial herb native to southern Africa, including Lesotho and several South African provinces. It forms spreading rosettes and runners, with deeply divided leaves densely covered in white woolly hairs underneath. Its daisy-like flowers have yellow centers and white or yellow outer petals, but the plant can become invasive where introduced.

Edible succulent plant probably native to southern Africa. Its long ground-hugging stems root at their joints to form carpets, with fleshy pointed leaves and deep-magenta flowers. Leaves may be eaten raw, cooked or pickled; fruit should be fully ripe and may be laxative in large quantities.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw, cooked or pickled; fully ripe fruit is edible but has little flesh and may be laxative in quantity.

stories.summary: Bulb-growing perennial ornamental native to the Mediterranean region from Portugal to Turkey. It bears clusters of as many as eight white flowers with yellow centres and contains a fragrant compound that humans can scarcely detect but honeybees readily sense.

A corm-growing perennial herb endemic to South Africa's Cape Province, it grows in winter, flowers in spring and rests during summer. Its tall spikes carry neat rows of bright orange-red or scarlet flowers with yellow to orange lower parts.
A perennial maidenhair fern native to California and Baja California. Its trailing leaves have many rounded, lobed green segments, with spore-bearing patches underneath.

A deciduous broadleaf tree native to western North America, red alder is among the world’s largest alders. Its leaf edges curl under, unlike those of other alders, and the leaves darken and wither rather than turning yellow before falling.

A flowering plant native to South Africa's Cape Province, the red hot poker has lily-like leaves and tall flowerheads of red, orange and yellow. Its many varieties bloom at different times during the growing season.

A perennial herb native to Europe and temperate Asia, oxeye daisy spreads through seeds and shallow creeping underground stems. Its flower heads have white rays around yellow centres, and its unopened buds can be marinated like capers.
stories.edibilityNote: Unopened flower buds can be marinated and used like capers.

stories.summary: A biennial flowering plant native to Europe, western and central Asia, and north-western Africa, garlic mustard forms low leaf clusters in its first year and flowers the following spring. Its crushed leaves smell of garlic, while its small white flowers are cross-shaped and grow in dense clusters.
stories.edibilityNote: Chopped leaves, especially young ones, flavour salads and sauces; flowers and fruit are sometimes included. Young first-year plants contain cyanide, whose gas is eliminated by chopping.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree or shrub considered under a recent definition to be native to most of Europe, parts of Asia and northern Africa. It has paired leaflets and clusters of creamy-white flowers followed by red fruit; the bitter raw fruit is commonly debittered by freezing, cooking or drying before being made into preserves, drinks and other foods.
stories.edibilityNote: Bitter raw fruit is usually frozen, cooked or dried, then made into preserves, juice, alcoholic drinks, tea, flour or savoury accompaniments.

stories.summary: Herbaceous perennial native to Eurasia, meadow buttercup has glossy yellow flowers on ungrooved stems and finely cut, hairy leaflets. Its flower buds begin developing in late summer before the flowering year, and it overwinters as a rosette. The Cherokee cook its leaves and eat them as greens.
stories.edibilityNote: The Cherokee cook the leaves and eat them as greens.

stories.summary: A flowering perennial native to much of Europe and parts of Asia, sweet woodruff has foliage whose sweet scent strengthens as it wilts and persists when dried. It was, and to some extent remains, used to flavour drinks, preserves, ice cream, tea and other foods.
stories.edibilityNote: Historically and partly still used to flavour alcoholic and soft drinks, jelly, jam, ice cream, herbal tea and other sweets.

stories.summary: Perennial herb native to much of Europe, western and central Asia, and parts of Africa and China. Its yellow flowers bear black glands, while translucent leaf glands make the leaves look perforated; each plant can produce thousands of seeds.

A deciduous hardwood tree native to the eastern United States, though its exact native range is uncertain, black locust has deeply furrowed bark and paired prickles that vary greatly between trees. It spreads through root suckers, sometimes forming dense colonies.
stories.edibilityNote: In parts of Europe and Japan, flowers are fried or made into jam; reports call shelled seeds and young pods edible, though bark and leaves are toxic.

stories.summary: A fast-growing mulberry tree native to China and India, white mulberry is widely cultivated for leaves that feed silkworms. Its pollen is released at about half the speed of sound, while its fruit ranges from white or pink in cultivated plants to deep purple in the wild.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten fresh or dried and made into syrups, wines, spirits, paste or tea; leaves are prepared as tea in Korea.

stories.summary: Sprawling perennial herb native to Europe. Surface runners form dense mats of purple-tinged leaves, while spring stalks carry many blue or purple flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw, in salads or as tea; only small amounts are advised, and older leaves become more bitter.

stories.summary: A moss widespread across temperate regions worldwide, grey-cushioned Grimmia forms small grey-green to orange-yellow cushions, sometimes with silvery leaf tips. Its capsules bend back into the leaves when dry and stand out when moist, and it grows on rocks, concrete and tree trunks.

A small annual or biennial flowering plant native to Eurasia, shepherd’s-purse has heart-shaped seed pods and mucilaginous seeds that trap nematodes. The plant can be eaten raw, with young leaves preferred, and it is cultivated as a leaf vegetable in Asia.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is eaten raw or cooked; young leaves are preferred, and it is cultivated as a leaf vegetable in Asia.

stories.summary: A biennial herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. It forms shiny dark-green basal rosettes and dense clusters of bright yellow spring flowers, usually with a peppery taste. Young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, buds and flowers are edible, and flower shoots are eaten after cooking.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten raw or cooked; buds and flowers are edible, while flower shoots require cooking.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa, it has trailing or climbing, hairy stems. Its shallowly lobed leaves resemble ivy, and solitary pale lilac or blue flowers grow from the leaf axils.
A bulbous perennial native to western Atlantic Europe, the bluebell bears sweet-scented violet-blue flowers in nodding, one-sided clusters in spring. It can carpet the floor of ancient woodlands.
stories.edibilityNote: Bluebells, particularly their bulbs, are normally considered toxic.

stories.summary: A large deciduous tree native to Europe and western Asia. It can live for centuries and has deeply fissured bark, while its acorns grow in clusters on long stalks. Though bitter and high in tannins, roasted and ground acorns can serve as a coffee substitute.
stories.edibilityNote: The bitter, tannin-rich acorns can be roasted and ground as a coffee substitute.

stories.summary: Bulbous perennial native to central and southeastern Europe. Its tightly packed, nearly round flowers resemble grape clusters; lower fertile flowers point downward, while paler sterile ones point upward.

Perennial flowering plant native to Eurasia. Its delicately scented flowers appear singly in early spring and are typically pale yellow, although wild white and pink forms occur. The flowers open flat, while the leaves often form a heavily wrinkled, evergreen rosette in favourable habitats.
stories.edibilityNote: Flowers and leaves are edible; leaves may be cooked in soup or used for tea, while young flowers can make wine.

stories.summary: A bulbous perennial native to southern and central Europe and north-western Africa. Its white, star-shaped flowers open late in the day and show a green outer stripe when closed; it can spread aggressively through bulb offsets.
stories.edibilityNote: Historically, some regional cuisines used dried and ground or boiled bulbs, and baked flowers into bread; medical authorities advise against eating any part.

stories.summary: A bulb-forming perennial native to Eurasia, growing in moist woodland. It has broad, pointed leaves and flower stems that are triangular in cross-section; in the British Isles it flowers from April to June.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are documented as edible; leaves are eaten raw or boiled. Poisonous lookalikes cause mistaken-identity poisonings.

stories.summary: Perennial flowering rush considered native across much of Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas. It forms large clumps of smooth, pith-filled cylindrical stems, with yellowish flower clusters that appear to emerge from the stem's side.
stories.edibilityNote: Reported as an ingredient of hui sup tea, although the source marks this claim as needing a citation.

stories.summary: A perennial native throughout Europe and into western Siberia, common soapwort has sweet-scented pink or sometimes white flowers that open in the evening and smell stronger at night. Boiled leaves or roots produce a lathery cleaning liquid. Despite toxic potential, it is used commercially in tahini and brewing, while the root is often added when making halva in the Middle East.
stories.edibilityNote: Despite toxic potential, it is used commercially in tahini and brewing; in the Middle East, the root is often added while making halva.

stories.summary: A moss native to Eurasia and North America. It is rare in Iceland, where it is known from only two locations and locally listed as vulnerable.
A perennial herb native to Europe, the Mediterranean region and eastward to central Asia. It has a strong smell resembling mould or damp soil and clusters of hairy reddish-purple flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: Syrup can be made from the fresh plant; no purpose or preparation details are given.

stories.summary: A flowering perennial native to Europe and parts of Asia, common valerian bears sweet-smelling white or pink flowers in summer. Its creeping rhizomes have an unpleasant smell.
