stories.edibilityNote: It can be consumed as tea.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Valeriana officinalis
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: Herbaceous perennial native to Western Europe, North Africa and Asia. It has showy mauve-purple flowers with dark veins and commonly grows in meadows, hedgerows and fallow fields. Young leaves and shoots are eaten raw or cooked and have a long history as wild food.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves and shoots are eaten raw or cooked; boiled young leaves were used as a vegetable in parts of 19th-century Europe.

stories.summary: Perennial herb native to Europe. It has upright stems, toothed lobed leaves and delicate spikes of two-lipped mauve flowers, and has a long history as a medicinal plant.

An annual herb native to Europe and Asia, it often has a brown or black spot at the centre of each leaf. Dense spikes carry tiny pink flowers, followed by shiny black, three-edged fruits. Young leaves may be eaten as a leaf vegetable.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves may be eaten as a leaf vegetable.

stories.summary: Annual flowering herb apparently native to central Mexico. Its heavily branched stems produce side shoots at nearly every node, while its stems, leaves and flower bracts range from sparsely to densely hairy. Numerous small flower heads have yellow centres and widely spaced white rays.
stories.edibilityNote: It can be eaten as a pot herb or in salads, though culinary use outside its native range is uncommon except in China.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to most of Europe and western and central Asia. Its rough, hairy foliage and red-flecked stems accompany flowers that change from pink to vivid blue; when eaten, the plant is toxic to horses and cattle.

Annual climbing herb native to Europe and western Asia. Its leaves end in supporting tendrils, while its short-lived whitish or pale-blue flowers produce small, often densely hairy pods, usually containing two seeds.

A deciduous tree native to much of continental Europe, Britain, southwest Asia and the Atlas Mountains of North Africa. It has five blunt, rounded leaf lobes and paired winged fruits that spread in opposite directions.

A shrub native to China, Korea and Japan, Japanese aucuba grows naturally in moist, shaded forest habitats. Often grown in variegated form, it has clusters of small purplish-brown flowers and red fruit.

Perennial herb native to wetlands in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Its bright, petal-like sepals are usually yellow, while its floating seeds can be splashed from the fruits by raindrops.
stories.edibilityNote: Early spring greens and buds are eaten cooked but are poisonous raw; very young flower buds have also been prepared like capers.

stories.summary: A fragrant herbaceous perennial native across most of Europe. It forms ground-level leaf rosettes and large yellow flower heads, but is toxic when taken internally.
stories.edibilityNote: It should not be taken orally; eating large amounts, or using small amounts of concentrated arnica, can cause poisoning.

stories.summary: A biennial herb native to Europe and parts of western Asia and northern Africa, common centaury grows in fields and roadsides. It forms a small basal rosette, then an upright leafy stem bearing many flat, pinkish-lavender flowers with yellow anthers.

An annual herb native to most of Europe, northern Africa and much of Asia, it grows on cultivated or disturbed ground. Its single upright stem branches near the top and bears small yellow-green flowers from mid-spring to late summer. The raw plant is poisonous and may cause nausea, vomiting, allergic reactions or skin irritation.
stories.edibilityNote: The raw plant is poisonous and may cause nausea, vomiting, allergic reactions and skin irritation.

stories.summary: A low, spreading evergreen shrub native to mountainous central, eastern and southern Europe. Its dark reddish-pink, slender bell-shaped flowers appear from late winter to early spring, sometimes while the plant is still covered by snow.

A small evergreen shrub native to boreal forest and Arctic tundra throughout the Northern Hemisphere. It spreads into dense colonies and bears edible red berries that are initially bitter, later sweetening on the branch; they are widely eaten raw, cooked, sweetened or preserved.
stories.edibilityNote: The berries are eaten raw or prepared as jams, sauces, drinks, baked goods and other dishes.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to the mountains of central and south-central Europe, with possible populations in Russia's Republic of Karelia.

A large liverwort with a worldwide distribution, common liverwort usually grows on shaded, moist soil and rocks. It forms flattened, fork-branched rosettes and has separate male and female plants with distinctive disc-like or star-rayed reproductive structures. It is frequently among the first vegetation to appear after a large wildfire.

A liverwort of unstated native origin. It forms rounded, yellow-green rosettes with perforated upper surfaces and usually grows on moist, exposed mud near lakes, ponds and reservoirs or in other damp disturbed ground.

An aquatic floating liverwort whose native origin is not stated. It forms thick mats on and beneath pond surfaces, provides a retreat for young aquarium fish, and can be attached to submerged logs or rocks.
Liverwort with a cosmopolitan distribution.
A liverwort described in the source as native to damp forests in southeastern Asia. It is grown in freshwater aquariums, where its submerged growth resembles miniature coral.
A liverwort with a cosmopolitan distribution, widely found along both North American coasts, in Europe and in eastern Asia.

Extraordinarily tiny leafy liverwort that tolerates drying and is often overlooked. It favours bright, dry places with acidic, lime-poor soil, while its variable but consistently present underleaves help distinguish it from related species.

A liverwort with a subboreal distribution, it is reported across Europe, Macaronesia, northern Africa, Asia and North America. Its rounded, square-to-rectangular leaves form green to nearly black-green mats, often in wet, shaded places such as forest streams, springs, bogs and swamps.

An evergreen shrub endemic to Oregon and California in the United States, blueblossom has glossy green leaves and spring clusters of tiny flowers ranging from shades of blue to nearly white. It attracts birds, butterflies and other pollinators, while honeybees often visit for pollen.

A perennial flowering herb of unstated native origin, naturalized in parts of Western Australia. Its distinctive square stem bears evenly arranged, hairless green leaves that shimmer in direct sunlight, along with pink-purple flowers.

An annual flowering plant native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa. It sprawls across the ground, with fresh green leaves and small flowers that are usually white to pale blue, sometimes lilac; its fruit has two parallel lobes.

A wild carrot occurring in both North and South America. It bears clusters of white or pinkish flowers, and its small taproots are edible carrots. It should not be confused with highly poisonous poison hemlock.
stories.edibilityNote: The small taproots are edible carrots.

stories.summary: A bulb-forming herbaceous perennial endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. Its hanging purple flowers sometimes have a green stripe along the centre of each petal-like segment, and its populations are scattered and usually small.

An edible flowering plant native to Eurasia. Its long fruits have an elongated beak lined with comb-like bristles. In Europe it has long been eaten as a leaf and salad vegetable, both cultivated and gathered wild.
stories.edibilityNote: Long used in Europe as a leaf and salad vegetable; formerly cultivated and also gathered wild.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to parts of Europe and introduced elsewhere, including North America. It has rough, branching stems, unequal white petals tinged pink or red, and greenish or pinkish fruits covered with straight or curved prickles.

A fan palm endemic to Guadalupe Island, Mexico. Its native trees occupy a small grove on the island’s steep northern end, where the maritime climate and terrain produce a rare North American fog oasis.

Annual or biennial flowering plant native across parts of Europe, northern Africa and western Asia. It bears bright-purple flower heads guarded by tough, sharp yellow spines. In western Crete a local variety's leaves are eaten boiled, while southern Italian Arbëreshë communities boil and fry young whorls with other wild greens.
stories.edibilityNote: In western Crete, local leaves are boiled; southern Italian Arbëreshë communities boil and fry young whorls with other wild greens.

stories.summary: Annual, biennial or perennial herb native to western and southern Europe. It grows upright with many branches ending in dandelion-like flower heads, and occurs on hillsides and in sandy clearings.

A small creeping aquatic perennial native to North Africa, Europe, the Caucasus and parts of the Levant. It grows in wetlands, marshes and swamps, producing shiny, rounded leaves with umbrella-like veins.
stories.edibilityNote: Described as edible, with a slight carrot smell, but the source flags this claim as needing citation.

stories.summary: A rootless parasitic plant native from Macaronesia across most of Europe to northwestern China, and also present in western North Africa, clover dodder has thread-like pink, red, yellow or purple stems. It coils around many kinds of host plant and draws water and nutrients from them.

A bulb-growing herbaceous perennial native to Europe and western Russia, south through Turkey to Syria. It usually has two shiny, fleshy leaves and bears upward-facing violet-blue spring flowers, which are occasionally white, pink or purple.

Herbaceous plant native to the Mediterranean region across Eurasia, North Africa and Western Asia. It has notably long, stiff, awl-shaped leaves and has become naturalized in western North America, South America, Hawaii and Australia.

Clumping perennial herb native to South Africa. It usually has slender linear leaves with dull green upper surfaces and white woolly undersides, plus solitary bright-yellow flower heads that close at night; the rare variety ovalis instead has more oval leaves and is restricted near Grahamstown.

A vernal-pool plant with no stated native origin, it is found mainly in California and extends into Oregon and northern Baja California. Its tiny flower heads resemble white cotton balls, giving individual plants the informal name Q-tips.

Low-growing annual, rarely a short-lived perennial, native to the Mediterranean Basin and Macaronesia. It bears dense clusters of small, honey-scented flowers, and its petals, leaves and tender stems can be eaten raw or cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: Petals, leaves and tender stems can be eaten raw or cooked.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to the western Mediterranean Basin in Europe and northern Africa. Its slender, much-branched stems bear narrow-lobed upper leaves and small yellow flowers; after maturity, the dead plant uproots and tumbles in the wind, spreading seed.
stories.edibilityNote: The spicy leaves can be used to make wasabi or mixed into salads and other dishes.

stories.summary: A petite annual herb native to Europe, it also occurs as an introduced plant in places including parts of North America. It grows in disturbed sites such as pavement cracks and bears solitary flowers that usually have four sepals and no petals.

Small annual herb native to several parts of North America and found in many habitats. Its threadlike green or purplish stems may stand upright or trail, and each slender flower stalk carries one flower, usually with five tiny white petals.

An annual plant native to Europe, Macaronesia, Siberia, northwestern India, northwestern Africa and the highlands of eastern tropical Africa. Its tiny flowers have five white petals, and seeds buried in soil can survive for several years.

Annual or perennial spikesedge widespread across Europe, central and southeastern Asia, the Americas, and probably introduced in Australia. Its creeping underground stem produces short, grasslike stems and tiny pointed flower spikes in marshes, seasonal pools, and bogs.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial native to Europe, western Asia and northwest Africa. Pale spore-bearing stems emerge in early spring before the green, heavily branched sterile stems, which last from late spring to autumn.

Annual plant native to most of Europe, northern Africa and western Asia, typically occurring on cultivated or disturbed ground. It has smooth stems, green flowers and kidney-shaped glands with long, thin horns. Its whole plant, including the root, was formerly eaten as Polish famine food after boiling in milk.
stories.edibilityNote: In Poland, the whole plant, including its root, was formerly eaten as famine food after being boiled in milk.

stories.summary: A perennial shrub or small tree native to southeastern Australia, it has rigid, prickly leaf-like structures crowded in whorled bundles. From July to December it produces densely packed pale-yellow flower spikes, followed by narrow, flattened seed pods.

An evergreen shrub native to South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania. It produces short clusters of yellow flowers periodically throughout the year. Indigenous Australians ate its gum after softening it in water to relieve chest pains.
stories.edibilityNote: Indigenous Australians ate the gum after softening it in water, historically to relieve chest pains.

stories.summary: An annual or short-lived perennial native to Africa and Eurasia, black medick bears tight bunches of small yellow flowers. Its single-seeded pods harden and turn black when ripe.

Perennial legume that appears to have originated in south-central Asia. It has a deep root system and usually lives four to eight years, though some varieties in suitable climates can exceed 20 years; it is widely used as ruminant feed in temperate, dry regions.

A yellow-flowered annual herb native from Macaronesia and northern Africa through Europe to temperate and tropical Asia. Its three-part leaves release a sweet, cloying scent when crushed, and the plant can maintain strong germination and growth in salty soils.
Annual or biennial legume native to Eurasia. It has a characteristic sweet smell, yellow flowers and ribbed, hairless fruit.

Flowering annual herb native to Europe and western Asia. Its leaves have three leaflets, while its distinctive yellow flower heads resemble hops. The flowers turn brown as they age and dry, enclosing a single-seeded pod.

Hairy annual flowering herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its erect stems carry three-part leaves and pink flower clusters with fine-haired cups whose needle-like lobes may harden into bristles as the plant ages.

Annual flowering herb native to much of Eurasia, the Mediterranean region and North Africa. It begins as a flat rosette of deeply lobed leaves on red stalks, then bears purple-streaked lavender flowers and long-beaked fruit.
A weedy annual or biennial herb native to much of Eurasia and North Africa. It smells musky when bruised, and its long-beaked fruits open to reveal feathery, wind-dispersed seeds.
stories.edibilityNote: The species is described as edible, but no plant part or preparation is specified.

stories.summary: An annual grasslike rush with a native range described as circumpolar across tropical to subarctic areas of both hemispheres. It forms green clumps of thin stems with a few threadlike leaves and grows in moist, muddy places.

A perennial rush found in creek beds and freshwater marshes of the Southwestern United States. It has flat, tapering leaves and small green flowers that usually remain enclosed in reddish-tipped bracts. Its shoots can take up and store selenate, so the plant is used for phytoremediation.

This flowering mint is native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, though its native range is thought to centre on the eastern Mediterranean. Crushed leaves smell strongly of spearmint, and small mauve flowers form dense, widely spaced whorls along the stems.
stories.edibilityNote: Historically used as a cooking herb and still used to flavour foods; pennyroyal is toxic, and its concentrated oil can be fatal if swallowed.

stories.summary: A bulbous flowering plant native to Spain and Portugal and naturalised in many other regions. It has narrow, rush-like leaves and bears clusters of scented yellow or white flowers in late spring. It has also been cultivated in France since the 18th century for perfume oil.

Tree with natural forms distributed across the Mediterranean Basin, parts of Africa and Arabia, Northwest India, Southwest China, Madeira and the Canary Islands. The species includes the cultivated olive and wild Mediterranean forms; one wild variety is smaller and shrubbier, with smaller leaves and fruit.
A grass native to northern Africa, western Asia and southern Europe, it has spikelets resembling those of the unrelated Bromus briziformis. Its seeds and leaves are edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds and leaves are edible.

stories.summary: Grass native to southern Europe, northern Africa and southwestern Asia east to India. Its small stature, self-fertility and rapid life cycle make it a widely used experimental model for temperate grasses and cereal crops.

An annual grass native to the Mediterranean Basin, little quaking-grass forms narrow clumps of upright stems. Its flower clusters bear several small, cone-shaped spikelets that hang from slender stalks.

An annual or biennial grass native to northern Africa, western and central Asia, the Caucasus and much of Europe, barren brome has rough, hairy leaves that may be green or purplish. Its loose flower heads are open and nodding.

An annual grass native across Europe, North Africa and eastward to central Asia, sea barley grows mainly on bare coastal ground and inland salt flats. Its flower spikes break into fruit clusters dispersed by winter floods or livestock, and it thrives only where competition is limited.

A short, tuft-forming perennial grass widespread across much of Eurasia and North America. It has blue-green basal leaves and nearly cylindrical flower heads bearing shiny tan spikelets, sometimes tinged purple.
stories.edibilityNote: The seed can be ground into powder and boiled as porridge or made into flour or bread.

stories.summary: A stout perennial bunch grass originating from southern Europe and the Caucasus. It has grayish-blue leaves and dense, spike-like flower heads, eventually forming large bunches. Its alkaloids are implicated in livestock toxicity.
A flowering grass whose listed subspecies are native to mainland Portugal; subsp. pratense is introduced in the Azores.

An annual bunchgrass native to North Africa, Europe and South Asia, lesser canary grass grows in tufts and bears spike-like flower clusters. It is widely naturalised elsewhere and is used for livestock forage and birdseed, although it is poisonous to some mammals.

An annual grass native to the Old World, it now occurs worldwide as an introduced species and sometimes a noxious weed. Its dense, greenish flower head looks soft and feathery because the spikelets bear long, fine, whitish bristles.
An annual or biennial plant native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, clustered dock has also been introduced to North America.
An annual or sometimes biennial herb native to Europe. It grows in wet places such as irrigation ditches, with shiny yellow flowers followed by spherical clusters of spiny fruits.

An evergreen shrub native from California to northern Mexico, it has yellow-green flowers without petals and red berries containing two nutlets. Native Americans in the western United States ate the fruit, though large quantities reportedly turned the body red.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Americans in the western United States ate the fruit; large quantities reportedly gave the consumer's body a red tint.

stories.summary: A dense deciduous shrub native to western North America, Pacific ninebark has reddish-gray bark that peels away in many thin layers. Its dark green leaves resemble grape or maple leaves, while creamy white flower clusters appear from late spring into midsummer.

An evergreen or deciduous shrub native from southern Europe and the Caucasus to parts of western Asia, scarlet firethorn has sharply thorned stems. It bears clusters of white flowers followed by small, bright red fruit.

A deciduous tree native to northeastern and central China and Taiwan, tree-of-heaven grows rapidly and spreads aggressively by seeds and root sprouts. All parts have a strong smell, often compared with peanuts or rotting cashews, and the tree can quickly recolonize after cutting.
stories.edibilityNote: Roots are poisonous to humans; illness has also been reported after ingesting other plant parts or water contaminated by flowers.

stories.summary: A perennial flowering herb native from Macaronesia and North Africa through Europe and Central Asia to the central Himalaya. Its sprawling reddish stems bear sticky blackish fruits, while its windblown pollen is a major cause of asthma and rhinitis around the Mediterranean.

Perennial herb native to the Mediterranean region. It bears numerous pink or red flowers, rarely white, in dense clusters and often grows on cliffs, rocks and walls. Its strongly scented leaves may be eaten raw in salads or cooked as vegetables.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves may be eaten raw in salads or cooked as vegetables, though their strong aroma may be unappealing.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to southern and central Europe and western Asia. Its hairy climbing stems use leaf-tip tendrils for support, and it bears yellow or purple-marked pea-like flowers followed by hairy pods.

Annual flowering herb native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa. Its leaves have several pairs of narrow leaflets, and it bears solitary flowers or clusters of up to three with yellow or purple-tinged petals.

An erect annual crop whose wild ancestor and origin are unknown, the fava bean has square stems and grey-green leaves without climbing tendrils. Its white flowers have true-black wing spots. The beans are widely eaten, but people with favism must avoid them; boiling for ten minutes destroys most of their relatively low toxin levels.
stories.edibilityNote: Beans are eaten raw or cooked; young pods and leaves are also edible. People with favism must avoid them, while boiling reduces most lectin toxins.

stories.summary: An annual flowering plant native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, lentil vetch has pale-blue flowers and leaves ending in a simple tendril. Its pods typically contain four seeds. In mainland Portugal it was assessed as regionally extinct after not being recorded since 1883.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Vicia tetrasperma
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An annual legume believed to have originated in the Middle East, yellow vetchling has yellow flowers, sometimes streaked with violet. Its true leaves are reduced to tendrils, while leaf-like structures take their place.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruits are eaten in parts of South Asia and may supplement grain diets, but large quantities are narcotic and potentially toxic.

stories.summary: Legume native to parts of Europe and western Asia. It is grown for forage, winter ground cover and green manure, but its hard seeds and early seed shedding can leave it as a field weed.

An evergreen cashew-family tree native to arid and Andean South America. Its upper branches droop, and its bark, leaves and berries are aromatic when crushed; dense fruit clusters turn from green to red, pink or purple and may remain year-round. The berries are sold as pink peppercorns, although the fruit has caused vomiting and diarrhea in children and lacks US GRAS status.
stories.edibilityNote: Pink/red berries are sold as peppercorns; extracts flavour drinks, while Wari and Inca fruit preparations included fermented drinks, syrup and maize gruel.

stories.summary: A perennial shrub native to North America, it is thornless and has leaves made up of many hairy, oval leaflets. Its flower spikes feature single purple petals and prominent yellow-tipped stamens, followed by pods containing one or two seeds.
An evergreen shrub native to the Pacific coast of North America, it has large, long-lasting leaves and usually pink flowers. It contains a toxin that can poison honey from nearby hives.

A bulbous perennial native to southern and western France, Portugal and Spain, the hoop-petticoat daffodil has grass-like leaves and deep yellow flowers in mid-spring. Its unusually large central trumpet is surrounded by tiny pointed segments.
A rhizomatous flowering perennial native to Europe and temperate Asia. Arching leafy stems carry hanging white tubular flowers with green tips, and the plant can spread through shady areas.

An annual flowering plant native to the Iberian Peninsula and northwest Africa, Linaria amethystea has bluish-green stems and violet hairs on its upper leaf surfaces. Its spring flowers are usually amethyst-blue and white, with two lips and a long spur, although some subspecies have yellow flowers.

A perennial shrub endemic to Madeira, it inhabits some ravines in the island’s laurel forest. It has woody, hairy branches, heart-shaped leaves and usually dense clusters of orange-brown flowers, which appear from May to June.
A hairy perennial herb native to Western Europe and Tunisia. Its pale green or yellowish flowers face one side, lack an upper lip and bloom from June through August.
Edible perennial grassland herb native to Europe and Asia. It has square stems, purplish-red flower spikes and persistent tuberous runners that help it spread.
stories.edibilityNote: Described as edible, with no particular part or preparation specified.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Stachys palustris
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A rhizomatous perennial orchid native across Europe, Asia and North Africa, it grows mainly in light or damp woodland. Its white, yellow-lipped flowers usually open only during the warmest, brightest hours, and some individuals lack green pigment and obtain all their nutrition from fungi.

A perennial twining herb of unstated native origin, hedge bindweed has a subcosmopolitan temperate distribution. It climbs counter-clockwise, bearing arrowhead-shaped leaves and white, sometimes pale-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is toxic and contains calystegine alkaloids.

stories.summary: A Mediterranean perennial found in sandy and stony places on limestone. It is sticky and glandular, woody at the base, and bears yellow flowers marked with reddish-brown stripes from April to July.
stories.edibilityNote: Its branches are used in raisin preparation, but the source does not state that they are eaten.

stories.summary: Evergreen partly parasitic shrub native to Europe and western and southern Asia. It grows on tree stems and produces white or yellow berries with very sticky pulp. Concentrated tea may be fatal and berries can cause serious illness, although mistletoe is an ingredient in Istrian biska liquor.
stories.edibilityNote: An ingredient in Istrian biska liquor; concentrated infusions can be fatal, and berries have caused serious illness.

stories.summary: Perennial thistle native to western and central Mediterranean regions, with a native presence in Portugal. It has violet-purple flower heads with fleshy receptacles and green-purple bracts ending in spines; its natural milk-coagulating effect is used in cheesemaking.
stories.edibilityNote: Its natural milk-coagulating effect is used to make cheeses such as Serra da Estrela and Nisa.

stories.summary: A flowering orchid of the Palaearctic and North Africa, the lesser butterfly-orchid has two shining green basal leaves. Its slim flower spike carries white, yellow-green-tinged flowers that are scented at night.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Platanthera bifolia
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An annual herb native from the Canary Islands across Europe to northern Iran and southern Turkmenistan, the dwarf violet grows in disturbed or grazed soil. It remains very short and bears characteristically asymmetrical violet flowers.

Spring-flowering bulbous perennial native to the western Iberian Peninsula, excluding the far northwest. Compared with the common bluebell, it has larger, paler and less drooping flowers, broader leaves, blue anthers and little or no scent; pink- and white-flowered forms also occur.

A fern indigenous to Asia, southern Europe, tropical Africa and Australia. It often grows around limestone or in cracks in concrete structures. It absorbs unusually high levels of arsenic and is used to clean polluted sites.
Flowering legume whose variety pusilla is native to mainland Portugal.

An annual, sometimes biennial, flowering herb native to Europe, Africa and western Asia. Its small flowers have yellow anthers and are about half the diameter of those of the similar Geranium robertianum.

A bushy evergreen perennial native to woodland locations in Europe, Turkey and the Caucasus, wood spurge has slightly hairy dark-green leaves and green-yellow flower clusters in late spring and early summer. It thrives in dry tree shade and spreads rapidly through underground stems; its milky sap is toxic and irritates skin.
A large perennial subshrub native only to Madeira. It usually has a candelabra-like shape, densely hairy leaves and elongated clusters of blue or purple flowers that attract bees and butterflies.

Rhizomatous perennial native to China, Korea and Myanmar. It forms spreading clumps and usually bears blue to violet flowers with darker markings around a fringed white crest; a white form also exists.
stories.edibilityNote: Most parts, including the rhizomes and leaves, are poisonous if ingested and may cause stomach pain and vomiting.

stories.summary: Red alga with no stated native origin, widely found on moderately sheltered rocky shores around Europe. This small, tufted seaweed can vary from yellow-buff through red to almost black and never grows below low tide.
stories.edibilityNote: Harvested and dried in Scotland and the Channel Islands as a curry-flavoured spice; also used in gin-making in northwestern Ireland.

stories.summary: Marine red alga native to southern Australia and New Zealand. Its sparse branches bear long creeping stems with harpoon-like hooks, while mature plants form dense, intertwined pink clumps whose barbs attach to the seabed.

Perennial flowering plant native to northern Argentina, southern Brazil and Uruguay. It has pink-to-violet flowers and rosettes of three heart-shaped leaflets, whose undersides usually show orange granules. Thick, woody rhizomes allow it to spread into colonies.
stories.edibilityNote: Rich in ascorbic acid and eaten as a vegetable by people in Jharkhand, India.

stories.summary: Bulbous perennial from woods and meadows of the eastern Mediterranean, from Greece and Turkey to the Caucasus, including Armenia. It has simple basal leaves and short stems bearing mainly purple or blue flowers, though some varieties are white or pale pink. It blooms in mid-spring, and some selections are fragrant.

An aquatic perennial herb native to northern temperate and some subtropical regions of Europe, northwest Africa and western Asia. It has floating and submerged leaves and fragrant, solitary yellow flowers. It has been used as food since prehistoric times.
stories.edibilityNote: Documented as food from prehistoric times; the supplied information does not identify particular edible parts or preparations.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. Its sometimes-climbing stems carry white or cream flowers tipped with purple, which gradually turn pink after pollination.

A short-lived perennial flowering plant reported as native across the Old World from southern Africa to Eurasia. It is semi-aquatic, with pale violet-blue flower spikes, and can spread when flood-broken pieces root downstream.

A tufted perennial sedge of unstated native origin, it is widespread across higher latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere. It forms tight clumps in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor bogs and bears white flower clusters in August, followed by dry fruits with beak-like caps.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Rhynchospora alba
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: Small herbaceous plant found in Australia and New Zealand, mainly on hillsides and in weedy areas. It is New Zealand’s smallest Oxalis species, with leaves ranging from green to purple.

A perennial aquatic plant found nearly worldwide in freshwater habitats. It forms dense floating mats of small green discs with dark-red undersides, and rarely flowers. It is hardly used for human nutrition and is not cultivated for it because of contamination, heavy-metal and calcium-oxalate concerns.
stories.edibilityNote: Hardly used for human nutrition and not cultivated for it because of contamination, heavy-metal and calcium-oxalate concerns.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to the tropical Americas. It branches freely, and larger plants become tumbleweeds after dying and drying; in Cambodia, its leaves are sometimes cooked and eaten by people.
stories.edibilityNote: In Cambodia, the leaves are sometimes cooked and eaten by people.

stories.summary: An annual flowering plant native to Macaronesia and Europe’s Atlantic, Baltic and Mediterranean coasts. It grows in salty, sandy coastal soils and was historically burned to produce soda ash for glassmaking.

A perennial herb naturally found from eastern Europe across central and eastern Asia, extending south to northern India and Mexico; its North American presence may reflect prehistoric human introduction from Asia. Its small, narrow leaves taste sweet and mildly spicy and are used fresh or dried as seasoning.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are used fresh or dried in pickles, stews, salads, béarnaise sauce, vinegars and other culinary infusions.

stories.summary: Annual flowering plant whose native origin is unresolved in the supplied information. Its female flower heads become buoyant, hooked burs that catch in animal hair. Small amounts of mature plant parts may be consumed, but seeds and seedlings should not be eaten in large quantities because they contain an extremely toxic chemical.
stories.edibilityNote: Small amounts of mature parts may be consumed; seeds, seedlings and large quantities are dangerous, and famine consumption caused deaths in Bangladesh in 2007.

stories.summary: An annual flowering plant native to the Mediterranean regions of Europe and Africa. Its leaves are dotted with resin, and the structures surrounding its flower heads end in spines.

An annual flowering herb of unknown native origin, possibly from South America and perhaps Chile, it is now a widespread weed of disturbed ground. Long, yellowish three-pronged spines grow near the leaf forks, while hooked burs spread by attaching to animals, people and objects or floating on water.

Perennial herb native to the Americas and northern Australia. It has fleshy stems and thick leaves, with coiled double rows of small white flowers whose throats may be purple or yellow. It commonly grows in salty soils such as beaches, alkali flats and salt marshes.

A winter annual herb native to the Middle East, North Africa and southern Europe, it commonly occupies dry, disturbed ground. Developing seedpods rise above its compact yellow flower heads. Its spicy leaves, seeds and flowers are edible, while cured pods can be parched, ground into meal and cooked in soup or stew.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, seeds and flowers are eaten; cured pods can be parched, ground into meal and made into soup or stew.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, eastern rocket has a hairy, branching stem. Its lower leaves are deeply divided, while pale yellow flowers at the stem tips develop into long, narrow fruits.
Annual flowering herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its creeping stems are coated with small, fuzzy, pale green leaves, and its flowers have hairy green sepals but no petals.

Low-lying shrub of the southwestern United States, California, Idaho and northern Mexico; its native status is not specified. It grows in sandy, often salty and strongly alkaline ground, with fleshy, knobby green stems, scale-like leaves and seeds used as food in prehistoric North America.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds were used as food in prehistoric North America.

stories.summary: A fast-growing annual whose native range is obscure but reportedly spans temperate Eurasia, the Indian subcontinent, North Africa, Ethiopia, and the eastern and central United States. Its lower leaves are toothed and roughly diamond-shaped, while upper leaves have a whitish, mealy underside. Young shoots may be eaten raw or cooked; leaves, flower buds and flowers are preferably cooked, and the seeds also have traditional food uses.
stories.edibilityNote: Young shoots may be raw or cooked; leaves, flower buds and flowers are cooked. Seeds have traditional food and drink uses.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to Eurasia and parts of Africa, it has branching stems that root at their joints and form spreading patches. Its round flowerheads change from white to pink, then develop pinkish, net-patterned fruit clusters resembling strawberries.

Annual flowering plant native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. Its wild form is hairy and glandular, with intricately divided, lacy leaves and coiling clusters of blue or lavender flowers. Its seeds germinate only in darkness.

A herbaceous perennial native to temperate Europe, western and central Asia, the Himalaya, eastern Siberia and North America, corn mint spreads by creeping rootstocks. It has hairy, coarsely toothed leaves and pale purple flowers, occasionally white or pink, clustered around the stems. Its leaves can be eaten raw or made into tea.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves can be eaten raw or made into tea, traditionally to treat colds or aid digestion.

stories.summary: Aromatic evergreen shrub native to the southern coastal mountain ranges of California and Baja California. Its spring-green leaves mature to grayish white, while arching branches may root where they touch the ground. Tight clusters of pinkish-purple flowers rise on similarly coloured stems.

Annual or perennial herb native to northern Africa, southern Europe, and western and central Asia. It has broad, shallow-lobed leaves and small white or pink flowers, and the entire plant is eaten raw or cooked with a mild, chard-like flavour.
stories.edibilityNote: The entire plant is eaten raw or cooked and has a mild flavour resembling chard.

stories.summary: A small deciduous tree or large shrub native to the south-central United States. Its bumpy yellow-green fruit releases sticky white latex when damaged, while its strong, flexible, durable wood was traditionally prized for bows.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is generally not eaten by humans and is mostly inedible; its seeds are called edible, but only squirrel use is documented.

stories.summary: A small to medium-sized tree native to eastern Australia, it often has a crooked trunk and a domed canopy of greyish foliage. Its bark may be fibrous below and smooth, mottled grey, cream and yellow above; groups of seven buds produce white flowers in the Australian spring.
Tree native to eastern Australia and southern New Guinea. It has smooth bark mottled white, grey and blue as irregular sheets are shed, along with white flowers and woody, hemispherical fruit.

Plantain native to the Mediterranean region and naturalized in parts of Asia and North America. Its ground seed husks are an indigestible source of soluble dietary fiber and are widely used in commercial psyllium products.
stories.edibilityNote: Ground seed husks are consumed as indigestible soluble dietary fiber in commercial psyllium products.

stories.summary: A large deciduous plane tree native to California and Baja California, especially waterways, canyons and floodplains. Its bark forms a striking patchwork of pale colours, while its broad lobed leaves turn golden to orange-red before falling.

A deciduous willow native to dry areas of northern China, Korea, Mongolia, Japan and Siberia. It grows rapidly but is short-lived, with narrow leaves that turn golden yellow in autumn. Its strongly drooping form is a cultivated selection.

A deciduous tree native to China, Korea and Manchuria, the golden rain tree has a broad, dome-shaped crown. Large end clusters of yellow flowers are followed by inflated, bladder-like pods that ripen from green to orange and pink in autumn.

A poisonous herbaceous perennial native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, sacred datura bears sweetly fragrant white trumpet flowers and spiny round seed capsules. All parts contain dangerous alkaloids and may be fatal if eaten, with the roots considered the most potent part.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts may be fatal if eaten; the roots are considered the most potent and alkaloid-rich part.

stories.summary: Flowering shrub or small tree native to South America and introduced widely elsewhere. It has smooth, bluish-green, rubbery leaves and yellow tubular flowers; every part is potentially poisonous to people and livestock.
stories.edibilityNote: Poisonous cooked or raw; ingesting the leaves can be fatal because they contain high levels of anabasine and nicotine.

stories.summary: A bushy annual herb endemic to the western United States, it bears white, greenish or purple-tinged flowers with long tubular throats. Indigenous peoples traditionally cultivated it along parts of the western coast and the middle Columbia River.
A flowering wetland plant whose native origin is not specified. Sea clubrush grows widely in coastal and inland saline wetlands, often dominating mineral-rich mud where water levels fluctuate.

Flowering plant native to southern California and Baja California, chaparral yucca forms a stemless rosette of rigid, sharp-pointed, finely toothed leaves. Its single flower stalk grows extremely quickly and carries hundreds of fragrant white to purplish flowers; the flowering shoot usually dies afterward, while most subspecies produce basal offshoots. Before European settlement, Native Americans ground its seeds into flour and ate pit-roasted hearts, roasted stalks and often parboiled petals.
stories.edibilityNote: Before European settlement, Native Americans ground seeds into flour, pit-roasted hearts, roasted slightly bitter stalks and often parboiled petals.

stories.summary: A winter annual grass native to Europe, southwestern Asia and northern Africa. Its hairy leaves and drooping flower clusters are distinctive. It readily invades disturbed ground and spreads through rapid growth and prolific seed production.

A warm-season grass native to Europe, Africa, Australia and much of Asia, Bermuda grass spreads by creeping stems and underground rhizomes, forming dense mats. It has deep roots, recovers quickly from damage and produces durable turf in hot, dry regions.
A flowering grass native to continental Portugal and Madeira.

A grass native to Eurasia and North Africa, it forms dense clumps with swollen stem bases, especially in drier places. It rarely produces viable seed and usually reproduces through these detachable bases and bulbils held in green, leaflike flower clusters.

A flowering grass whose native origin is not specified, it occurs in tropical regions. It has tall, thick stems, long leaves and pyramid-shaped flower clusters that bloom in the first year. It may be grown as an annual or perennial.

A perennial herb found throughout tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, it thrives in marshes and other wetlands and can tolerate highly saline water. In southern Iraq’s Mesopotamian Marshes, its pollen is reportedly made into a dessert called khirret, though the source flags this claim as needing a full citation.
stories.edibilityNote: In southern Iraq, its pollen is reportedly made into khirret dessert; the source marks this claim as needing a full citation.

stories.summary: An aromatic annual herb probably originating in western and central Asia. Its white or lilac flowers usually appear from July to September, and its delicately aromatic, spicy flavour is valued as a culinary seasoning.
stories.edibilityNote: Used as a culinary seasoning; in Bulgarian cuisine it is mixed with salt and paprika to make sharena sol.

stories.summary: An evergreen pine native to Eurasia, Scots pine is readily recognized by its short blue-green needles and orange-red bark. Mature trees often have a long, bare, straight trunk topped by a rounded or flat mass of foliage.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Pinus sylvestris
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An evergreen conifer with a Holarctic distribution across the cool temperate Northern Hemisphere, common juniper varies from a small tree to a ground-hugging shrub. It has needle-like leaves in threes and berry-like cones that ripen over 18 months from green to waxy blue-black. The bitter cones are not eaten raw; dried and usually crushed, they flavour meats, sauces, stuffings, beer and gin.
stories.edibilityNote: Bitter cones are not eaten raw; they are dried, usually crushed, and used sparingly to flavour foods, beers and spirits.

stories.summary: A small deciduous shrub native to Japan and eastern Asia. It has spiny brown branches, pale yellow spring flowers, leaves that turn red in autumn, and glossy red-to-orange edible berries that persist through winter. It is widely naturalized in China and North America and invasive in many places.
stories.edibilityNote: The glossy red-to-orange berry is edible and matures from late summer through autumn.

stories.summary: A crabapple tree native to China, it bears white flowers and yellow or red fruit. Some varieties are grown for their fruit.
stories.edibilityNote: Some varieties are grown for their fruit.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to southern Ontario and the eastern United States, silky dogwood bears opposite oval leaves and small blue fruits. Its rusty-brown twigs can spread into dense thickets, particularly in wetland habitats.

A floating aquatic fern native to warm-temperate and tropical regions of the Americas. Its tiny branching plants may be green with pink, orange or red edges and can rapidly cover an entire lake surface. It largely dies back during temperate winters but survives through submerged buds.

A perennial fern native to places including Finland, brittle bladderfern grows mainly in shady, slightly moist rocky cracks and ledges. Its leaves are finely divided, with many rounded spore clusters underneath.
An annual plant believed native to the central and possibly eastern United States, procumbent pigweed has smooth, hairless surfaces. It flowers from summer into fall.
stories.edibilityNote: Several Native American groups ate the seeds; Zuni people initially ate them raw and later ground them with black cornmeal and formed them into balls.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb that may be native to the Neotropics or central and eastern North America, redroot amaranth is now introduced across most continents. It can form a tumbleweed and bears dense flower clusters threaded with spiny green bracts.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, stems, young shoots and seeds are eaten raw or cooked; discard boiling water because leaves contain oxalic acid and may contain nitrates.

stories.summary: A strongly scented herb native across much of Eurasia, Macaronesia and North Africa, celery grows naturally in damp, often salty places. Cultivated forms are vegetables selected for edible leaf stalks, swollen stem bases, or leaves and stems, which may be eaten raw or cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: Wild celery was historically a condiment; cultivated forms provide raw or cooked stalks, swollen stem bases, leaves and stems.

stories.summary: Waterside carrot-family plant of unspecified native origin, widespread across much of Europe, Asia, Australia and North America. Its hollow stems bear thread-like leaves underwater and broader leaves above water, while crushed stalks smell of carrot or parsnip. The Zuni use it in schumaakwe cakes.
stories.edibilityNote: The Zuni people use the plant as an ingredient in schumaakwe cakes.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Berula erecta
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An aquatic plant native to North America and parts of South America. It floats or creeps in wet, sandy places and has rounded leaves; it is eaten in salads or cooked as a pot herb.
stories.edibilityNote: Used raw in salads or cooked as a pot herb.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to mountainous and wooded parts of California and Arizona, it is hairy and aromatic. Its narrow fruits are ribbed and bristly, while its tiny flowers are greenish yellow.

A flowering plant native to southern Africa, brass buttons spreads stems along the ground and raises bright yellow, button-like flower heads. It is highly salt-tolerant and favours muddy wetlands and brackish habitats, with fleshy leaves and reddish stems.

A branching subshrub native to southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia as far east as Pakistan. It smells of camphor and has narrow leaves coated in sticky resin. The resin can cause allergic reactions and severe dermatitis, so gloves are advised when handling it.

A flowering plant native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, telegraphweed is tall, bristly and glandular. Its hairy, toothed or lobed leaves become smaller up the stem, ending in bright yellow, daisy-like flower heads and later spherical seed heads with long white tufts.

Annual herb native to parts of Europe, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent. It sprawls through disturbed, shady ground, with many-branched stems and loose clusters of small flowers.

A fast-growing annual herb widespread in North America, with toothed lower leaves and seeds marked by distinctive honeycomb-like pits. It was cultivated by Indigenous peoples in prehistoric North America and remains a crop in Mexico.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, young shoots and seeds are eaten; cooking reduces oxalic acid, and seeds are soaked and rinsed to remove saponins.

stories.summary: A small succulent native to Eurasia, particularly the Mediterranean Basin. Its fleshy foliage changes from green through orange to deep red as it matures, and tiny flowers appear between opposite pairs of pointed leaves.

A fast-growing annual plant native to North America. Its spreading stems form ground-hugging mats, and its small hairy leaves usually bear a central brown spot. Broken leaves or stems release poisonous milky sap that can irritate skin and cause stomach irritation and vomiting if swallowed.
stories.edibilityNote: The poisonous milky sap has been ingested medicinally as a laxative or to induce vomiting, but can irritate the stomach and cause vomiting.

stories.summary: An annual or biennial legume native to much of Asia, southern Europe and northeastern Africa. Its small white flowers form narrow, often drooping clusters, and the whole plant has a sweet scent that intensifies when dried.

An annual or biennial flowering herb native to Europe, it commonly grows in moist places such as marshes, wet fields and rice paddies. Its branching stems carry spikes of small pinkish flowers followed by oval capsules containing many minute seeds.

Annual-to-perennial herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its narrow leaves form a ground-level rosette and are toothed or deeply divided, resembling a buck’s horn. The leaves are grown as a vegetable, especially for salad mixes.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are cultivated as a vegetable called erba stella, mainly for salad mixes.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial native to Eurasia and temperate Africa, greater plantain forms a broad leaf rosette and narrow flower spikes bearing many small, bitter seeds. Young tender leaves are eaten in salads, older leaves can be stewed, and the seeds can be ground as a flour substitute or extender.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten raw; older leaves are cooked in stews. The tiny seeds can be ground as a flour substitute or extender.

stories.summary: A prostrate annual-to-perennial herb considered native in most places and on every continent except Antarctica, but introduced in Venezuela and the Falkland Islands and absent from southern Asia. It inhabits springs, streams and seasonally wet grassland, sometimes forming mats or floating. In Spain and Portugal, wild plants are gathered and eaten as salad, though they are not cultivated.
stories.edibilityNote: Wild plants are gathered for salad in Spain and Portugal but are not currently cultivated.

stories.summary: Succulent plant of unclear native origin, now ranging from North Africa and southern Europe through Asia to Australasia; much of this spread is assumed to be human-assisted, and its status in the Americas is uncertain. It has reddish, mostly ground-hugging stems and small yellow flowers that open briefly on sunny mornings. All parts are edible raw or cooked, and the seeds can be eaten or made into flour, though the leaves contain high oxalate levels.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are edible raw or cooked; seeds are also eaten raw or made into flour.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to the Mediterranean Basin, parts of the Middle East and nearby Atlantic islands, tiny bedstraw has very short upright stems with small leaves arranged in whorls. Its tiny greenish flowers grow singly or in pairs, followed by fruits covered in hooked hairs.

An annual herb native to the Mediterranean area and Western Europe, including northern Africa, Turkey, Iran and eastern North Atlantic islands. Its thin, branching stems carry rings of narrow leaves and tiny greenish-white or purple-tinged flowers; hooked bristles densely cover the fruit. It readily occupies rocky habitats and old stone walls.
A semiaquatic annual flowering herb native to much of the temperate world. It forms low fleshy tufts in mud or wet sand, with spoon-shaped leaves and tiny white flowers sometimes tinted pink or blue.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Limosella aquatica

stories.summary: A flowering biennial native to Eurasia and North Africa, moth mullein forms a basal leaf rosette in its first year and a slender flowering stem in its second. Its yellow or white flowers have orange stamens covered in purple hairs, resembling moth antennae. It has naturalized widely in North America and is considered invasive there.

A hairy biennial herb native to Europe, northern Africa and Asia. It forms a large leaf rosette followed by a tall stem densely packed with small yellow flowers. Its abundant seeds may remain able to germinate for decades.

A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, turkey tangle frogfruit occurs across tropical regions worldwide and is often grown as ground cover. Its flower heads have a purple centre ringed by small white-to-pink flowers, giving them a match-like appearance.

An annual sedge native to southern Europe, most of Africa and Asia, and Australia. It grows in wet habitats and rice fields, with thin stems, wispy basal leaves and rounded clusters containing many tiny brown flowers.

Tufted herbaceous sedge native to subtropical and tropical South America. It has a short woody rhizome and umbrella-like clusters of small flowers. In some regions, people eat its nut-like tubers raw or cooked, and the stem base is also edible.
stories.edibilityNote: In some regions, the small nut-like tubers are eaten raw or cooked; the stem base is also edible.

stories.summary: A herbaceous emergent plant of unspecified native origin, three-square bulrush is widespread across much of the Americas, Europe, New Zealand and Australia. This long-lived marsh perennial has rough, dense dark-green foliage and small flowers in compact spikelets.

A tiny duckweed native to parts of the Americas, though its exact native range is unknown, least duckweed is the smallest Lemna species. Its translucent green body grows singly in shade and usually in pairs in full sun, and it produces a short-lived flower.

Duckweed native to much of the Americas, Valdivia duckweed is a minute flowering plant that forms mats on calm freshwater. Its flat, translucent, pale green body produces a root and a tiny, short-lived flower, often enclosed in a membrane.

A tufted grass native to much of northern North America and most widespread in the west, western fescue usually grows in forests and woodlands. It has hairlike basal leaves, does not spread through underground stems, and flowers from late June into July.

An aquatic perennial native to Eurasia and the Americas, longleaf pondweed grows in ponds, lakes, ditches and streams. Its submerged leaves are narrow while its floating leaves are oval, and both types are carried on notably long stalks.
Flowering grass native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, but introduced to São Miguel and Terceira in the Azores. Its reddish colour is a distinctive feature.

A clump-forming perennial native to Europe, chives have dark-green rounded leaves and pale-pink, pompom-like flowers. Their mild onion-flavoured fresh leaves and stems are used raw in salads and as seasoning in many dishes.
stories.edibilityNote: Fresh leaves and stems are eaten raw or used as seasoning in salads, soups, potatoes and egg or cheese dishes.

stories.summary: A self-supporting perennial herb native to Europe and Egypt.

A small herbaceous perennial found in Europe, the eastern Mediterranean and North Africa, ground-pine resembles a tiny pine tree. Its three-lobed leaves smell like pine needles when crushed, and its seeds can remain alive in soil for up to 50 years.

An annual or biennial herb native to central and southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, field marigold has bright yellow to orange flower heads on slender, hairy stems. Its fruits occur in three shapes, including ring-shaped forms.
An annual herb of unspecified native origin, southern bird's-foot-trefoil has a self-supporting growth form and broad, compound leaves.
Annual wild pea native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. It has branched curling tendrils and single flowers in varying shades of red.
stories.edibilityNote: Historically eaten as cicerchia in Milan in 1288, although the species is known to cause lathyrism.

stories.summary: An annual flowering plant native to the Mediterranean region. Garden forms range from yellow flowers surrounded by sea-green leafy bracts to purple flowers with blue bracts; in Europe it flowers from May to August.
A perennial flowering herb endemic to the Mediterranean basin, broad-leaved anemone has fragrant solitary flowers ranging from bluish white or mauve to red-purple. It flowers from March through May.
An annual herb whose native origin is not stated in the supplied information. It is a small, self-supporting plant with broad compound leaves.

A herbaceous annual native to disturbed ground in Europe and naturalized as a weed elsewhere, including North America. Its pink flowers resemble miniature snapdragons, followed by hairy green fruit said to resemble a weasel's snout.

A flowering plant native to southern Europe and some Mediterranean islands, spring sowbread has wide, heart-shaped leaves that are often coarsely toothed or lobed. Its late-spring flowers have long, slender petals and may be deep carmine-pink or white.

Annual flowering herb native to temperate and boreal North America and Eurasia, usually growing beside ponds, streams and other wet ground. It has deeply divided, mostly hairless leaves and small yellow flowers. All parts are considered poisonous, and ingestion can cause burning, pain, tongue inflammation and increased salivation.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are considered poisonous; ingestion can irritate the skin and mucous membranes.

stories.summary: Orchid native to the Mediterranean Basin, including parts of southern Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. Its dense bright-pink flower clusters appear in April, and each flower has a lobed lip resembling a naked person wearing a hat.
An orchid found widely across Europe and Asia, as far north as Germany. It grows in wet meadows with alkaline soil; mass flowering can occur in Jersey and Guernsey from late May to early June.

stories.summary: A flowering orchid native to western Eurasia and northern Africa, the green-winged orchid usually bears purple flowers, though they may range from white to deep purple. Its green-veined side petals resemble wings, and its flowers produce no nectar.
A flowering orchid found in Southern Europe and Northern Africa, it favours dry, stony ground.

A herbaceous perennial orchid native to Europe, northern Africa and western Asia. Its flowers resemble human figures, with petals and sepals forming the head and the divided lip forming a hanging torso and limbs; it usually grows in sunny, often calcareous grassland.
Terrestrial orchid native to the Mediterranean region from Portugal and Morocco to Turkey. Its flower is said to resemble a sawfly, though this resemblance is only purported.

An orchid native across the Mediterranean region from Portugal and the Canary Islands to Turkey and Lebanon, it has flowers resembling female Eucera bees in appearance and scent. Male bees attempting to mate with the flowers carry pollen between plants.

An orchid native to southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, from Portugal and Morocco to Syria. Its flowers may be yellow or have blue-grey or brown velvety spots. Male Andrena bees pollinate it while facing away from the pollen structures, collecting pollen on their abdomen.

An annual herb native to Eurasia, it commonly grows as a weed in disturbed ground and has been introduced elsewhere. Long hairs and bristles cover the plant, including its sharply lobed leaves and the pointed structures surrounding its yellow flower heads.
Annual herb of unspecified native origin, with broad compound leaves. Its flowers are visited by several kinds of mason bee.

Bulb-growing wildflower native to western North America, from southwestern British Columbia to northern California. It has mottled basal leaves and nodding white flowers with yellow-based, upward-curving segments.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Americans reportedly ate the roots raw or cooked; the source does not identify the groups or period.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to western North America, from southern Alaska and British Columbia south to Utah and California. Its hand-shaped leaves have numerous leaflets, while wild plants usually bear tall spikes of blue-to-purple flowers. Newer garden hybrids are highly poisonous and should never be eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Newer garden hybrids are highly poisonous and should never be eaten; low-alkaloid cultivars mentioned are bred for animal fodder.

stories.summary: A small tree or shrub native to foothill woodlands and chaparral, the western redbud is found primarily in Oregon and Northern California. Its bright pink or magenta flowers emerge before the leaves, while clusters of thin, brown or reddish-purple pods persist through winter.

A coniferous tree native to scattered groves on the western slopes of California’s Sierra Nevada. Giant sequoias are the most massive individual trees on Earth, and the oldest known specimen lived for more than 3,200 years.
A biennial plant native to Europe. It has very large leaves and pink-to-purple flower heads whose hooked outer bracts attach to people and animals.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leafstalks, leaves and flower stalks are eaten raw or cooked; roots require boiling with changed water and become woody after one year.

stories.summary: A deciduous conifer native to the mountains of central Europe, with isolated lowland populations in northern Poland. Its light-green needles turn bright yellow before falling in autumn, and old cones may remain on the tree for years. A lifespan near 1,000 years is confirmed, while ages around 2,000 years are considered likely.

A grass native to the southeastern United States, Grenada, Central America and South America. Its folded or flat leaf blades have fine hairs along their edges and may turn purple or reddish when mature; it is often used as permanent pasture.

A root vegetable native to Eurasia, wild parsnip is related to carrot but is paler and more strongly flavoured. Its root and the part just above it are eaten cooked in stews and soups, while other plant parts are toxic. Cultivated since ancient times, it served as a staple before potatoes were introduced.
stories.edibilityNote: The root and adjoining lower stem are eaten cooked; other plant parts are toxic.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to Eurasia, including central and western Europe. It forms a rosette of finely hairy leaves and bears delicate pink-white flowers from May to September.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is documented as edible; fresh leaves have reported nutritional values.

stories.summary: A parasitic broomrape native to the Mediterranean basin in Europe and North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, and Western Asia as far as Iran, bean broomrape commonly lives on faba beans. It lacks chlorophyll, and its stems are gathered and eaten in Apulia, southern Italy.
stories.edibilityNote: Its stems are gathered and eaten in Apulia, southern Italy.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to the Mediterranean region, garland daisy has aromatic, deeply divided leaves and small yellow flower heads. Its greens are eaten in many Asian cuisines, while the stronger-tasting stalk can also be used; overcooking may make them bitter.
stories.edibilityNote: Greens and stronger-tasting stalks are eaten, often simmered, steamed, stir-fried, deep-fried or added to soups; overcooking may make them bitter.

stories.summary: Evergreen pine native to the southeastern United States, from eastern Texas to Florida and north to southern New Jersey. It has yellowish- to grayish-green needles in bundles of three, sometimes twisted, and older trees develop reddish-brown bark with deep fissures and broad, scaly plates.
An annual flowering herb endemic to California. Its spring flowers are bowl-shaped and white with dark veins, dots and a purple spot at each lobe tip.

A herbaceous perennial native to temperate parts of western Asia, Africa and Europe, the sand crocus has thin, narrow, often curled leaves. Its usually solitary pink, pale purple or violet flower has pointed petals, darker veins and a yellow or golden throat, blooming from February onward or between March and May.

A corm-forming iris-family plant native to the Mediterranean region—southern Europe, northern Africa and the Middle East—and Sudan. It has long, slender leaves and small six-part blooms; most varieties flower purple or violet, but some are white or yellow.
A rhizomatous evergreen perennial native to the Juan Fernández Islands, central and southern Chile, and southern Argentina.

A herbaceous perennial native to central and northwestern Europe, marsh gladiolus has sword-shaped leaves and rosy-violet or magenta flowers. Despite its name, it does not grow in marshes, preferring moist, lime-rich meadows and forest clearings that alternate between wet and dry.

Corm-forming herbaceous perennial native to temperate northern Africa, western Asia and southern Europe, from the Mediterranean to the Caucasus. It is a vigorous plant with linear leaves and bright pink flowers in spring.
Plant species with no supplied native origin. It belongs to the family Iridaceae.

A herbaceous elder native to southern and central Europe and southwest Asia, dwarf elder forms large groups of upright stems from an extensive underground stem. It bears flat-topped clusters of white, occasionally pink, flowers and glossy black berries. All parts are toxic, especially the seeds, though cooking can neutralize the toxicity.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are toxic, especially the seeds, but cooking can neutralize the toxicity; explicit human food use is not described.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to western North America, silverleaf phacelia grows in habitats from scrub to forest, usually on sandy or rocky soil. Fine silvery hairs cover the plant, and its white or lavender flowers are urn- or bell-shaped.

Herbaceous perennial native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, where it is scarce within its range. It lacks chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise, instead drawing resources from fungal networks associated with trees; its fleshy, fungus-like growth may be yellow, red or yellowish-white.
