stories.summary: Small annual terrestrial carnivorous plant native to the Americas, Africa and Australia. It is almost pantropical and is described as the most widely distributed species in its genus. In mainland Portugal it is assessed as regionally extinct, with the last collection dating to 1967 despite later searches.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Utricularia subulata
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A shrub or small tree native to Cuba, sweet acacia is evergreen in most places but deciduous in part of its range. Paired thorns grow beside each leaf, and its flowers are used in perfume. Young leaves, flowers and seed pods can be eaten raw or cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves, flowers and seed pods are edible raw or cooked.

stories.summary: An annual or herbaceous perennial native to tropical South America, from Colombia and Brazil to Argentina and Chile. It has tall, slender square stems with long gaps between leaves, topped by tight clusters of fragrant lavender to rose-purple flowers from midsummer until the first autumn frost.

A perennial flowering herb native to Canada, the United States, Europe, the Azores and northern Africa. Its creeping stems root at their joints, and plants growing underwater become brownish and look different from those on land. It bears pink flowers with deeper pink lines and heart-shaped seed capsules.

An annual climbing vetch native to Turkey and Malta, and also native in Greece. It has purple-and-white flowers, branched leaf tendrils and hairy seed pods. It is not cultivated for human consumption, and its seeds contain high levels of vicine, which causes favism in susceptible people.
stories.edibilityNote: Not cultivated for human consumption; seeds contain high vicine levels that cause favism in susceptible people.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Vicia bithynica
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, the Azores and Madeira, and a member of the pea family.

Perennial flowering herb native to Europe and North America, with smaller native areas in northern Africa and western Asia. It grows in wetlands and along streams, often forming small summer colonies joined by rooting runners. Flowers are usually lilac, pale blue or pale violet, but sometimes nearly white.

A grape native to the United States, sand grape is naturally concentrated in the Ozark Hills of Missouri and Arkansas, with scattered populations farther east and southwest. It is a self-supporting bush of rocky riverbanks and streambanks and has been widely used to breed hybrid grapes and rootstocks.

A climbing flowering vine native to the Mediterranean, Central Europe and southwestern Asia. It attaches to supports with tendrils and bears clustered berries that may be green, red or purple in cultivated plants. Grapes are eaten fresh or dried, their leaves are used in many cuisines, and juice is fermented into wine or vinegar.
stories.edibilityNote: Grapes are eaten fresh or dried; leaves are used in cooking; juice is made into wine and vinegar.

stories.summary: A tall palm native to southern Baja California, Mexico, the Mexican fan palm is also found in Sonora. It is highly variable and now occurs in many regions around the world.

A perennial flowering herb native to South Africa's Cape Provinces, bulbil bugle-lily produces showy spikes of orange, reddish or purplish flowers. It often spreads through small cormlets formed along the flowering stem, sometimes creating dense colonies.

A tiny aquatic flowering plant native to Europe, Africa and parts of Asia, rootless duckweed is described as Earth’s smallest vascular plant. Its rootless, rounded green body floats on quiet water and buds into new plants. Long used as inexpensive food in Myanmar, Laos and Thailand, it is rich in protein and starch.
stories.edibilityNote: Long used as inexpensive food in Myanmar, Laos and Thailand; its green part is protein-rich and its dormant turions are starch-rich.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Wolffia arrhiza
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An aquatic plant of fresh and brackish water, recognisable by long, thread-like leaves that give it a stringy appearance. It has long, tendril-like roots and distinctive horn-shaped seeds.

A plant native to Asia, Russia, Ukraine and Romania, Syrian bean-caper has thin stems with sparse, fleshy, waxy leaflets. Its long taproot can produce new plants from fragments, and it forms colonies in dry, gravelly, salty or disturbed places.

A medium-sized tree whose native origin is not stated, found across Africa from Senegal to northern South Africa. It bears large hanging clusters of brown, sausage-shaped fruit and foul-smelling, bell-shaped flowers that open at night and are pollinated by bats. Its fibrous fruit contents are often considered inedible, but are locally eaten cooked; the Maasai also ferment the pulp into strong beer.
stories.edibilityNote: Fibrous fruit contents are often considered inedible but locally eaten cooked; Maasai ferment the fruit pulp to make strong beer.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native to mainland Africa, the African baobab has an exceptionally broad trunk that may comprise several stems fused around a hollow core. It can remain leafless for about eight months in the dry season, while its large white hanging flowers stay open and fertile for only one night.
stories.edibilityNote: Traditionally eaten in Africa: roots and fruit are edible; dry fruit pulp is soaked for juice, and young leaves are cooked.

stories.summary: A flowering plant found in South Africa, although the supplied information does not establish whether it is native there.

A flowering succulent perennial endemic to southeastern Southern Africa, including South Africa, Malawi, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. It forms large, sprawling clusters with spiny-edged leaf rosettes at branch tips and produces vivid red-orange flowers, often blooming in winter.
A free-floating flowering plant native to Europe and Asia. It has circular floating leaves and small white flowers, and can form dense invasive mats in North American waterways.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Hydrocharis morsus-ranae
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An evergreen shrub native to the southeastern United States, it has sword-like blue-green leaves edged with distinctive white threads and masses of hanging cream flowers in early summer. Its fruit can be cooked and eaten after the seeds are removed, while the large petals are eaten in salads.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits are cooked after seed removal; large flower petals are eaten in salads.

stories.summary: A bulbous orchid native to the Mediterranean Basin, the giant orchid flowers from January to April. Its bulb is edible when cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: The bulb is edible when cooked.

stories.summary: An orchid found in Europe, the Mediterranean and the Near East eastward to Iran.
Annual succulent herb whose native origin is not stated. It has simple, broad leaves and a self-supporting growth form.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to the southern and eastern United States. It often has several stems and produces clusters of dark-red tubular flowers in spring, followed by smooth light-brown fruit; its seeds are poisonous.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruits contain poisonous saponins, and the seeds are poisonous to humans.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to the eastern and central United States, violet woodsorrel grows from an underground bulb and has three heart-shaped leaflets and lavender-to-white spring flowers. All parts are edible and used in salads, but only moderate amounts are advised because its oxalic acid can be poisonous in large quantities.
stories.edibilityNote: Flowers, leaves, stems and bulbs are edible and traditionally eaten, including in salads, but large quantities may be poisonous because of oxalic acid.

stories.summary: Perennial ornamental plant native to the United States, Canada and northeastern Mexico. Its hairy, grass-like leaves surround shorter stems bearing yellow, star-shaped flowers, which open in the morning and usually wilt in hot afternoon sun; despite its appearance, it is not a grass.

A small palm native to the southeastern and south-central United States and northeastern Mexico, the dwarf palmetto grows in habitats ranging from swamps and floodplains to occasionally drier sites. Its rounded fans of leaves and unusual cold tolerance among North American palms make it distinctive, and older plants can become tree-like.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean from western Morocco and Portugal to Greece and western and southeastern Turkey, it bears reddish-purple spring flowers and red-to-black fruit. In Cyprus the fruit is baked into village bread, in Crete it flavours pomace brandy, and in the Northern Sporades the shoots are eaten as a vegetable.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit is baked into bread, used to flavour pomace brandy, or roasted for a coffee-like drink; shoots are eaten as a vegetable.

stories.summary: A non-photosynthetic orchid native to Europe and Russia, with sporadic presence in North Africa and parts of the Middle East. Usually beige-brown rather than green, it blends into woodland leaf litter and obtains its nutrition through soil fungi linked to tree roots.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Neottia nidus-avis
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A carnivorous plant native to the New World, the yellow pitcher plant ranges from southern Alabama through Florida and Georgia to the coastal plains of Virginia and the Carolinas. Its vibrant yellow rolled leaves form pitchers whose slippery surfaces, downward-pointing hairs and digestive fluid trap insects.
An annual flowering plant occurring in southern Europe. It has hairy stems and leaves, a stiff-haired capsule, and red flowers marked at the base with a black spot edged in yellow.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Glaucium corniculatum
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A deciduous flowering tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar. It has rounded, two-lobed leaves and conspicuous fragrant pink flowers, followed by long seed pods. Young leaves and flowers are edible; in Philippine cuisine, the citrusy, sour leaves flavor soups or are prepared as a pickle condiment, while flowers are used in pickles and curries.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves and flowers are edible; leaves flavor Philippine soups or pickles, and flowers are used in pickles and curries.

stories.summary: This herbaceous perennial orchid has no stated native origin; it is widespread in mountainous regions across much of Europe and is also found in Algeria, Morocco and western Siberia. Its leaves carry dark oval spots, while dense flower spikes range from pale pink to purple or white with darker streaks.
A shade-loving fern native to central and southern China, Korea, Japan, the Ryukyus, Taiwan and Vietnam. It commonly grows on old walls and has been introduced to many other parts of the world.

An aromatic deciduous shrub native to cool temperate Eurasia and North America, often forming dense colonies from root suckers. Its spring catkins usually occur as male and female flowers on separate plants, though plants may change sex between years. Dried leaves and fruits have seasoned food and beer, and leaves make tea; people who are or may be pregnant should not consume it.
stories.edibilityNote: Dried leaves and fruits are used as spice or beer flavouring, and dried leaves as tea; avoid during possible pregnancy.

stories.summary: A large, clump-forming herbaceous perennial native to the coastal Serra do Mar Mountains of southern Brazil. Its enormous leaves have spikes underneath and along their stalks, while tiny red-green flowers form conical branched clusters. Many European cultivated and feral plants labelled as this species are actually the hybrid Gunnera × cryptica.

Deciduous fern native to Europe, North Africa and West Asia, growing in woodland bogs and beside streams. Its stout underground stems can eventually form a woody, trunk-like base, while brown spore-bearing tips make some fronds resemble flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: In some places, young shoots called fiddleheads are eaten and said to taste like asparagus; the source marks this claim citation needed.

stories.summary: A tall wetland perennial native to Kazakhstan's Irtysh River valley, sweet flag has iris-like leaves with crimped edges and a fragrant smell when crushed. Young inner stems are eaten raw, while peeled roots have been boiled and simmered in syrup for candy; however, ingestion may be toxic, and food use is banned in the United States.
stories.edibilityNote: Young inner stems are eaten raw; peeled roots are boiled in syrup for candy. US food use is banned because ingestion may be toxic.

stories.summary: A tussock-forming, grass-like evergreen perennial native to Europe, the Atlas Mountains, Turkey, Iran and Central Asia. It has bright-gold foliage with green edges and grows in wetlands such as marshes, fens and shallow-water margins.

A tall perennial of wetlands and river margins, forming colonies with hairy, often three-lobed leaves. Its large flowers range from white through pink to deep red, usually with a dark maroon centre, and attract bees.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaf buds, young leaves, flowers, seeds and roots are documented as edible; immature seed pods can be prepared like okra.

stories.summary: A large deciduous shrub native to temperate eastern Asia, including China, Mongolia, southeastern Siberia, Korea and, rarely, central and northern Honshū in Japan. Its paired flowers change from white to yellow or pale orange, and children sometimes suck their sweet nectar, but its red to black berries are mildly poisonous and should not be eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Children sometimes suck sweet nectar from the flowers; the berries are mildly poisonous to humans and should not be eaten.

stories.summary: Clubmoss with a pan-tropical distribution and possible native status in the Azores. It favors bogs and is described as the largest clubmoss, with long rhizomes and tall leafy uprights.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Palhinhaea cernua
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native throughout eastern and central North America, late figwort grows in dry woods. Its rounded flowers are deep reddish-purple inside, greenish to brown outside, and resemble a horse’s mouth with an overbite; hummingbirds commonly visit them in late summer.

Herbaceous perennial native to the Balkans through Greece, Crete and the Aegean Islands, and southwestern Anatolia. Its large purple floral structure smells like rotting meat and attracts fly pollinators, while its broad divided leaves may have cream-flecked veins.

A perennial flowering plant native to the western and central Alps, rare in much of its Swiss, Austrian and Italian range but commoner in the French Maritime Alps. Its nodding light-blue to blue-purple flowers have straight or slightly curved nectar spurs, unlike the hooked spurs often seen on hybrids sold under this name.

An evergreen succulent perennial native to southeastern Europe and Asia Minor. Its sprawling stems carry fleshy blue-green leaves, while inconspicuous spring flowers are surrounded by bright yellow bracts. Ingestion causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, and its milky sap can severely irritate skin and eyes.
stories.edibilityNote: Ingestion causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea; the milky sap can also severely irritate skin and eyes.

stories.summary: Fern native to eastern North America and across Eurasia. It grows in wet habitats such as swamps, bogs, marshes and streambanks, with fertile fronds bearing spore clusters underneath.

An aquatic fern native across parts of Europe and Asia, from central and southern Europe to Vietnam. Its four-part leaves resemble four-leaf clover and may float in deep water or stand upright in shallow water or on land. In mainland Portugal it underwent severe decline during the last century and was assessed as Critically Endangered.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant has reportedly been used as food in some places for more than 3,000 years.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Marsilea quadrifolia
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: Evergreen fern native to the Balearics, Corsica, Crete, Sardinia and Scilly, with a wider range across Europe, Asia and North Africa. Pale reddish-brown scales cover the frond undersides, which become visible when the leaves roll up in summer. It can withstand drying and recover when rewetted.

A fern found mainly around the Mediterranean Basin and eastern Atlantic, with isolated records as far north as Ireland and Poland. It is difficult to distinguish from black spleenwort; leaflet shape is unreliable, while spore size viewed under a microscope is more consistent.
A deciduous tree or densely branched shrub native to the Mediterranean region. Its small, glossy, three-lobed leaves have smooth edges and fall unusually late in autumn.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean Basin, mastic has a strong resinous smell and leathery, deep-green leaves. Its aromatic resin is harvested as a spice and chewing gum, while its tart, raisin-like fruit is edible but not commonly eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is edible but uncommon as food; the aromatic resin is used as a spice, flavouring and chewing gum.

stories.summary: A flowering plant endemic to the Mediterranean region, shrubby hare's-ear is an evergreen shrub of sunny hills, walls and rocky places. It has simple blue-green leaves and clusters of tiny yellow flowers that bloom from June to September.

stories.edibilityNote: Listed as edible; no plant part or preparation is specified.

stories.summary: A flowering plant whose two listed subspecies are native to mainland Portugal.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it belongs to the carrot family.

A perennial herb of unstated native origin, Oenanthe globulosa grows in temporarily flooded depressions with muddy, clay-rich soils. In mainland Portugal, a 2020 assessment knew only a few populations concentrated around Sintra and classified it as Vulnerable amid continuing habitat decline.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Oenanthe globulosa
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A flowering perennial native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia, hemlock water-dropwort grows in damp grassland, wet woodland and along waterways. It has hollow, grooved stems, fleshy tubers that release yellowish oily fluid when cut, and leaves that smell deceptively like parsley or celery. All parts are extremely toxic.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are extremely toxic; roots mistaken for parsnips have caused severe and sometimes fatal human poisoning.

stories.summary: A tall perennial herb of the Mediterranean coast, it occurs from Spain and Morocco to Lebanon, Syria, Israel, Cyprus and Turkey. It has alternate leaves and yellow, unisexual flowers in rounded clusters, and grows in scrubland and rocky areas.

An evergreen flowering subshrub native to Western Europe, including the Iberian and Italian peninsulas, France and Sardinia, intermediate periwinkle forms broad mats. Its whitish-blue flowers bloom from late winter to early spring.

A perennial plant native to central and southern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, the southern daisy has creeping underground stems. Its apparent flower is actually a cluster of many tiny flowers, with white outer florets surrounding yellow tubular ones.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.
A flowering plant in the daisy family, Pulicaria odora grows in pine woods, bushy places and sandy ground. Its leaves are cooked and may then be edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves may be edible after cooking.

stories.summary: A plant with no native origin stated in the supplied information, Mediterranean phagnalon can grow up to 50 centimetres high.
Shrub native to Mediterranean-basin countries in Europe, North Africa and Western Asia, as well as Iran, Iraq, the Arabian Peninsula and the Canary Islands. It has simple broad leaves and dry fruit.

A compact evergreen shrub native to southwestern Europe. It has narrow, aromatic green leaves and tight yellow flower heads in summer. The leaves are used in Mediterranean dishes and cocktails for an olive-like flavour.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves add an olive-like flavour to Mediterranean dishes and cocktails.

stories.summary: An annual or perennial shrub depending on locale, Helichrysum stoechas grows in dry, rocky and sandy places; its native origin is not stated. It has greyish-green leaves and small, round yellow flowers that may appear in spring or in July and August. Its leaves and flowers have an intense fragrance used in perfumery and aromatherapy.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, Echinops strigosus belongs to the daisy family.
A wild thistle native to Portugal, Spain, Morocco, Algeria and Gran Canaria. It is used locally to curdle milk in traditional sheep's and goat's cheesemaking.
stories.edibilityNote: Used locally as a coagulant in artisanal sheep's and goat's cheesemaking.

stories.summary: A highly branching perennial of unstated native origin, it is common throughout the Mediterranean Basin. Its narrow toothed leaves are sticky, hairy and unpleasant-smelling, while a single plant can carry many yellow flower heads.

An annual flowering plant found across the Mediterranean Basin and western Europe, although its native range is not explicitly identified. It has white petals around a yellow-orange centre and blooms during rainy seasons. Its whole flowers are crushed for essential oil, whose composition varies with where it grows.
A Centaurea species of unstated native origin, it is found in southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa.
Low-growing annual herb native to the Mediterranean region. It has orange-yellow flowers from April to June and colonizes dry coastal areas.
A herb with subspecies recorded from southern Europe, North Africa, the Canary Islands, Madeira and Turkey. It has broad leaves and usually yellow or orange, many-petalled flowers.

An evergreen perennial native to the Mediterranean region, with aromatic silvery-white leaves and sprays of yellow, daisy-like flowers. In Maghrebi mint tea, it is used during winter as a bitter substitute for or supplement to spearmint.
stories.edibilityNote: Used in Maghrebi mint tea during winter as a bitter substitute for or supplement to spearmint.

stories.summary: A daisy-family plant native across parts of North Africa, Macaronesia, southwestern Europe and southeastern Europe.
A hardy perennial flowering plant native to southern Europe and Morocco. It has narrow, serrated leaves and clusters of small flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves may be chopped and eaten raw as a herb or added to soups and stews.

stories.summary: A flowering plant with documented native origins at subspecies level: subsp. microcarpa is endemic to mainland Portugal, while subsp. procumbens is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula.
A hardy flowering perennial native to Portugal, Morocco, Algeria and Libya. It forms a sprawling mass of red flowers throughout summer and readily self-seeds.
An annual bellflower herb, it is self-supporting and can grow to 11 centimetres tall.
Flowering plant native to the Mediterranean region, adapted to clay and marl soils.
A flowering plant native to Portugal and Spain, the Lusitanian bellflower is the namesake of a group of closely related species.

A biennial herb found across western Asia, northern Africa and most of Europe, rampion has light blue or violet bell-shaped flowers and a thick, turnip-like root. It was once widely grown in Europe for leaves eaten like spinach and an edible root used like a radish.
stories.edibilityNote: Historically in Europe, its leaves were eaten like spinach and its parsnip-like root like a radish; the thick root is explicitly edible.

stories.summary: A climbing flowering plant native to the Mediterranean region of southern Europe and northern Africa. It can grow to 2.5 metres or more and is sometimes cultivated as a garden plant beyond its native range.

An evergreen shrub, rarely a small tree, native to Mediterranean Europe and North Africa. Its white or pale pink flowers emerge from reddish-pink buds in winter, followed by dark blue-black fruit with an unusual metallic blue colour.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.
A plant native to Lebanon and surrounding Mediterranean areas.

A fodder shrub widespread through the Mediterranean Basin, North and East Africa, and the Arabian Peninsula, Mediterranean saltbush has small gray leaves. Its leaves are edible, and the plant tolerates severe drought and highly alkaline or saline soils.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are edible and were reportedly gathered and eaten by poor returnees from Babylonian exile around 352 BCE.

stories.summary: A shrub native to south-western Europe and western North Africa. It has wavy grey-green, hairy leaves and pink-to-purple flowers with five petals.
A flowering shrub native to southwestern Europe and western North Africa, grey-leaved cistus bears pink to purple flowers. Dense short hairs give its three-veined leaves a greyish-white appearance.
An endangered ornamental plant whose native origin is not stated.

A shrubby flowering plant native to Europe and Africa, silver broom occurs across the western and central Mediterranean, including parts of southern Europe, the Balkans and northwestern Africa. It has also been introduced to Germany.

A medicinal flowering plant native to Europe, northern Africa and Western Asia. It bears spherical flower heads, usually with yellow petals, though var. coccinea has red petals, and favors dry grassland and rocky, lime-rich ground.

A bush native to the western Iberian Peninsula and northwestern Maghreb, Erica umbellata has clusters of three to six flowers at the tips of its stems. Its flowers are intensely pink or purple, but occasionally white.

An evergreen flowering shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean Basin and parts of East Africa. It has needle-like leaves and many small, honey-scented white flowers, while its exceptionally hard, heat-resistant wood is used for smoking pipes.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean Basin and Western Europe. Its rough red berries are edible and sweet when reddish, and they ripen in autumn alongside the next crop of white, bell-shaped flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: Red berries are edible and sweet when reddish; eaten fresh but more often made into jam, marmalade, yogurt, brandy and other alcoholic drinks.

stories.summary: A climbing herb native across southern and central Europe, northwest Africa and western Asia, it has anticlockwise-twining stems, heart-shaped leaves and bright red berries. Most of the plant, including its tuber, is poisonous, but young shoots are reportedly harvested while their saponin content is low and eaten as a vegetable.
stories.edibilityNote: Most parts, including tubers, are poisonous; young shoots are reportedly harvested while saponin is low and eaten as a vegetable.

stories.summary: A shrub of unspecified native origin, it has a self-supporting form, simple broad leaves and dry fruit.

Pine native to the Mediterranean region, with an outlying population in the eastern Mediterranean. It has paired, slender yellowish-green needles and narrow cones that mature glossy red-brown, then open gradually over several years or faster when exposed to heat.
stories.edibilityNote: Its pine nuts are used in Tunisian and Maltese desserts, while its resin flavours Greek retsina wine.

stories.summary: A pine native to southern Atlantic Europe and parts of the western Mediterranean, maritime pine has the longest and most robust needles among European pines. Its large cones open slowly over several years or after heating by a forest fire, releasing winged seeds.

Evergreen shrub endemic to Portugal. It forms compact, densely branched cushions with a bright green exterior, dry brown stems and sharp spines, and often grows on limestone near the central-west coast.
A gorse native to France, the Iberian Peninsula and parts of the Maghreb.
A flowering perennial occurring in southern temperate Europe and Siberia; it is not native to Ireland. It forms an upright bush with wiry, usually spiny stems and deep pink-and-white flowers.
Flowering bush native to the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa.

A perennial flowering plant native to parts of Africa, Europe and Asia, it scrambles over nearby vegetation using tendrils. It has winged, floppy stems, pairs of narrow leaflets, pinkish-red flowers and seed-filled pods.
A flowering legume native to the Mediterranean. Its seeds are cultivated on Santorini and cooked into fava santorinis, a purée typically served with onion, olive oil and lemon juice.
stories.edibilityNote: The cooked seeds are made into the Greek purée fava santorinis.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it was described in a 1913 account as a low, hairy annual of dry hills in Estremadura, coastal Alentejo and the Algarve. That account noted purplish flowers in dense heads and pods covered with bristle-bearing scales.

Perennial flowering legume native to the southeastern United States, especially sunny, dry habitats. Its wiry, hairy stems bear leaves of three leaflets and yellow-orange flowers during summer and fall.

Leguminous tree native to East Africa, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and southern Africa. Its long, woody seed capsules contain bright red and black seeds, which are used decoratively and as fish poison.

An aquatic perennial native from East Asia through northern Indochina to central and northern India, with isolated Caspian locations. Its flowers can regulate their temperature, and seeds have germinated after about 1,300 years. Rhizomes and seeds are widely eaten; petals, leaves and rhizomes should be cooked because eating them raw risks parasite transmission.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are edible; petals, leaves and rhizomes are recommended cooked because raw consumption risks parasite transmission.

stories.summary: Flowering plant native to continental Portugal.

Poisonous evergreen shrub native to the northern and western Mediterranean region. It has dense, narrow dark-green leaves, fragrant white flowers and red autumn fruits; all parts are considered highly poisonous if consumed.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are considered highly poisonous when consumed.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to Israel, with a wider Irano-Turanian and Mediterranean distribution. It is covered in star-shaped hairs that feel unpleasant, and a touched or damaged flower abruptly sheds its entire corolla after about 30 seconds.
An annual herb with simple leaves.

A herbaceous perennial with no native origin specified, wild madder has woody, square climbing stems and glossy evergreen leaves arranged in whorls. Its small, pale green-yellow flowers appear from April to June, followed by fleshy berries that turn black when ripe.
Small shrub native to the Mediterranean and now established in various other parts of the world.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.
A flowering plant native to continental Portugal, Geum sylvaticum belongs to the rose family.

An evergreen shrub from Mediterranean-climate scrub between Gran Canaria, Morocco and Portugal and the Levant, Mediterranean buckthorn has glossy, leathery leaves and small, fragrant yellow-green flowers. Its red-brown fruits darken to black when ripe.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.

Flowering plant native to the western Mediterranean region, including mainland Portugal. Populations may have yellow or white flowers, and in Portugal it occurs in scrub clearings and woodland edges, particularly from the central coast and west to the southern Algarve.
A perennial grass native to Europe, Africa, western Asia and the Arabian Peninsula. It is self-supporting, with simple broad leaves and dry fruit.

Terrestrial orchid native around the Mediterranean and Middle East, from Morocco and Portugal to Hungary and Iran. It grows from underground tubers and flowers between March and June in its native habitats. Its brown, velvety lip has three rolled lobes and a complex blue-to-violet marking.
An annual herb of unstated native origin, with a self-supporting form and simple, broad leaves. Its flowers are visited by several insects, including brown argus butterflies.
Evergreen shrub native to the western and central Mediterranean. It has narrow, leathery dark-green leaves and scented creamy-white flowers, followed by purplish-black berries.
Annual flowering herb native to northern Africa south to Tanzania, southern Europe and southwestern Asia. It is locally naturalised elsewhere, including Great Britain.

A terrestrial orchid occurring throughout the Mediterranean, it has a glossy, iridescent purple-blue patch surrounded by reddish-brown velvety hairs. Its flowers are pollinated exclusively by the wasp Dasyscolia ciliata.
Tree native to the Mediterranean Basin, from Morocco and Portugal east to the Levant. It is commonly known as the green olive tree or mock privet.
Deciduous tree native to Central and Southern Europe, northwest Africa and southwest Asia. Its pale brown buds distinguish it from the black-budded common ash, while its leaflets are notably slender.
A flowering plant native to the western Mediterranean. Among mallows in its genus, it is unique for the two-lobed structure just beneath each flower.
A perennial herb native to the Mediterranean Basin, West Asia and Macaronesia. It is a small, self-supporting plant with simple broad leaves and an association with freshwater habitats.
Small, self-supporting annual herb native to southern Europe, western Asia, North Africa, the Horn of Africa and some oceanic islands, including Madeira, the Canary Islands and Socotra.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.

An erect subshrub endemic to Portugal, particularly the southwest. Its graceful, four-sided stems bear cream or white flowers with purple stamens, and it inhabits sandy acidic soils, especially stabilized dunes.

An edible wild garlic native to the Mediterranean and nearby areas from Portugal and Morocco to Turkey and Palestine, rosy garlic has loose, fragrant pinkish-to-lilac flowers. Its bulb has a powerful smell and flavour.
stories.edibilityNote: Documented as edible; the bulb is specifically described as having a powerful smell and flavour.

stories.summary: A flowering plant with a mainland-Portuguese endemic subspecies and an Iberian-endemic subspecies. The mainland-Portuguese subspecies is legally protected, while the Iberian-endemic subspecies is not.
A perennial herb endemic to the central Iberian Peninsula in Spain and Portugal, it has white flowers. Oil from the flowers is used in some pain-relieving lotions.

Perennial evergreen flowering vine found across parts of Africa, Mediterranean Europe and Asia. It has flexible thorny stems, leathery heart-shaped leaves with spiny edges, fragrant yellowish or greenish flowers, and berries that turn from red to black but are unpalatable to humans.
stories.edibilityNote: The berries are described as insipid and unpalatable to humans, but not explicitly inedible.

stories.summary: An evergreen shrub native to Eurasia and parts of northern Africa, butcher's-broom has flat, stiff shoots that resemble spine-tipped leaves. Small greenish flowers appear singly at their centres in spring, followed on female plants by red berries.
stories.edibilityNote: The berries caused reported poisonings, mostly in children, including 107 cases in 1995–2007 and four acute cases in Lombardy in 2010–2011.

stories.summary: A bulb-forming herbaceous perennial found in the Mediterranean Basin, Armenia and northwestern Iran. It produces a pyramidal cluster of star-shaped, milky-white flowers, each marked by a pale green central vein. It grows in fields, dry grassland, waste ground and rocky terrain.

A perennial herb native to the Mediterranean region of southern Europe, northern Africa and the Middle East. Its highly branched stem and small fruits help distinguish it from similar asphodels, while its numerous white flowers have a central brown streak.
A flowering plant native to the western and central Mediterranean, Asparagus albus occurs in coastal shrubland and disturbed places.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and recorded in mainland Portugal.
A flowering herb native to the Iberian Peninsula and northern Morocco. It has thin leaves and white flowers, and wild plants in Spain and Portugal are gathered for use fresh or dried as a food herb.
stories.edibilityNote: Wild plants are collected in Spain and Portugal and used fresh or dried as a food herb.

stories.summary: An annual herb, Italian woundwort has a self-supporting growth form, and its flowers are visited by the Green-striped White butterfly.

A small plant, sometimes a shrub, native to southern Mediterranean regions including Iberia, Sicily, northwestern Africa and the Canary Islands. It has grey woolly stems, fernlike silver-green leaves and dark blue or violet flowers held above the foliage; its aromatic leaves smell more like oregano than other lavenders.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and present in mainland Portugal.

A tall perennial herb native to the British Isles, Mediterranean Southern Europe, North Africa, the Near East and the Caucasus. It has hairy stems and soft purple-to-violet summer flowers. This aromatic sage flavours food and tea, and its flowers can be added to salads.
stories.edibilityNote: Used as a food flavouring and tea; flowers can be added to salads.

stories.summary: Flowering plant of unstated native origin, found in the western Mediterranean. It belongs to the St John’s-wort family.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira and introduced in the Azores.
A flowering plant native to southern Europe and the Mediterranean region.

Evergreen oak shrub or tree native to the Mediterranean region and North African Maghreb, from Portugal and Morocco east to Cyprus, Anatolia and the Levant. It is usually a low shrub and historically hosted kermes scale insects used to make crimson dye.

A spreading shrub oak native to Portugal, western Andalusia and rarely Galicia in Spain, and Morocco. It usually lies low and spreads by runners. Its insect-induced galls are harvested commercially for dyeing.

An evergreen oak native to the western Mediterranean, with most of its population in the Iberian Peninsula and smaller populations in Northwest Africa. It has a dense, rounded crown and small, leathery leaves. Humans have eaten its acorns since Neolithic times, including toasted and ground as flour for soups or breads in southern Iberia.
stories.edibilityNote: Acorns are eaten; in Neolithic southern Iberia they were gently toasted, ground into flour, and used in soups or breads.

stories.summary: An annual, self-supporting herb with broad leaves, Ononis mitissima is notably tiny, reaching only about five centimetres tall.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, Scorpiurus vermiculatus occurs in fields, fallow ground and grassland. A 1913 description records hairy upright or rising stems and thick pods coiled in one plane, with stalked, broadened warts covering their backs.
A herbaceous flowering perennial found across most of southern and central Europe and North Africa. It has broad simple leaves, square stems and small two-lipped flowers in loose clusters.

A shrub of the Mediterranean region, found in southern Europe and northern Africa, Mediterranean buckthorn has a tangled, many-branched form with thorn-tipped young stems. Its inconspicuous greenish-yellow flowers appear in winter, and its yellowish fruits ripen black.
stories.edibilityNote: The berries are very bitter and purgative, and are toxic to humans in large quantities.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to the Mediterranean Basin. Its variable leaves and flowers accompany red blooms, usually appearing from December to May.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is edible, but its acid-lemon-flavoured leaves contain high oxalic acid levels that may be dangerous in large amounts.

stories.summary: A deciduous or semi-evergreen oak native to the western Mediterranean region of the Iberian Peninsula, the Portuguese oak can live for up to 600 years. Its leaves usually fall in mid-to-late winter, while its oblong acorns mature within six months.
A low-growing woody flowering plant native to Spain and mainland Portugal. It favours scrubland and flowers from November to May.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.
Flowering plant whose subspecies Nepeta tuberosa subsp. tuberosa is native to mainland Portugal. It belongs to the mint family.

A bushy evergreen shrub native to Iberia, Morocco and western Turkey. Its narrow aromatic grey-green leaves contrast with dense heads of small dark-purple flowers, topped by large purple bracts resembling butterfly petals.
A flowering plant whose subspecies Erophaca baetica subsp. baetica is native to mainland Portugal.

A flowering tree or shrub native to China and Japan, Japanese camellia grows naturally in forests. Its leathery dark-green leaves accompany rose or white wild flowers, while thousands of ornamental cultivars offer many flower colours and forms. Its processed leaves can be made into aromatic tea and contain caffeine and catechins.
stories.edibilityNote: Processed leaves are used to make aromatic tea and contain caffeine and catechins.

stories.summary: Evergreen shrub native to the Appalachians of eastern North America, from Alabama to coastal Nova Scotia. It keeps waxy, deep-green leaves for up to eight years and bears showy white, pink or pale-purple flowers, mainly in June. In the southern Appalachians it often dominates the forest understory, forming dense thickets called “laurel slicks” or “laurel hells.”
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves may be poisonous, but no human food use or ingestion context is given.

stories.summary: Herbaceous perennial native to the Mediterranean region, although its exact natural range is uncertain after 2,000 years of cultivation. Its fringed flowers have a spicy, clove-like fragrance; wild flowers are bright pinkish-purple, while cultivars come in many colours.
stories.edibilityNote: Its fragrance was historically used in vinegar, beer, wine, sauces and salads.

stories.summary: A large deciduous shrub or small tree native to the southern Balkan Peninsula, common lilac bears dense clusters of sweet-smelling flowers, usually lilac to mauve but occasionally white. Its flowers are edible and used to flavour honey, sugar, food and other sweets.
stories.edibilityNote: The flowers are used to flavour honey, sugar, food and other sweets.

stories.summary: A large evergreen flowering tree native to the southeastern United States coastal plain, from Virginia to central Florida and west to eastern Texas. It has stiff, dark-green leaves and large, waxy white flowers with a strong lemon-citronella fragrance.

A herbaceous perennial native across much of western, southern and central Europe, the Caucasus and eastward to central Asia, alpine forget-me-not has a highly restricted British presence. There it occurs at two sites: limestone grassland in the North Pennines and high ground around Ben Lawers.

A perennial orchid native to southwestern Eurasia, from western Europe through the Mediterranean to Iran. Its compact flower head has a distinctive pyramidal shape, with pink to purple, rarely white, flowers and a scent described as foxy.
A small palm native to North America. Its extracts are used medicinally, including traditional use for urinary and prostate conditions.

An agave found only in the Chihuahuan Desert, lechuguilla often spreads through underground offshoots into large colonies. It flowers once, then dies, and has tough, rigid leaves tipped with points sharp enough to penetrate clothing or leather.
stories.edibilityNote: In Mexico, salt- and mineral-rich water stored in flowering stalks is sold as a sports drink.

stories.summary: A palm native to the Philippines, the areca palm grows straight with numerous crowded leaflets. Its nuts are chewed with slaked lime and betel leaves for stimulant and narcotic effects, but they are addictive and linked directly to oral cancers.

A deciduous flowering shrub native to woodlands of the southeastern United States, oakleaf hydrangea has large lobed leaves with silvery-white undersides that turn red, bronze and purple in autumn. Its upright, cone-shaped flower clusters open white and age to pink or brown, depending on the cultivar or seedling.

A critically endangered conifer native to southern Brazil and also naturally found in northeastern Argentina, Paraguay and northern Uruguay. It has thick, triangular leaves with razor-sharp edges, and large cones containing many edible, nut-like seeds that are extensively harvested in southern Brazil.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds are edible, widely harvested in southern Brazil and eaten as a winter snack, including boiled.

stories.summary: An Australian rainforest tree naturally distributed from northeastern New South Wales to tropical Queensland. Its bright red flowers form circular, wheel-like clusters, while its boat-shaped fruits hold many thin seeds.

Perennial herb native to eastern Australia, with long, strap-like leaves arising from underground stems. Its leaf tip has three prominent points, with the side points as long as or longer than the middle one. Seeds may be ground into flour, while the flowers and leaf bases are also edible.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds may be ground into flour for Indigenous Australian damper; flowers and leaf bases are also eaten, with leaf bases chewed for water.

stories.summary: A woody climber native to Australia, Malesia and the southwestern Pacific region. Its juvenile and mature leaves differ, and it bears white or cream tubular flowers with purple markings followed by capsules containing winged seeds.

Fruit tree native to the eastern and central United States. Its deeply plated bark is distinctive, and its orange fruit is astringent when unripe but sweet when ripe; ripe fruit may be eaten raw, usually after softening, or cooked or dried.
stories.edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten raw, usually after softening, or cooked, dried, fermented or made into desserts, jam, molasses and candy.

stories.summary: Deciduous tree native to China, the Japanese persimmon has broad, stiff leaves and sweet, slightly tangy fruit. Astringent varieties are edible only when soft-ripe, while non-astringent varieties such as ‘Fuyu’ can be eaten firm.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten ripe or dried; astringent varieties require soft ripening, while non-astringent varieties may be eaten firm.

stories.summary: A rock-growing orchid endemic to eastern Australia. It usually grows on rocks, sometimes forming large colonies, and bears spikes of usually pink flowers from late winter to spring, though timing varies with climate.

A large plant widespread in eastern Australia, the Queensland grasstree can develop a tall, many-branched trunk and grey or bluish-green leaves. Ngunnawal people make a sweet drink by soaking its flower spike and eat the growing leaf-stem portion and white leaf bases.
stories.edibilityNote: Ngunnawal people soak the flower spike for a sweet drink and eat the growing leaf-stem portion and white leaf bases.

stories.summary: Shrub or tree endemic to eastern Australia, including Lord Howe Island. It has thin bark, usually white flowers borne singly on short side shoots, and fruit that can remain on the plant for a few years.

Palm tree endemic to the east coast of Queensland and New South Wales, Australia. Its single trunk has a swollen, regularly scarred base, while its long fronds often twist so their outer leaflets stand nearly vertical. Ripe fruits are bright red and contain one seed.

A large shrub or small tree native to the eastern coast of tropical South America, extending south to Uruguay and parts of Paraguay and Argentina. Its ribbed fruit changes from green through orange and scarlet to maroon; the edible fruit ranges from tart to sweet with cultivar and ripeness and is used mainly in jams and jellies.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten and used in jams and jellies; taste varies from tart to sweet with cultivar and ripeness.

stories.summary: A shrub native to eastern Asia—northeastern China, Japan, Korea and southeastern Siberia—the rugosa rose naturally grows along sandy coasts. It forms dense, prickly thickets and has deeply wrinkled leaves with scented flowers ranging from dark pink to white. Its hips are edible raw or prepared as jam, syrup or tea.
stories.edibilityNote: The hips can be eaten raw or made into jams, syrups or tea.

stories.summary: A deciduous succulent endemic to southern Madagascar, it grows as a spiny shrub or tree with thick, water-storing stems. Its leaves fall during the long dry season, and young plants begin as tangled stems before developing a strong central trunk.

A perennial herbaceous orchid widespread across central and southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. Its flower has a hairy, variably patterned petal resembling a bee’s abdomen; northern populations are almost exclusively self-pollinating, while a solitary bee pollinates it in the Mediterranean region.
stories.edibilityNote: Root tubers were ground into salep in the Ottoman Empire; salep remains used in traditional dishes in Turkey and across the Middle East.

stories.summary: A liverwort, it was typically absent from urban sites in one tropical Ecuador study despite occurring at a nearby pristine site. The study suggested sensitivity to human effects such as wastewater and heavy-metal pollution.

A sprawling annual weed whose native origin is not stated, red nightshade occurs in Europe, western Asia and northern Africa and is naturalized in Australia and North America. It is hairy, with white or purple-tinged flowers followed by dull red or orange-yellow berries, depending on the subspecies.

A medium-sized deciduous tree native across Europe and temperate Asia and to northern Morocco, silver birch is mainly mountainous in the southern parts of its range. It has white, peeling bark and slender, often drooping twigs, while its roughly triangular leaves turn yellow in autumn.
stories.edibilityNote: In spring, tapped sap may be drunk fresh, concentrated like maple syrup, or fermented into wine.

stories.summary: A flowering bromeliad indigenous to warmer parts of the Americas, from the southern United States to northern Argentina and Chile. It forms rounded clumps on trees, fences and wires, using hosts mainly for support rather than nourishment.
stories.edibilityNote: The Pima of Mexico occasionally eat its flowers for their high sugar content.

stories.summary: An Arctic–alpine fern native to Europe and parts of Asia. It produces separate sterile and fertile fronds and colonises acidic rocky slopes, often where snow remains late in the year.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Cryptogramma crispa
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An evergreen trailing rock-rose native to most of Europe. Its bright yellow, saucer-shaped flowers have touch-sensitive orange stamens, while garden varieties range from white to deep red. Individual blooms are short-lived, but flowers appear in abundance through summer.
Annual flowering herb native to Great Britain, Iceland, central Europe and Western Asia. It blooms in July and August and is a known host of flax rust.

A perennial flowering herb whose native origin is not specified, wild basil has square, upright, hairy stems and pink, violet or purple two-lipped flowers. Its leaves are used to flavour food and make herbal tea.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are used as an aromatic herb in food dishes and to make herbal tea.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree endemic to woodlands of the southeastern and south-central United States, winged elm grows slowly and tolerates many soils. Broad, thin corky wings develop along older branchlets, and the leaves turn bright yellow in autumn.

A large deciduous tree native to the Balkans, horse-chestnut has fallen-leaf scars shaped like horseshoes with seven “nails.” Its spring flowers are usually white with yellow-to-pink markings, followed by green spiky fruits containing glossy brown conkers.
stories.edibilityNote: Raw seeds, leaves, bark and flowers are toxic and should not be eaten; young, fresh seeds can cause sickness.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to the Americas east of the Rocky Mountains and south to Bolivia. It bears large clusters of white summer flowers and drooping clusters of dark purple-black fruit; only ripe berries cooked with their seeds removed are suitable for food.
stories.edibilityNote: Only ripe berries should be cooked and have their seeds removed; traditional jams, jellies and syrups use cooked, strained fruit.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial of unstated native origin, lady's bedstraw is widespread across most of Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia. In medieval Europe its dried plants stuffed mattresses and its flowers were used in cheese making; in Denmark, it is traditionally infused into spirits.
stories.edibilityNote: In Denmark it is traditionally infused into spirits; its flowers were used in medieval European cheese making.

stories.summary: Annual herb of unstated native origin, found on Mediterranean scrubland hills and beneath stonework or concrete structures. It has alternate leaves that may be divided two or more times.
A flowering plant of unstated native origin, introduced in the Azores.

A perennial flowering herb native to Europe and Asia, greater knapweed bears purple, thistle-like flower heads crowned by ragged purple-pink outer parts. Its deeply divided leaves form a clump at the base, and its flowers attract bees and many butterflies.

A perennial flowering herb native across temperate Eurasia from Britain to Japan. Its violet-blue or purplish-blue bell-shaped flowers grow in tight clusters and bloom from June to September. Garden varieties also include white, pink and blue forms.

Epiphytic fern native to tropical southeastern Asia, eastern Australia, Hawaii, Polynesia, Christmas Island, India and eastern Africa. Its large, banana-like fronds form a nest that collects water and decaying plant matter. Sprouts are eaten in Taiwan, while young fronds are eaten in Polynesia, often cooked with coconut cream.
stories.edibilityNote: Sprouts are stir-fried or boiled in Taiwan; young fronds are eaten in Polynesia, often cooked with coconut cream.

stories.summary: A slow-growing tree fern native to Hawaii, hāpu‘u pulu produces fiddleheads that supply pulu, a material used as mulch or padding. Women also used pulu as a menstrual absorbent.

A tropical flowering tree native to tropical Asia and Australia. It has glossy leaves, bright pink or red flower clusters and bell-shaped fruit that ripens red, pink or white-streaked. The ripe fruit is eaten raw despite its bland flavor; flowers are eaten in Indonesian salads, and the skin is cooked into syrup in Guyana.
stories.edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten raw; Indonesians eat the flowers in salads, and in Guyana the fruit skin is cooked into syrup.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to south Texas, Mexico, Belize, Venezuela and the Caribbean. It bears yellow flower heads throughout the year and commonly grows as a weed in lawns, roadsides and paths.

A tall perennial flowering plant native to North Africa, most of Europe and parts of Asia. Its robust stems and narrow leaves are densely hairy, while the large purple-pink flowers have four notched petals.

An evergreen shrub native to Mexico and naturalized in Florida. Its white flowers emerge from chains of red or salmon-pink bracts resembling shrimps, and its long blooming periods attract hummingbirds and butterflies.

A perennial yam vine native to Africa, Asia and northern Australia, air potato forms bulbils on its stems and potato-like tubers underground. Its twining stems always twist counterclockwise around supports.
stories.edibilityNote: Some varieties have edible tubers; boiling removes their bitterness. Tiwi people ritually cook and eat the tubers during the kulama ceremony.

stories.summary: A low, spreading deciduous shrub native to central and eastern Canada and the north-central and eastern United States, lowbush blueberry has glossy blue-green leaves that turn red in autumn. Its white or pink bell-shaped flowers produce small, sweet, dark blue to black berries.
stories.edibilityNote: Wild blueberries are used in Maine’s state dessert, blueberry pie.

stories.summary: A biennial flowering plant native to central and eastern North America. It has square, narrowly winged stems and fragrant pink, occasionally white, flowers with yellow markings that form a central star.

Perennial sunflower native to North America, including south-central Canada, the eastern and central United States, and northeastern Mexico. Its stems and leaves have stiff hairs, and it spreads through underground rhizomes in sunny open forests and forest edges.

An evergreen shrub native to southern Argentina and Chile and symbolic of Patagonia. It has shiny, box-like leaves, arching thorny branches and blue-black berries eaten fresh or made into jam and alcoholic drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: The blue-black berries are eaten fresh, made into jam and added to alcoholic drinks such as calafate beer.

stories.summary: A flowering plant primarily native from eastern Siberia to Korea and northern and central Japan.

A woodsorrel that likely originated in North America and is now found worldwide. Its clover-like leaves have three leaflets, and its small flowers have five yellow petals; it is often considered a weed.

An evergreen tree native to the Brazilian states of Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, Goiás and São Paulo. Its round, purplish-black fruit grows directly on the trunk and contains sweet white or pink flesh; it is eaten raw or made into preserves, juice and alcoholic drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten raw or made into jellies, jams, juice, wine, tarts and liqueurs; it has been cultivated in Brazil since pre-Columbian times.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native to the Appalachian, Ozark and Ouachita mountain regions of the eastern United States. Its large leaves cluster at branch tips like umbrellas, while its large, unpleasant-smelling spring flowers develop into red, cone-shaped fruits.

A shrub or occasional small tree native to eastern North America, eastern Mexico, the Bahamas and Cuba, groundsel tree often grows in salty or brackish wetlands. Female plants develop conspicuous snowy-white, cotton-like flower heads in autumn. Its seeds are toxic to humans.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds are toxic to humans.

stories.summary: An evergreen shrub or tree originating in Southeast Asia, rose-apple has glossy mature leaves and white or greenish-white flowers with many long stamens. Its ripe fruit has a strong floral scent, crisp watery flesh and usually one or two loose seeds; it is eaten raw, cooked in regional recipes or served with spiced sugar in Southeast Asia.
stories.edibilityNote: The ripe fruit is eaten raw or cooked in regional recipes and is often served with spiced sugar in Southeast Asia.

stories.summary: Non-stinging nettle-family plant that grows on walls and rubbish. Its pollen can cause allergies.
stories.edibilityNote: It was once used to make certain metheglins.

stories.summary: A very small fern native to Europe, East Asia and eastern North America. It grows exclusively on limestone and other calcium-rich rocks, with bluish-green, heavily divided fronds.

Herbaceous perennial native to Europe, from Spain north to Belgium and Poland and east to Ukraine. It has slender green to grey-green leaves and tight clusters of usually dark pink to purple flowers, which are occasionally white.

A creeping aloe native to South Africa’s Western Cape and adjacent parts of the Northern and Eastern Cape. It sprawls over rocky ground, while its leaf-bearing tips often turn upright; drought can redden and curl its fleshy leaves inward. Unlike most aloes, it flowers in summer.

Lily native across Eurasia, from Portugal through Europe and Asia to Mongolia. Its scented, backward-curving flowers are usually spotted pink-purple but can range from nearly white to nearly black, with numerous blooms on vigorous plants.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Lilium martagon
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A flowering perennial native to Europe, Africa and western Asia, with grey-green leaves and pale lavender or blue flowers from summer into autumn. In the European wild, it favours grassland on lime-rich soils.

A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, lesser skullcap has a southern temperate European distribution. It bears narrow, opposite leaves and small pinkish-purple flowers, and grows in wet heaths and open woodland on acidic soils.

Hairless flowering perennial native in southern Britain only to counties including Somerset, Dorset and Hampshire, but distributed more widely through Europe, western Asia and North Africa. Its egg-shaped root tubers sit away from the stem base, and its fruiting heads are distinctively flat-topped; unlike other water-dropworts, it can occupy dry lowland habitats within its natural range. In Turkey, locals reportedly eat the tubers roasted, cooked with yoghurt and bulgur, or pickled and cooked in winter.
stories.edibilityNote: In Turkey, tubers are reportedly eaten roasted, cooked with yoghurt and bulgur wheat, or pickled and cooked during winter.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to Europe from Britain to the Caucasus, zigzag clover resembles red clover but has narrower, unmarked leaflets. Its narrow stipules lack bristle points.

A perennial pea native to Europe and parts of Asia. It has dark root tubers and red flowers that become bluer with age. The tubers can be eaten raw but are better cooked like chestnuts; they were historically eaten in the Scottish Highlands during food shortages.
stories.edibilityNote: Tubers are edible raw but preferably cooked like chestnuts; they were historically eaten during Scottish Highland food shortages and used to suppress appetite.

stories.summary: A willow shrub distributed across much of Europe, eared willow is distinguished from the similar grey willow by reddish leaf stalks and young twigs. Kidney-shaped appendages persist along its shoots.

A palm tree endemic to New Zealand and the only palm native to its mainland. It has a smooth, bulging crownshaft, lilac-to-pink flowers and red ripe fruit; island forms vary, with the Chatham Islands form having larger fruit and hairier fronds.
stories.edibilityNote: Māori traditionally ate inner leaf bases and young flower clusters raw or cooked, rarely harvested palm heart, and ate unripe berries; ripe berries are inedible.

stories.summary: A long-lived tree native only to New Zealand, with stiff, needle-like leaves and bark that peels in papery flakes. Its rot-resistant wood has traditionally been prized by Māori for building large canoes.
stories.edibilityNote: The red fleshy part of the berry-like cones is documented as edible.

stories.summary: A rhizomatous herbaceous perennial native to North America from eastern Canada to northern Mexico, obedient plant bears dense spikes of tubular pink flowers resembling snapdragons. A flower pushed aside often stays in its new position.

A perennial herb native to parts of Eurasia. It bears numerous drooping, usually bright blue-violet flowers and can be extremely invasive in North America, spreading through abundant seed and underground rhizomes and tubers.
stories.edibilityNote: Historically grown for food; roots are eaten raw or cooked, while shoots and leaves are edible and basal leaves are often cooked.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial native to Europe, western Asia and northern Africa, it grows in meadows, fields and woodland borders. Wild plants usually have bluish-violet flowers with an arched upper lip, above a clump of ruffled, toothed leaves.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant was historically used as a flavouring for alcohol.

stories.summary: An herbaceous perennial native to eastern and central North America, sweet Joe-Pye-weed forms clumps of upright purple stems with rings of leaves. Its large, loose clusters of purplish flowers bloom from mid to late summer and attract many nectar-feeding insects.
A cactus native to southern Mexico, queen of the night opens its large, very fragrant flowers at night, and they wilt before dawn.
Cut-leaved selfheal is a plant whose native origin is not provided. It sometimes hybridises with two other selfheal species.

A tall herbaceous perennial native to Europe and parts of western Asia, white hellebore has pleated leaves and white flowers marked with green. Every part is poisonous, and mistaken identity with wild garlic or yellow gentian has caused poisonings.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; accidental consumption after confusion with wild garlic or yellow gentian has caused poisoning.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Veratrum album
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A perennial wild onion from mountainous Eurasia, including Europe, the Caucasus and the Himalayas. It has broad leaves, a sheathed bulb and whitish-green flowers; East Asian and Alaskan populations formerly included in this species are now often treated as Allium ochotense.
A herbaceous perennial native to western and central Europe, from the UK to Ukraine, Cheddar pink bears fragrant rose-pink flowers in May and June. It cannot tolerate wet winter soil.

Woody evergreen flowering subshrub reported as native to southern Europe from the western Mediterranean to southern Italy. Its small grey-green leaves are highly aromatic, and it is the main source of thyme used in cooking.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is the main source of the herb thyme, used as an ingredient in cooking.

stories.summary: A sedge native to the northern United States, Canada, Iceland, Europe, the Atlas Mountains, the Transcaucasus and parts of Siberia. It favors calcareous mires and damp woodland, particularly peaty soil flushed by water from nearby limestone.

Herbaceous perennial native to North American floodplains, stream banks and moist forests. It has deeply divided leaves and late-season flowers with greenish centres and pale-yellow rays, and can spread rampantly through underground stems.
stories.edibilityNote: Young wild leaves were traditionally gathered in early spring and eaten as cooked greens; raw use is suggested by some references.

stories.summary: Evergreen perennial native to Corsica and Sardinia. It has large, leathery leaves divided into three spiny-toothed leaflets and produces green, bowl-shaped flowers in late winter and early spring.

Evergreen conifer native to the northern temperate and boreal forests of Canada and the United States. Its narrow, conical young crown becomes column-shaped with age, and its thin bark flakes into small plates. New growth or tips are used in beer, gin, soda flavouring, candy, pickles and preserves.
stories.edibilityNote: New growth or tips are used in alcoholic drinks, flavoured soda, candy, pickles and preserves.

stories.summary: Large forest tree native primarily to the Appalachian belt, with scattered populations elsewhere in the southeastern United States and southern Ontario, the cucumber-tree is among the largest and cold-hardiest magnolias. Its small yellow-green flowers grow high in the tree, while cucumber-shaped green fruit ripens to a striking reddish orange and releases bright red seeds.

A deciduous tree native primarily to the Midwestern and Upper South regions of North America, it is distinguished from most oaks by shiny, laurel-shaped leaves with smooth margins. Its hard wood was historically important for making shingles.

A deciduous tree native to the eastern United States, commonly occurring in floodplains and swamps. Young bark peels in thin, curling salmon-pink to brown-grey layers, becoming darker, thicker and deeply furrowed with age. Unlike most birches, its fruit matures in late spring.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Americans used boiled sap as a maple-like sweetener and ate the inner bark as survival food.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to central and northern China, Japan and Korea. Its stems bear four corky wings, and it develops vivid red autumn foliage and brightly coloured fruit. All parts are toxic if eaten and cause severe discomfort.
stories.edibilityNote: All plant parts are toxic if eaten and cause severe discomfort.

stories.summary: Annual vine native to eastern North America. It trails in mats or climbs with tendrils, producing clusters of small, bristly fruits that each contain one seed and catch on animals for dispersal.
stories.edibilityNote: The foliage can be cooked and eaten as a green vegetable.

stories.summary: An herbaceous perennial native to parts of the eastern and central United States, fall phlox bears often strongly fragrant flowers from summer into autumn. Wild flowers are typically pink or purple and rarely white, arranged in branching clusters.

Herbaceous perennial native to eastern North America, where it grows in moist prairies and meadows. Its tall purple flower spikes resemble bottle brushes or feathers, and the flowers smell of vanilla when dried.

A red alga distributed across the Atlantic and Mediterranean. Its pink to dark-red body attaches to rock or other algae by creeping cylindrical filaments and develops flattened, irregularly branched upright axes; it commonly occupies dim, shallow rocky habitats year-round.

A bulb-forming flowering plant native to southern Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. Its spring leaves die away before a tall flower cluster appears in autumn, and all parts contain the toxic compound scilliroside.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts contain toxic scilliroside, and the plant has been used as a poison.

stories.summary: A mat-forming flowering perennial native along Atlantic and Baltic coasts of Europe and on several Atlantic islands. It has fleshy, wax-coated grey-green leaves and usually solitary white flowers with deeply notched petals and an inflated, bladder-like base. It grows mainly on stable coastal shingle, dunes and beach strandlines.

A flowering heath native in the British Isles only to Dorset, Devon, Cornwall and one County Galway location, it inhabits bogs and wet heaths there. It has glandular, hairy leaves and bright-pink flowers arranged in long clusters.

Deciduous shrub native to the Appalachian Mountains of the eastern United States, though it may be gone from Pennsylvania and Alabama. Its clustered, unscented flowers usually range from yellow through orange to red, sometimes with several colors on one plant.

A herbaceous perennial native to Europe, fragrant agrimony has yellow glands beneath its leaves that release a sweet aroma. Its brown, grooved fruits bear hooked bristles, some distinctively pointing back toward the stalk.
stories.edibilityNote: Herbal tea reports usually concern common agrimony, and it is unclear whether fragrant agrimony was distinguished.

stories.summary: A perennial flowering herb native to Europe and introduced in a small part of the north-eastern United States, saw-wort has spineless, hairless stems and reddish-purple, thistle-like flowerheads. Its leaves provided a yellow dye used until the 19th century.

An aquatic flowering plant with no stated native origin, found around European, Turkish and North African coasts. Its flowering stems rise above the water and carry small three-petalled flowers; a Newfoundland population was recently found and may have been introduced.

A biennial native to Europe, northern Africa and Asia, carline thistle grows in alkaline grasslands and dunes. Its tiny brown flowers have dry, spiky golden-brown surroundings, making the plant appear to be dying even when fully flowering.

An herbaceous perennial of unstated native origin, European goldenrod is widespread across much of Europe, North Africa and Asia. It flowers profusely in late summer, producing many small yellow flower heads at the tops of its stems.

A flowering perennial native to Western Europe, growing in wet, boggy moorlands. It bears spikes of bright yellow, star-like flowers and deep orange fruit; Shetland Islanders have used the fruit as a colourant replacing saffron.
A wildflower of unspecified native origin, marsh gentian grows in marshes and moorlands. It supports the Alcon blue butterfly and is the only plant on which that butterfly lays its eggs.

Flowering perennial native to Atlantic Europe from southwestern Sweden to southwestern Iberia, common sea-lavender grows in clumps in salt marshes and other coastal habitats. It is probably a group of closely related species.
A biennial or short-lived perennial herb native to Europe, Greenland and the Azores. It commonly trails along northern European coasts, with fleshy, finely divided leaves and daisy-like flower heads.

A liverwort with a Holarctic distribution across Eurasia and North America, it typically grows on tree bark and rocks where rainfall is adequate. Its rounded leaf tips have flat edges. It can remain dormant while dry for months or years and revive quickly when moisture returns.

A perennial orchid probably native to the Mediterranean. Its tiny white flowers, each marked with green, spiral around a slender stalk after summer; its leaf rosette appears around flowering and remains green through winter.

A cultivated autumn-flowering perennial probably originating in southern mainland Greece, it is unknown in the wild. Its sterile purple flowers bear three red or orange stigmas, which are used as the spice saffron, and the plant depends on vegetative propagation.
stories.edibilityNote: The flower stigmas are used as the culinary spice saffron.

stories.summary: A seagrass endemic to the Mediterranean Sea. It forms large underwater meadows of ribbon-like leaves, while its floating fruits are called “sea olives” and fibrous balls made from its foliage often wash ashore.

A green marine alga recorded from the Canary Islands to Ireland and elsewhere in Europe, its origin around Ireland may lie farther south. It forms a dark-green, velvety, spongy sphere and attaches to submerged rock by filaments.

A deciduous tree native to northern Europe and northern Asia, downy birch has dull grey-white bark and finely hairy shoots. Its inner bark was ground into bread during famines, while spring sap is drunk fresh or made into syrup, ale, wine and liqueurs.
stories.edibilityNote: Inner bark was used in traditional and famine breads; spring sap is consumed fresh or made into syrup, ale, wine and liqueurs.

stories.summary: Herbaceous perennial native to northeast Mexico and the south-central United States. Its mildly fragrant, canary-yellow, cup-shaped flowers open in the evening, close the next morning and last just one day; its seed pods have four wings.

An annual herb native to Southeast Asia and the Indian highlands, perilla has square hairy stems and a strong mint-like smell. Its leaves and seeds are eaten in several Asian cuisines, often fresh, pickled, ground or roasted, and toasted-seed oil is used for cooking; large amounts of seeds have caused anaphylaxis.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and seeds are eaten fresh, pickled, ground or roasted, and seed oil is used in cooking; large seed amounts have caused anaphylaxis.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to South Africa and Namibia. Its narrow leaves may be smooth-edged, toothed or deeply divided, while its white to yellowish ray flowers sometimes bear blue or purple markings.
