stories.summary: A plant species native to the Madeira archipelago. It has a zigzagging taproot with whitish, soft, brittle and juicy roots.

A legume-family plant found across much of the Iberian Peninsula, southwestern France and northern Morocco, although its native origin is not explicitly stated. It grows characteristically in low scrub on acidic ground, and its March-to-June flowers are used in cooking, including carqueja rice.
stories.edibilityNote: The flowers are used in cooking, including carqueja rice, and are also prepared as medicinal infusions.

stories.summary: A perennial shrub endemic to Madeira, it has a silky, silvery covering and yellow flowers in clusters at the ends of its branches.

A tree native to West Africa from Mauritania to Chad and Cameroon, where it grows in wooded grassland or savanna. It has thorny leaf stalks and clusters of bright red flowers. Its seeds are poisonous.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds are poisonous.

stories.summary: A thorny deciduous tree native to tropical and subtropical eastern Africa, the Indian subcontinent, northern Australia, and Indian and western Pacific islands east to Fiji, the Indian coral tree bears dense scarlet or crimson flower clusters and black seeds. Its raw seeds are poisonous but can be cooked and eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds are poisonous raw but can be cooked and eaten.

stories.summary: A shrub, or sometimes a tree, endemic to China, where it grows in southern and north-central regions and Manchuria. It has pink or milky-white flowers and almost circular leaves that taper to a point.
A flowering plant native to Brazil, it is planted as a street tree in several Brazilian cities.
A broadleaf evergreen flowering tree native to South America, Brazilian orchid tree has a dense, symmetrical crown that may be vase-shaped, rounded or spreading.

A flowering shrub probably native to Malaysia, parts of Indonesia and the Philippines, although extensive cultivation obscures its exact native range. Its hoof-shaped, two-lobed leaves and fragrant white flowers are distinctive. It is used in culinary dishes in Odisha, though the plant part and preparation are unspecified.
stories.edibilityNote: Used in culinary dishes in Odisha; the plant part and preparation are not specified.

stories.summary: A leguminous plant native to Australia, it has fluffy yellow, tube-shaped flowers in winter. Its evergreen foliage may fall during very cold weather.
An orchid native to Bangladesh, southern China, the eastern Himalayas and Indochina.

An evergreen perennial herb native to southern Asia, including the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. Its false trunk consists of tightly packed leaf sheaths, and many modern edible dessert bananas derive from it, although some are hybrids with Musa balbisiana.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit's starchy pulp is eaten; many modern dessert bananas derive from this species, while others are hybrids with Musa balbisiana.

stories.summary: A large non-woody evergreen perennial whose wild form is native from South Africa north to Ethiopia and west to the Congo. It has huge banana-like leaves and flowers only once, at the end of its life. In Ethiopia, its cooked heart and corm are eaten, while pulverised trunk and flower stalk are fermented into kocho or processed into bulla; the fruits are inedible.
stories.edibilityNote: Cooked hearts and corms are eaten; trunk and flower stalk become kocho or bulla. Fruits are inedible.

stories.summary: Perennial geophyte native to South Africa’s Eastern and Western Cape, it occurs from the Great Swartberg through the Langkloof to Butterworth and forms part of the fynbos and Albany thickets biomes.

A climbing perennial flowering plant native to most of Africa except North Africa, tropical South and Southeast Asia, and south-central China, it uses curled leaf-tip tendrils for support. Its bright yellow-to-red flowers have wavy segments that bend backwards; most parts, especially the seeds and tubers, are poisonous, and ingestion can be fatal.
stories.edibilityNote: Most parts are poisonous, especially the seeds and tubers; ingestion can be fatal.

stories.summary: A sedge native to Europe, the Atlas Mountains and western Asia, specializing in riverside forests. It forms bright-green, grass-like clumps with pale-green flower spikes arranged in a corkscrew pattern along the stem.
A perennial sedge native to parts of Spain and Portugal. It grows in compact clumps.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.

A geophyte of the western Mediterranean, found mainly in Portugal and Spain, it has a short upright underground stem and basal leaves. Its pinkish-white flowers have six segments, and in the Algarve they may appear as early as late April, after the leaves have withered.
A small air plant native to Central America and Mexico, Tillandsia ionantha is usually stemless, with densely covered, narrow triangular leaves. It produces one to three purple flowers.

A solitary palm native to Sri Lanka, India, Myanmar and Malaysia, and perhaps elsewhere in the Indo-Malayan region. Its flower clusters emerge successively down the trunk, and the tree dies after completing flowering and fruiting. Flower-shoot sap is boiled into syrup, while the cabbage is eaten raw or cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: Flower-shoot sap is boiled into syrup; cabbage is eaten raw or cooked; mature pulp is dried and powdered; fruit is eaten after stiff hairs are removed.

stories.summary: A thyme-moss originating in North America and now also found in Middle America, Europe, Africa and much of Asia. Its sharply toothed, gradually tapering leaves form green cushions; when dry, the leaves darken and curl.

Perennial plant native to northeastern Asia, including China, eastern Siberia, Korea and Japan. Its buds swell like balloons before opening into large blue flowers; cultivated varieties may have white or pink flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: In Korea, the fresh or dried roots are popular salad ingredients.

stories.summary: A shrub or small tree native across tropical and southern Africa and islands of the western Indian Ocean. Its bumpy fruit ripens from green through yellow to orange; the mild, pineapple-like pulp, flowers and leaves are eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit pulp, flowers and leaves are eaten; flowers garnish or spice meals, and leaves serve as vegetables.

stories.summary: Mint-family plant native to tropical Africa and the Indian Subcontinent. It bears striking rings of lipped flowers, usually orange but sometimes red, white or purple, above very soft, serrated dark-green leaves.

Herb native to northwestern Spain and central and northern Portugal. It usually grows in rocky places and bears purplish-pink flowers in which incomplete separation of male and female stages makes self-pollination possible.

Flowering plant almost endemic to the mountains of central and northern mainland Portugal. It grows above 1,000 metres in stony meadows and granite rock crevices and is assessed as Vulnerable, with only five known locations.

stories.summary: A bulbous daffodil endemic to Portugal. It grows mainly in limestone crevices, less often in rocky clearings, beside holm oak groves or under forest cover.
Daffodil species native to Portugal.
A daffodil native to the central Iberian Peninsula, Narcissus rupicola grows on rocky ledges and in crevices with very little soil.

Perennial flowering herb native to central and eastern North America. It blooms from late summer to late fall with white-rayed, yellow-centred flower heads; its widespread variety is hairy, while Pringle's aster is hairless or nearly so.
A flowering shrub native to Venezuela, Brazilian red-cloak is especially recognizable by its large, showy reddish-purple bracts. These surround hairy white flowers with two distinct lips.
A herbaceous perennial native to the mountains of central and southern Europe. It bears whorls of yellow flowers and has intensely bitter roots and herbage; root extracts are used in bitter liqueurs.
stories.edibilityNote: Root extracts are used in bitter liqueurs, and gentian was occasionally used in brewing.

stories.summary: Herbaceous perennial native to eastern North America, orange coneflower has bright yellow, daisy-like flower heads. It spreads by creeping stems and seed and grows in habitats including bogs, woodlands, bottomlands and limestone-rich slopes.
A flowering plant native to eastern Russia, Japan and northwestern North America, including Alaska, Washington and parts of western and northern Canada.
Fern native from Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean to tropical South America.

A deciduous fern native to eastern Asia, forming tufts of divided fronds from a creeping underground stem. The commonly cultivated pictum form has grey-green fronds with reddish midribs and thrives in shady gardens.

A fern found in southern and tropical Africa, tropical America, Asia and Australia, African spleenwort grows on rocks or sometimes on other plants. It is critically endangered in Victoria, Australia, and considered exotic in New Zealand.

A fern native from Florida through southern Brazil and northern Argentina, and from DR Congo to Madagascar and the Mascarene Islands. It is also recorded in the Azores, where it may possibly be native.

A fern native to parts of Africa, Atlantic islands, the Americas and Hawaii. Its upright leaves have shiny, hairless, reddish dark-brown to blackish central stalks, and each fertile leaflet usually bears a single spore patch near its toothless lower edge.

A tree fern occurring widely across Asia in shaded forests with humus-rich soil. Its persistent, spiny leaf stalks are purplish near the base and scaly, while dead fronds form a skirt around the crown. Its starch-rich stems are edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The starch-rich stems are edible.

stories.summary: Slow-growing evergreen perennial native to Japan, Korea and China. Glossy leaves on creeping stems spread into dense mats and may yellow in direct sun or winter. White flowers rise above the foliage in late March and April at temperate Northern Hemisphere sites; in the United States and Canada, the plant is described as highly invasive and spreads aggressively underground.

A tender herbaceous perennial native to Brazil, scarlet sage bears upright spikes of scarlet tubular or bell-shaped flowers through much of summer and autumn. Its many ornamental cultivars range from white to dark purple, and it is grown as an annual where winters freeze.

Climbing aroid native from Mexico through Bolivia in Latin America. Its usually arrow-shaped leaves develop varied pale, pink or yellow markings in cultivated forms. All parts are poisonous if eaten and can cause severe mouth pain.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous when eaten and cause severe mouth pain.

stories.summary: A low perennial native to Western Europe and the northwestern Maghreb, Roman chamomile has daisy-like white flowers and a sweet, crisp, fruity-herbal scent. Its dried flowers flavor tea, though chamomile is likely unsafe during pregnancy and its tea may adversely affect anticoagulant drugs.
stories.edibilityNote: Dried flowers flavor herbal teas and foods; chamomile is likely unsafe during pregnancy, and tea may adversely affect anticoagulant drugs.

stories.summary: Herb native to tropical America, especially Brazil. It has white to mauve flowers and becomes an invasive weed in many regions outside its natural range. Ingestion can cause liver lesions and tumours, and contaminated grain caused a mass poisoning in Ethiopia.
stories.edibilityNote: Ingestion can cause liver lesions and tumours; contaminated grain caused a mass poisoning in Ethiopia.

stories.summary: A peat moss distributed throughout the Northern Hemisphere, papillose peatmoss forms dense carpets or hummocks in nutrient-poor fens and acidic peatlands. Its robust golden-brown top and short, blunt branches are useful field marks, while tiny wall projections make its cells look rough.

A biennial or perennial herb native across much of Europe, northern to southeastern Asia, Canada and colder parts of the United States. It produces many small flower heads with pink, lilac or occasionally white outer florets around yellow centres.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native across central and southeastern Europe and temperate Asia; some classifications also include a separated eastern Asian population. It has matt, coarsely toothed leaves and paired reddish winged fruits.

A rare deciduous shrub native to scattered locations in Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas, Missouri, Alabama and Tennessee. It bears pink-grey summer flowers, followed by hair-covered spent flower stalks that create a smoky effect. Its autumn foliage turns brilliant scarlet and is considered by many to have exceptionally intense colour.

A deciduous tree native to Japan and Korea, ranging from small to tall and growing slowly. Its pleasantly fragrant white flowers, sometimes tinged pale pink, open in early spring before the leaves, although young trees do not flower.

A small to medium-sized tree native to central and western China. It is valued as a street tree for its autumn foliage and fruit, which changes from red to blue as it ripens, and it tolerates drought and harsh urban conditions.

A deciduous small tree or large shrub native to Europe and northern and northeastern Asia, bird cherry bears drooping clusters of flowers and black, strongly astringent fruit. In Russia, dried berries are milled into flour for cakes, while fresh fruit may be minced and cooked as jam; some parts, including the fruit, contain potentially poisonous glycosides.
stories.edibilityNote: In Russia, dried berries are milled into flour for cake; fresh fruit may be minced and cooked as jam. Fruit can contain potentially poisonous glycosides.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native to southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia. Its leaves are green above and densely covered with white hairs beneath, while strongly scented pale-yellow flowers appear in mid to late summer.

Annual herb native to Asia and introduced to North America and Europe. Its branching stems may root where lower joints touch the ground, while bristly leaf sheaths and elongated clusters of pink flowers make it distinctive.

Tree fern native to eastern Australia from southeastern Queensland to Tasmania. Its trunk is densely covered with fibrous roots and old frond bases, while numerous large fronds form a funnel-shaped crown. The trunk resists fire, and the crown can regrow after burning.
stories.edibilityNote: The pith and young curled fronds are edible; Indigenous Australians ate the starchy upper-trunk pulp raw or roasted.

stories.summary: A perennial flowering plant native to the forest understorey of Asia, it has long, pointed leaves and strongly scented white flowers with yellow bases. Its flower buds and young flowers are edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The flower buds and young flowers are edible.

stories.summary: Dwarf perennial plant native to South Africa. Its trailing stems and fleshy leaves form dense mats that may be covered by abundant vermilion, magenta or pink flowers, and the leaves turn red in cold winter temperatures.
stories.edibilityNote: In South Africa, roots and especially leaves help prepare khadi wine; the plant is also used as beer yeast. Fermentation reportedly produces toxic oxalic acid.

stories.summary: A deciduous oak tree native to the north-central United States and south-central Canada, primarily the Great Lakes region and Upper Mississippi Valley, northern pin oak has glossy, deeply lobed leaves. Its variable acorns mature from green to pale brown about 18 months after pollination, and its foliage turns bright red in autumn.
Bulbous perennial flowering plant native to the Pyrenees in Spain and France. Its spring flowers hang like bells, with recurved purple, brown and yellow parts and a strong chequered pattern.
A flowering plant whose subspecies Silene foetida subsp. foetida is endemic to mainland Portugal.
A tree or shrub endemic to southwestern Western Australia. It has drooping, very narrow leaves, often twisted or zigzagging branchlets, and clusters of white flowers followed by cup-shaped capsules.

A perennial monocot from Southwest Australia, it resembles a tree crowned with bunches of long, grass-like leaves. Its often fire-blackened trunk develops bands from old leaves and annual growth that record age and previous fires.

Herbaceous perennial native to parts of central and southern Europe, including European Turkey and several Mediterranean islands. Its upright, spreading stems are thick, hollow and densely hairy. From May to August, it bears yellow to orange flowers with darker centres and hairy sepals.
A flowering plant native to southeast and south-central China, it typically grows beneath mountain forests. It and its derived cultivars and hybrids are the only fragrant hostas.

A summer-flowering bulbous perennial widespread across much of Colombia, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, and naturalized in Ecuador and Peru. Its three-petalled flowers have strongly contrasting centres, opening early in the morning and closing before dusk. The roasted bulbs are edible and are used in Indigenous recipes, including as a potato substitute in Colombia’s Sibundoy Valley.
stories.edibilityNote: Roasted bulbs are edible and used by Indigenous peoples; Sibundoy Valley communities cook them in recipes or substitute them for potatoes.

stories.summary: Flowering plant native to Mexico. Its showy flowers are usually red but can be orange or occasionally yellow. Aztecs used its nutritious tubers as food, but this use largely died out after the Spanish conquest.
stories.edibilityNote: Its tubers were eaten by the Aztecs, though this use largely disappeared after the Spanish conquest.

stories.summary: Herbaceous perennial native to Mexico and grown worldwide as an ornamental. It has purple-splotched flower bracts, equally sized bright-blue petals and tuberous roots, and occurs wild in moist fields and open or pine-oak forests.

A perennial native to the Americas, Indian shot has edible, starch-rich rhizomes and exceptionally hard black seeds resembling shotgun pellets. In part of Peru, the rhizomes were traditionally wrapped in leaves and slowly baked underground for the Festival of Corpus Christi.
stories.edibilityNote: The starch-rich rhizomes are edible; in part of Peru they were traditionally slow-baked underground for the Festival of Corpus Christi.

stories.summary: Epiphytic orchid endemic to Colombia, the Christmas orchid has succulent leaves and a flower lip coloured yellow, blue and red. It grows in cloud forests and is endangered because of habitat destruction.

A climbing or trailing herb native to the Afrotropics and Asia, hyacinth bean has three-part leaves and flattened pods containing several seeds. Its edible seeds are cultivated for food, while the pods contain high levels of cyanogenic glycosides and must be cooked carefully for human consumption.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds are edible; pods contain high levels of cyanogenic glycosides and require careful cooking. In Piura, the beans commonly accompany ceviche.

stories.summary: Perennial flowering plant native to Europe, northern Africa and western Asia. It grows on sandy seashores, with many branching stems and crowded, overlapping fleshy leaves.

Herbaceous perennial native to southwestern, central and eastern Europe and southwestern Asia. Its leaves become deeply divided higher up the stems, and bright pink, scentless flowers appear from summer to early fall.
A small flowering herb found widely in Mexico's mountains from Chihuahua to Chiapas, it often grows in protected, shaded places.
A usually perennial evergreen plant found along South Africa’s southern coast. Its regularly branched growth bears stiff, sandpapery opposite leaves and bright blue flower heads with yellow centres.

A small evergreen tree or shrub native to tropical Southeast Asia, starfruit has crisp, juicy yellow fruit that forms a star when sliced. Its leaflets fold together at night and close when shaken, while fruit flavour ranges from very sour to mildly sweet.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is edible; sweet forms are eaten raw, while sour forms are pickled or made into jelly, jam and juice.

stories.summary: Small tree native to Mexico and Central America south to Costa Rica. It bears hard, cannonball-like fruit that can be hollowed and dried as food or drink containers and used for handicrafts. Its protein-rich seeds have a sweet, licorice-like taste and are used in Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua to make semilla de jícaro horchata.
stories.edibilityNote: Protein-rich, sweet seeds are used in Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua to make semilla de jícaro horchata.

stories.summary: A rhizomatous herbaceous perennial found from central Europe to parts of Asia around the Himalayas, it also occurs in North Africa. Its dull-purple flowers are memorable for their separated, star-like petals and deep violet-blue spurs.

Woody perennial shrub native to the Mediterranean, rue has blue-green leaves that release a strong aroma when bruised and small, dull-yellow flowers. It is used sparingly as a bitter culinary herb because it contains toxins; pregnant people and those with liver problems should avoid it.
stories.edibilityNote: Used sparingly as a culinary herb; excessive amounts are toxic, and pregnant people or those with liver problems should avoid it.

stories.summary: A towering forest tree endemic to southwestern Western Australia. It is the tallest tree growing in that state and among the tallest trees worldwide. Its smooth, mottled bark sheds yearly, exposing contrasting white and orange-yellow surfaces.
stories.edibilityNote: Karri honey is sought for its clarity, light colour and delicate flavour; major honey flows occur every four to five years.

stories.summary: Usually perennial, but occasionally annual, flowering herb native to Australia. Its golden-yellow or sometimes white flower heads have stiff, papery bracts resembling petals, and dried flowers can last for years in arrangements.
A flowering plant introduced to both the Azores and Madeira.

A herbaceous perennial native to Nuevo León in Mexico and parts of the United States, including Texas and Oklahoma. Its compact growth carries violet-blue flower spikes and narrow, unusually shiny leaves, unlike the dull, velvety leaves of many other sages.

Woody flowering shrub native to North America, from Nevada and South Dakota south to Arizona, Chihuahua and Texas. Its gray-green, threadlike leaves and hanging flower heads distinguish it, and it often dominates deep sandy soils.

Perennial wheatgrass native to Europe, including the UK. Usually self-pollinating, it grows in clumps with green, loose leaves and varies considerably between populations in features such as flower number, bristle length and leaf hairiness.

Tropical evergreen subshrub native to Mexico and the West Indies. Its small, bright red to orange tubular flowers have a thin white rim and two purple-black petals, resembling lit cigars and attracting hummingbirds and butterflies.

Herbaceous biennial endemic to Tenerife, mainly the Macizo de Anaga. It forms a dense rosette in its first year, followed by a tall spike of white flowers in its second. In Tenerife, it blooms from February to April.

A bulbous plant native to much of southern and eastern Africa, paintbrush lily grows in cool, shady ravines and forests, often in moist leaf litter. It bears bright red round fruits, each with one opalescent seed. Its bulb is considered poisonous in significant amounts, despite reported traditional medicinal and pregnancy-related herbal use.
stories.edibilityNote: The bulb is poisonous in significant amounts; traditional consumption during pregnancy is described as part of an herbal regime, not as food.

stories.summary: A perennial shrub native to Mexico, where it inhabits pine–oak forests. Its leaves smell like pineapple, and it bears tubular red flowers from August onward in Mexico, generally flowering later farther north.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves and flowers are edible.

stories.summary: A small deciduous tree native to southern Europe and western Asia. Deep pink flowers grow prolifically in spring on older branches and even the trunk, followed by heart-shaped leaves and long, hanging flat pods. The flowers are edible and reportedly taste sweet and tart.
stories.edibilityNote: The flowers are edible and reportedly have a sweet and tart taste.

stories.summary: Fern native across broad areas of Africa, Asia, Pacific islands and eastern Australia. It can grow on other plants or on moist, well-drained ground, and its frond juice is used in Assamese traditional medicine.

A herbaceous, shrubby perennial native to a wide area of central Mexico. Its leaves vary from smooth mid-green to hairy grey-green, while abundant whorls of deep purple to purple-blue flowers bloom for several months from late summer.

Non-flowering spikemoss widespread across the Mediterranean Basin. It is a small, moss-like plant with ground-hugging, forked stems and four rows of leaves; its male spore cases are red and female ones green.

A flowering plant occurring in Mexico and Guatemala, this large Echeveria forms leaf rosettes and bears red, tubular flowers from September to January. In Mexican folk medicine, it has been used as a contraceptive vaginal rinse after intercourse.
A semi-woody succulent shrub native to Mexico, dwarf tree stonecrop has a compact, tree-like growth form.

Large deciduous shrub or tree endemic to Mexico, where it grows beside watercourses and along forest edges; it has naturalized in parts of Ethiopia. Its furrowed dark bark contrasts with paired leaves and branching clusters of small fragrant white, cream or yellow flowers with orange-flushed throats.

A moss found across much of the world, including Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas. It forms low, loose yellow-green to golden-brown carpets, with strongly ribbed, toothed leaves that are often curved. It grows on soil, rock and rotting wood in wet, lime-rich places such as springs, riverbanks and marshes.
A moss common in Britain. It forms creeping mats on decaying tree stumps, hedgebanks and other shaded places, and can also live underwater.

Moss widespread in the temperate Northern Hemisphere, with no native origin specified. It forms loose, deep-green mats; sterile shoots lie flat while fertile shoots stand upright and bear capsules with long-beaked lids. It favours damp, shaded, lime-rich places, often beside streams or in woods.

A moss with a cosmopolitan distribution across all seven continents. It withstands cold, drought, salt, acid, heavy metals and intense ultraviolet radiation, and fungal infections can produce fairy rings.

A moss found throughout the Northern Hemisphere and at some sites in South America, New Zealand and Australia, it grows in bogs, marshes, wet meadows and beside water. It usually forms small yellow-green mats, with mostly sickle-shaped leaves; spore-producing structures are extremely rare.

Moss with a nearly cosmopolitan distribution across parts of the Americas, Eurasia and New Zealand. It forms clumps or lawns whose bright yellow-green leaves can glow against reddish-brown stems, and its cylindrical spore capsules are strongly ribbed.

A bryophyte native to every continent except South America and Antarctica. It usually grows in wet soil at disturbed sites, and its capsules mature from late autumn through spring. Its size, leaves and capsule shape vary both across its range and within individual populations.

Perennial flowering plant native to Great Britain, Ireland and eastern mainland Europe from the Pyrenees to eastern Norway. It is an evergreen, creeping woodland plant with bright green pointed leaves and solitary yellow flowers on long stalks.

Palm endemic to western and northern Madagascar, where it grows in open grasslands and low-grass savannas, usually on lateritic soils. It has a grey, ringed trunk and enormous, nearly round leaves divided into many stiff segments.

Deciduous tree native to tropical and subtropical forests of South America. Its bottle-shaped trunk bears large conical prickles, while its flowers have creamy-white centres and pink petal tips; its seeds are surrounded by cotton-like fibres.
stories.edibilityNote: Its seeds can yield vegetable oil described as edible and also useful industrially.

stories.summary: A herb native to North America, with upright, square-edged stems and leaves bearing five to seven main veins. Those leaf veins help distinguish it from other small-flowered St John's worts.

A rhizomatous ginger native to Maluku and the southwestern Pacific islands. Its showy magenta-to-red structures are modified leaves surrounding the much smaller true flowers, and its underground stems spread horizontally before sending up leafy shoots.

A lily native to Siberia, the Russian Far East, Mongolia, northeast China, Korea and Hokkaidō. It requires winter frost and produces upright, dish-shaped flowers whose six segments curve backward from the centre.

A shrub or tree native to the Americas from Mexico to Argentina, including parts of the Caribbean, it has fragrant white flowers and firm yellow fruit. Fruit flavour varies from bitter or tart and strawberry-like to sweet enough for some varieties to be eaten raw; it is also used for preserves.
stories.edibilityNote: Some varieties bear sweet fruit eaten raw; the fruit is also made into preserves, though other varieties taste tart or bitter.

stories.summary: A succulent perennial herb native to Central America and southern Mexico. Its knobby, swollen stem resembles a bottle, while orange-red flower clusters rise above the leaves and its ripe capsules burst to scatter seeds. All parts are considered toxic, particularly the seeds.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are considered toxic, especially the seeds, which contain purgative oil and the toxin curcin.

stories.summary: A unicellular green alga found especially in extremely salty waters, Dunaliella salina lacks a rigid cell wall and can accumulate enough beta-carotene to appear orange-red. It is commercially cultivated for beta-carotene and used as a pro-vitamin A food supplement.
stories.edibilityNote: Used as a pro-vitamin A food supplement because it contains abundant beta-carotene; it may also provide vitamin B12.

stories.summary: A tender shrub or small tree native to southeastern Brazil and thought extinct in the wild, it bears large, hanging trumpet-shaped flowers that are sweetly scented at night and in the early morning. Every part is poisonous, especially the seeds and leaves, and ingestion can cause severe effects including hallucinations, paralysis and death.
stories.edibilityNote: Every part is poisonous when ingested; seeds and leaves are especially dangerous.

stories.summary: A perennial ginger native to East Asia, it grows in upright evergreen clumps from underground stems. Its funnel-shaped flowers are white or pink with yellow centres marked by red spots and stripes; the leaves are used to wrap and flavour foods and make herbal tea.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are used to wrap zongzi and muchi, flavour Okinawan noodles, and make herbal tea.

stories.summary: A tropical flowering plant native to tropical America, although its exact native range is uncertain, tannia is an important starchy crop. Its secondary corms and leaves are eaten; corms should be boiled to reduce irritation, while primary corms are generally reserved for animal feed because they contain more oxalates.
stories.edibilityNote: Corms and leaves are eaten; corms should be boiled to reduce irritation, while primary corms are generally animal feed because they contain more oxalates.

stories.summary: A plant native to Central America, Mexico, the West Indies and northern South America, piñuela has prickly leaves and is commonly planted as a pasture fence in Jamaica. Its pulp can be processed into thread-making fibre, and in Nicaragua and El Salvador the plant is used to make gruel.
stories.edibilityNote: In Nicaragua and El Salvador, the plant is used to make gruel.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, it is introduced in the Azores.

Perennial culinary herb native to tropical parts of the Americas. It has velvety, heart-shaped leaves and white flower spikes that rise like candles. Its fragrant leaves are used in Mexican cooking as wrappers and to flavour mole, eggs and soups.
stories.edibilityNote: Fresh or dried leaves flavour Mexican foods and drinks, though drying reduces flavour and makes them too brittle for wrappers.

stories.summary: A tropical wetland tree native to Central and South American swamps, it has shiny, hand-shaped leaves and a slightly thickened root that stores water. Its very large flowers have narrow petals opening around brush-like stamens, and its leaves and flowers are often eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are often eaten.

stories.summary: Tropical evergreen shrub native to Peru. Its short-lived white flowers emerge one after another from overlapping bright yellow bracts throughout the warm months.

A palm tree found wild in tropical South American wetlands. Its chestnut-coloured fruit has shiny scales and yellow flesh around a hard nut. The fruit is eaten or made into drinks and foods; flower-cluster buds are eaten as a vegetable, and sap is drunk fresh or fermented.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten or processed into drinks and foods; flower-cluster buds are vegetables, and sap is drunk fresh or fermented.

stories.summary: Medium to large deciduous shrub native to most of Europe and western Asia. Its creamy-white flowers are followed by black, single-seeded berries. Some garden varieties reveal striking red stems after their orange-yellow autumn leaves fall.

A palm tree native to northeastern Brazil, the carnaúba has a rounded crown of fan-shaped leaves and small black fruits. It may live for up to 200 years. Its leaves carry a natural coating harvested as carnauba wax.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit and pith are eaten; fruit makes jelly, dried pulp makes flour, seeds yield oil, and roasted fruit is brewed as a coffee substitute.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial originating in the Neotropical Americas. It is now found across tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.
A plant native to Mexico and southern Florida, Mexican alvaradoa is common in Mexico but endangered in Florida.

A liverwort possibly originating in Southeast Asia, it is now widely distributed across temperate Northern Hemisphere regions. Its highly divided leaves give its loose, pale-green to yellowish-white mats a feathery or fuzzy appearance, especially in moist, shaded places near springs and streams.

An annual herb native to Europe and Western Asia, Mediterranean hartwort has softly hairy, divided leaves and white flowers with enlarged, deeply two-lobed petals. Its round, flattened fruit is elaborately textured. The leaves are eaten in Greece as a cooked green and salad vegetable, while in Italy the plant is used as a condiment.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten in Greece as a potherb and salad vegetable; in Italy, the plant is used as a condiment.

stories.summary: A perennial grass with no native origin stated, tall wheatgrass has broad leaves and yellow flowers. Its self-supporting stems can reach about five feet.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It occupies open patches in heaths and other low scrub on acidic mountain ground above 900 metres. In mainland Portugal it has a restricted, declining population and was assessed as Endangered, with recurring fires identified as the main pressure.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Thymelaea broteriana
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in wet meadows; in mainland Portugal it was assessed as endangered, with only three known locations and a severely fragmented population.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Succisella carvalhoana
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A moss of unstated native origin, matted feather-moss occurs chiefly in temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere and also in northern, central and southern Africa. It forms soft, often extensive green mats, with creeping, nearly feather-branched stems that cling firmly to rock, walls, concrete or tree bases.

A moss of unstated native origin, it forms dense, slightly glossy green, yellow-green or brownish mats with creeping stems and rising branches. It grows mainly in wet places along lime-free streams and rivers, especially on silicate rock, and occurs widely across the Northern Hemisphere and Oceania.

A tree native to southern and Southeast Asia, Australia and Polynesia, bishop wood was introduced to North America as an ornamental and is now considered invasive there. Its dense, dark red wood is used for furniture and bridges; its fruits make wine, its seeds are edible, and its leaves are eaten with chilli sauce in southern Laos.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits are made into wine, seeds are edible, and leaves are eaten with chilli sauce in southern Laos.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to a range extending from Europe to China.

A tropical perennial native from tropical Africa and the Arabian Peninsula through parts of South and East Asia. This semi-succulent subshrub has large, serrated leaves and upright clusters of purple-blue flowers; its roots contain forskolin.
stories.edibilityNote: Herbal teas are made from the plant, although the passage does not specify which parts are used.

stories.summary: A tree native to northern Australia, New Guinea and the Maluku Islands of Indonesia, the weeping paperbark has thick white, pinkish or cream papery bark and drooping branches. Its cream to greenish-white flowers may appear at any time of year and were traditionally used by Aboriginal people to make a sweet drink.
stories.edibilityNote: Aboriginal people traditionally used the flowers to make a sweet drink; bark was used to wrap food before underground-oven cooking.

stories.summary: Herbaceous perennial legume native to parts of northern Africa, western Asia and Europe. It contains galegine, which contributed to the development of diabetes drugs, and the plant can be poisonous to mammals.

Flowering plant native to the Americas, from the southwestern United States through Central America to Argentina. Native peoples in Central America and Mexico have used wilted fresh leaves brewed and fermented in cool water for shamanic purposes.
A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, introduced in the Azores.

A herbaceous perennial native across parts of South, East and Southeast Asia, it has broad heart-shaped leaves and small greenish-yellow flowers framed by white bracts. Its fishy-tasting leaves are eaten fresh or cooked, while tender roots and rhizomes are used in regional Asian dishes; dried leaves may be brewed as tea.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw or cooked; tender roots and rhizomes are used in regional dishes, while dried leaves may be brewed as tea.

stories.summary: A coastal plant whose native origin is unresolved, Carpobrotus aequilaterus is naturalised as a weed in several regions. Its edible fruit is said to taste like strawberry but has poor structure.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is edible and reportedly tastes like strawberry, although it has poor structure.

stories.summary: Tropical subshrub or shrub native to tropical Asia, New Guinea and Queensland, Australia. Its nutritious leaves are widely eaten as a vegetable, including in Philippine soups and salads, Indonesian bubur Manado and everyday cooking in Papua New Guinea.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten as a vegetable in Philippine and Indonesian dishes and are a widely consumed indigenous green in Papua New Guinea.

stories.summary: A large shrub native to tropical America and Central and South Africa. It has broad leaves, yellow flowers and long simple stem hairs, and its prolific seed production makes it invasive in some regions.

Annual flowering plant native to the southeastern United States, with upright, freely branching, densely hairy stems. It has petal-free male and female flowers on the same plant and reddish-to-black seeds; it flowers from spring to fall through most of its range, but year-round in southern Florida.
A herbaceous perennial native to central and southwestern Asia. It has rough, hairy, fern-like foliage and large, uneven clusters of small, rigid, old-gold flowers in mid to late summer.

A wild, erect perennial herb whose native origin is not specified, devil's horsewhip is distributed throughout the tropical world and introduced as a common weed in many places. Its hairy stems and leaves carry long spikes of small green, spiny flowers, with flowering and fruiting reported from September to April.
Perennial climbing vine native to Japan, Korea, northern China and the Russian Far East. Its edible kiwiberries are small, smooth-skinned fruits that can be eaten whole without peeling.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten whole or processed; young leaves are eaten as a vegetable, and sap reportedly served as famine food in Korea.

stories.summary: A small fern native across parts of Africa and Asia, Malesia, mainland Australia, New Zealand and Pacific islands, rough maidenhair fern grows in clumps from short, dark rhizomes. Young growth can be pinkish before maturing to dark green.
A fern native to South America, it has shiny, dark leafstalks resembling human hair. Its triangular fronds begin semi-upright and droop gracefully as they age.

An ornamental plant native to North Africa, Western Asia, the Mediterranean and Europe. Its flowers are often scarlet with dark basal spots, while its leaves and roots are poisonous to humans and livestock.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves and roots are poisonous to humans and livestock.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Adonis annua
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: Annual, or rarely biennial, herb native to Europe, western Asia and northwestern Africa. Its divided leaves smell unpleasant, and the fresh whole plant is poisonous, though drying destroys its toxins.
stories.edibilityNote: The fresh whole plant is poisonous, but drying destroys its toxins; no human food use is documented.

stories.summary: A perennial mint-family plant native to much of northern North America, especially the Great Plains and other prairies. It has anise-scented leaves used for seasoning, tea and salads, and bears abundant bright lavender flowers from June to September.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are used as seasoning or tea and may be crumbled into salads.

stories.summary: An agave endemic to Arizona, the golden-flowered century plant has bright yellow flowers carried on a towering stalk.

A succulent perennial believed to have originated in northeastern Mexico, it forms suckers and has arching or backward-curving leaves beneath a very tall flowering stalk. It is cultivated for ornament, fibre and production of the alcoholic beverage pulque.
stories.edibilityNote: It is cultivated to produce pulque; early Mexican specimens were also reported as cultivated for making this alcoholic beverage.

stories.summary: A flowering shrub native to Texas, Cuba, and northeastern and east-central Mexico. Unlike many related species, it is evergreen.

Sprawling perennial herb native to western Mexico. Its often woody stems bear purple hairs and can root where they touch the ground. Coarsely serrated leaves and dense heads of white flowers help distinguish it.
stories.edibilityNote: Near Sangau, India, dried leaves and flowers are prepared as herbal tea and taken to reduce blood pressure and blood sugar.

stories.summary: Flowering plant native to the Philippines and northeastern Sulawesi. Its hybrid cultivar 'Silver Queen' is grown as a houseplant.

A perennial grass native across most of Europe and temperate Asia. It spreads by above-ground runners rather than underground stems and is common in damp places, including ditches and lake margins. Its short green growth is popular for lawns.

A wild onion native to Turkey, Cyprus, Syria, Lebanon and the Palestine region, it unusually lacks the onion or garlic scent common to its group. Its dense flower clusters have white, star-like flowers with green midveins, while the ovaries vary in colour with age and location.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Allium nigrum
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A bulbous perennial wild onion from Eurasia, field garlic grows in dry places. Its pinkish-brown flower heads sometimes carry small bulblets, and the two-part papery covering has long points that often overtop the flowers.

A rhizomatous perennial grass native to Eurasia and northern Africa, creeping foxtail forms sod in damp or saline grasslands and along waterways. It is used for forage and erosion control, and flowers between April and July depending on location.
Perennial herb native to Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay, with underground tubers. Its clusters of three to eight flowers are red to reddish-purple, sometimes with brownish spots.

Flowering herb native to forests from northeastern Mexico through Central and South America to northeastern Argentina. Its young red, green or purple stems are finely hairy, while its leaves are often vividly reddish-purple. Small vanilla-coloured, pom-pom-like flowers grow in compact clusters.
stories.edibilityNote: It is harvested from the wild for regional use as food, although the parts and preparation are not specified.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to central and southern Europe, the Mediterranean Basin, north Africa, Turkey and central Asia, excluding the Balearic Islands, Corsica, Crete and Cyprus. It has hairy, deeply divided lower leaves resembling hemp and usually bears pink or reddish-purple, heart-shaped flowers from July to September.
An annual flowering plant native to Mexico, northern Central America, the Caribbean, the Galápagos, and parts of the south-central and southeastern United States.

A small perennial semi-shrub native to North America. Its tiny purple flowers have yellow stamens, while dense hairs give its compound leaves a lead-grey appearance; its deep roots suit dry prairies, bluffs and open woodlands.
stories.edibilityNote: Indigenous peoples used the leaves to make tea.

stories.summary: A moss with no native origin specified in the supplied text. It forms yellow-green to brown-green cushions on persistently wet, shaded mountain rocks and, because it rarely produces spore capsules, usually spreads through detached leaves.
Moss native to North America and parts of Europe. It can form extensive black or brown cushions on wet, acidic, exposed rocks, and its leaves may curve to one side, especially when wet.

A moss found mainly around the Northern Hemisphere, black rock moss grows as dark, cushion-like tufts on exposed, usually acidic rock. Its mature spore cases lack a stalk and split along four vertical lines, opening when dry and closing again when moist.

A flowering plant native to Europe and central Asia, wild angelica is an annual or short-lived perennial. It has upright purplish stems and rounded clusters of tiny white or pale pink flowers in late summer.
stories.edibilityNote: Eaten as a vegetable until the 20th century; stems were eaten fresh, while leaves were boiled for storage or cooked with milk.

stories.summary: A leafy moss distributed across the Northern Hemisphere, chiefly in limestone areas, grows on shaded rocks and trees. It forms vigorous, non-glossy yellow-green or fresh-green carpets, with creeping stems producing sparsely branched ascending shoots.

A hornwort occurring across temperate Europe and North America, mainly in moist lowland fields and ditches. Its thin, dark-green body forms a rosette, while upright spore structures blacken as they mature and split open.

A perennial herb native to northern North America, mainly from Alaska across Canada, with isolated populations farther south. Its small, nodding flowers combine blue-to-lavender outer parts with white or pale-yellow petals and appear from May into July or August.

A perennial flowering plant native to the Rocky Mountains of the United States and Canada, it grows in mountain meadows, open woods and alpine slopes. Its nodding flowers usually have yellow sepals, though these may be yellowish-pink or raspberry-pink, with white or cream petals and curved nectar spurs.

A perennial flowering herb native to mountainous parts of Europe, North and East Africa, Central and Eastern Asia and North America, it inhabits damp gravel and scree. Loose heads of white, four-petalled spring flowers rise above strongly toothed basal leaves and stalkless leaves that clasp the stem.

An evergreen perennial herb native to Crimea, Turkey, Iran, the Caucasus and the Mediterranean. It grows in limestone crevices, by streams and in alpine meadows, producing white flowers in early spring; cultivated forms may have pink or double flowers.

Deciduous small tree or shrub native to eastern Asia, from Russia and China through Taiwan, Korea and Japan. Its rough gray bark bears prickles, and large leaves accompany clusters of small white flowers followed by black fruit. In Japan and Korea, young spring shoots are eaten after cooking or pickling.
stories.edibilityNote: Young spring shoots are eaten in Japan and Korea, commonly blanched, fried or pickled.

stories.summary: A flowering evergreen shrub or tree native to Central America, Mexico and the southwestern United States, Texas madrone has smooth orange-brown bark that peels in thin sheets. Its white or pale pink bell-shaped flowers are followed by rough red berries that are reportedly edible, though related species have narcotic properties.
stories.edibilityNote: The red berries are reportedly edible, although related species have narcotic properties.

stories.summary: A palm endemic to Queensland, Australia, the Alexandra palm has a solitary trunk and a crown of feather-like fronds with silvery-grey undersides. Its fruit turns bright red when ripe, and the Kuku Yalanji people of Far North Queensland ate its palm heart.
stories.edibilityNote: The Kuku Yalanji people of Far North Queensland ate the palm heart.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to sand dunes along the west coast of South Africa’s Cape Province, white arctotis is rare within its native range. It has also been introduced to New Zealand.
A compact flowering shrub native to East Asia, coralberry has thick, glossy dark-green leaves with tightly waved edges. Its clusters of glossy red berries can remain on the plant throughout the year.

A deciduous vine native to the Caribbean and Central America, it bears exceptionally large flowers smelling of rotting meat. The heart-shaped, purple-veined flowers have long tails and attract flies, while the plant contains carcinogenic aristolochic acid.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.

A perennial aromatic herb native across much of Eurasia, from France to Japan. Its strongly scented, heavily branched stems are often purple-tinged, while young sea-green, silky-haired growth becomes yellowish and smooth at maturity. Young leaves are recorded as edible when cooked, although this use is minor and not widely documented.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves are recorded as edible when cooked, but this use is minor and not widely documented.

stories.summary: A sunflower-family plant native to parts of China, Japan, Korea, the Russian Far East and the Aleutian Islands. Its pale green to white leaves are thickly hairy on both sides, giving them a silvery appearance. Tall clusters of yellow flowers bloom from July to late August.

Sprawling perennial herb native to the tropical Americas. Its reddish stems and buds lead to pink or purple flowers with prominent stamens, and its leaves have tiny reddish, bristly teeth. The tender stems are edible and can be used as food.
stories.edibilityNote: The tender stems are edible and used as food.

stories.summary: A fern native across parts of Africa, western and central Asia, Europe, Macaronesia, the southwestern United States and Hawaii. Its thick triangular leaves are repeatedly divided, carried on reddish-green stalks, and bear chains of spore-producing patches beneath.
A perennial flowering herb native to most of Europe except Ireland, Iceland and the Greek islands, and also native to parts of western and central Asia, wild liquorice is sometimes used to make tea.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is sometimes used to make tea.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Astragalus glycyphyllos
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: Spreading herb whose original range is unclear; subsp. gangetica was likely limited to Asia and subsp. micrantha to Africa. Its stems root readily at the joints, while its capsules dry from green to brown and explosively release their seeds. Some African communities eat the leaves as a vegetable.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are eaten as a vegetable in some parts of Africa.

stories.summary: An annual coastal plant native to Europe, North Africa, and western and eastern Asia. It has a shrubby appearance, narrow green or grey-green leaves, and small flower clusters, often forming dense stands on beaches, saltmarshes, and tidal riverbanks. Its leaves are edible when cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are edible when cooked.

stories.summary: An annual plant native across parts of Middle and western Central Asia, Asia Minor, North Africa and Eastern Europe. It has a white branched taproot and produces two fruit types differing in size and colour. It commonly grows in salty soils and disturbed places such as roadsides, railways and dumps.

A tufted grass native to Europe, with seeds smaller than those of common oats. Its seeds are edible, and it was formerly cultivated as human food in Scotland, though it is now grown as livestock forage in South America.
stories.edibilityNote: The edible seeds were formerly cultivated as human food in Scotland.

stories.summary: A grass with no native origin stated, broadleaf carpetgrass forms low groundcover in moist, nutrient-poor soils and shaded places. It is used for permanent pasture and low-maintenance turf but is generally too short for harvested fodder.
Flowering bamboo native to China, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Sri Lanka, Taiwan and northern Indochina. Its slender stems and dense foliage form clumps suitable for hedges and living fences.

A leafy liverwort recorded from Arctic Europe south to the Pyrenees and Bulgaria, and also across parts of Asia and North America. It forms yellow-green spongy mats, often mixed with other mosses, and has leaves divided into four broad, spine-tipped lobes.

A moss with no native origin specified, bird's-claw beard-moss is common across temperate regions but rare in the tropics. Its bright yellow-green, opaque leaves often twist around the stem when dry and spread outward when moist.

A perennial vine native to the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia and New Guinea. It grows quickly on soft stems and has thick, heart-shaped leaves with a mild flavour and slippery texture; the leaves and shoots are cooked in curries, soups and stir-fries.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten in numerous cooked dishes across Asia; cooked shoots are commonly used in Africa.

stories.summary: A large annual herb native from Central Europe across Asia, it develops red autumn foliage and can detach and roll in the wind as a tumbleweed. In Japan, its dull black seeds are boiled, soaked and hulled to make tonburi, a garnish prized for its caviar-like texture.
stories.edibilityNote: In Japan, boiled, soaked and hulled seeds are eaten as the garnish tonburi.

stories.summary: An evergreen, sprawling shrub native to Angola, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Eswatini and parts of South Africa. Its two rounded leaf lobes resemble a camel's foot, and wild plants generally bear brick-red flowers; cultivars may instead flower pink or orange-red.

Upright herbaceous perennial native to Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. It has glossy, succulent leaves and red, pink or white flowers, which bloom in summer or throughout the year in warmer places; its fruits have three wings.

A flowering, shrub-like begonia native to Colombia and Venezuela, it has hanging succulent stems densely covered with glossy oval green leaves and clusters of small white flowers. The commonly cultivated variety, B. foliosa var. miniata, instead has pink or red flowers.
Flowering plant native to Jamaica, Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Bolivia and southern Brazil. Its juice is applied to the skin to treat itching from insect bites.

A flowering herb from North America, widespread across much of Mexico and also found in Arizona and Guatemala. It produces numerous yellow or whitish flower heads and grows mainly in wet places such as marshes and streambanks.

A perennial bromeliad native to northern South America and parts of the Caribbean. It forms clumps of jar-shaped leaf rosettes that collect water and debris, and produces brush-shaped red or pink blooms, often nearly simultaneously in late summer or early autumn.

Grass native across much of Africa, the Middle East, southern and eastern Asia, Malesia and Australia. It is used as stored livestock feed and grazing for livestock and wild ruminants, and is sometimes planted to restore disturbed land.
An evergreen climbing shrub whose native origin is not supplied. It has thick thorny stems and drooping branches, with tiny white flowers surrounded by colourful papery bracts that resemble petals.
Moss native to much of the world outside South America and tropical regions, it can grow under artificial light in places without natural light, such as Crystal Cave in Wisconsin.

An orchid native to warmer parts of the Western Hemisphere, from southern Mexico and Florida through Central America and the Caribbean to northern South America. It is commonly called the tailed Brassia, spider orchid or cricket orchid.
A plant native to New Caledonia and Vanuatu in the western Pacific. Leafflower moths have been reared from its fruit there, and the fruit is presumed toxic and capable of causing liver injury.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is presumed toxic and may cause liver injury.

stories.summary: A perennial grass native and widespread in Britain and Europe except the extreme north. Fine stems carry distinctive green and purplish, hop-shaped flower clusters that droop from loose branches; in the UK it flowers from June to September.

A flowering grass native from the Mediterranean and Caucasus through the Middle East and Central Asia to Xinjiang, Afghanistan and Pakistan, large-headed brome thrives in disturbed habitats. It has been introduced at scattered sites in the Americas and central Europe.
A grass native from northern Italy through the Caucasus to China.

An annual grass native from the Mediterranean through Crimea, the Middle East, the Caucasus and Central Asia to Xinjiang and the northwestern Indian subcontinent. It is somewhat weedy and typically grows in grasslands.

An annual plant native to the United States, it has creeping stems that root at their nodes and younger shoots that climb with tendrils. It grows beside rivers and lakes and along woodland edges and damp thickets.

Tender deciduous shrub native across much of South and Southeast Asia, southern China, the Himalayas and parts of the western Pacific. Its sweetly scented flowers are usually white, occasionally pale violet, and appear in late winter in slender clusters at the ends of long, loose branches. It can grow as woodland understorey scrub or a small tree.
An evergreen flowering shrub endemic to Madagascar, where it grows among mountain scrub. It has fragrant autumn and winter flowers ranging from deep yellow and orange to pink.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.

A flowering plant native to the Mediterranean Basin and introduced elsewhere, including parts of North America. Its hairless, waxy stem passes through the fused bases of deep-green leaves, and it bears rounded clusters of yellow to yellow-green flowers.
Annual flowering plant native to the specified areas of mainland Portugal. It grows in wasteland, low-nitrogen meadows, damp shaded places and cultivated plots.
A moss with no stated native origin, it is widely distributed around the world. In one study, it showed intermediate sensitivity to the herbicide Asulam.

A robust perennial herb native to Mexico, the false bromeliad develops vigorous, bromeliad-like flowering shoots. Its leaves can turn burgundy-violet after prolonged sunlight, and its small fragrant white flowers appear from late winter to spring.

A succulent creeping perennial native from the southeastern United States through the West Indies to Argentina, creeping inchplant forms mats of delicate fleshy leaves that become smaller toward the shoot tips. Its rapid spread has made it invasive in Western Australia.
An aster-family plant native to China and the only species in its genus.
A plant of unspecified native origin, found in Canada and the eastern United States.

An annual or biennial flowering plant originating in southern Europe. Biennial plants form a leaf rosette in their first year and stems with long-lasting, bell-shaped violet-blue or rarely white flowers in their second; flowering runs from May to July in the Northern Hemisphere.

A biennial herb native to temperate Europe, it bears delicate upright, funnel-shaped flowers that are usually violet-blue but sometimes white. Their pointed petals spread outward, and surrounding vegetation may support the branches so the plant appears prostrate.

A herbaceous perennial native to European mountain ranges, including the Alps, it has narrow glossy foliage and cup-shaped lilac-blue or white flowers. It naturally grows in broad-leaved woods, woodland margins, meadows and rocky places.
Moss with a cosmopolitan distribution.

A fern native to the southeastern United States, Cuba, Costa Rica, Bolivia and Venezuela, long strap fern grows on other plants, generally in tree canopies. It has simple, hairless leaves and many fine rootlets covered with dark reddish-brown scales.

Aquatic perennial herb native to the wetlands of tropical America. Its narrow blue-green leaves are topped by large, delicate, pale-yellow flowers, and it grows at the margins of still or slow-moving water.

A fast-growing climbing plant native to eastern Argentina and Brazil. Its tough stem clings to supports, while its slightly fragrant creamy-white flowers develop into capsules that split into three parts and release hard, black, winged seeds.

A tuft-forming, spreading sedge native to parts of northern and western Europe. It has slender three-angled stems and narrow leaves that tend to droop at their tips, and grows in moist habitats including fen meadows and swamps.
A perennial sedge whose native origin is not stated, it commonly grows in dunes and other sandy habitats. It spreads through long runners beneath the soil surface.
Sedge native to Europe and North Africa. It grows in dense clumps and has widely separated flower spikes; in Europe it often inhabits wetlands, fens and coastal brackish marshes.
A sedge native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, it has become naturalized in Australia, New Zealand and scattered parts of North America.
A sedge native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, Carex extensa is known as long-bracted sedge.
A clump-forming sedge native to parts of Europe and North Africa. Its arching leaves are blue-green above and pale beneath, while its densely packed female flower spikes may stand upright or nod.
Sedge native across Europe. Its leaves and flowering spikes are characteristically hairy, though plants in wetter places may be less hairy.
A sedge found in Europe and western Asia as far as the Himalayas, and introduced elsewhere. It is poorly studied and treated as an unresolved species aggregate, with a history of taxonomic confusion.

An evergreen perennial sedge native to wetlands of Europe, western Asia, North Africa and eastern North America. It forms tussocks with bluish-green leaves and purplish-black flower spikes and seed heads in summer.
A sedge of unspecified native origin, it occurs in northern and western Europe and northeastern North America. Its leaves are pale blue on both sides, and its fruits are egg-shaped and spiked.

A sedge native to temperate Europe, spiked sedge grows in grassland, roadsides and waste ground, usually on heavy, slightly alkaline soils. Its stems are roughly triangular, while its roots, leaf sheaths and flower bracts contain distinctive purple pigment.

A biennial plant originating from the region between central Europe and Asia. It has delicately divided leaves and clusters of small white to pale-violet flowers. Its cooked roots, tender leaves and fruits are eaten, while the spicy, slightly sweet seeds flavour breads, cheeses, drinks and other foods.
stories.edibilityNote: Cooked roots are eaten as a vegetable; tender leaves, fruits and seeds are used in salads, dishes, baked goods, cheeses and drinks.

stories.summary: Clustering palm native to tropical Asia from India through Java to southern China. Its many leaflets resemble tail fins, while its ripe red or dark-purple fruits are harmful to people. Trunk pith can be processed into a flour resembling sago.
stories.edibilityNote: Trunk pith can be made into sago-like flour, but the fruit contains irritating crystals and is harmful if eaten.

stories.summary: A tree native to Australia and New Guinea, chiefly growing in stands along freshwater rivers and streams. It has fissured, scaly bark, often-drooping branchlets and leaves reduced to tiny scales arranged in whorls.
A flowering tree endemic to eastern Australia. It often produces root suckers, bears scale-like leaves on spreading or drooping branchlets, and grows near brackish rivers and estuaries.

A pod-bearing tree native to temperate provinces of China, Chinese catalpa bears bunches of creamy white flowers distinctly tinged with yellow. Its dark green leaves have three lobes, and its fruits are exceptionally narrow, long pods.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.

Tall perennial flowering herb endemic to Macaronesia. It has three-part leaves and flower spikes coloured purple, lilac or pink, and grows in laurel forest and other shady places, generally above 500 metres.

A tropical African herb that may grow as a tender annual or perennial, with tiny flowers packed into vivid, plume-like heads. Its leaves and flowers are edible, especially in West Africa and Southeast Asia; one variety, Lagos spinach, is a major boiled green in West Africa.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are edible; Lagos spinach is an important boiled green in West Africa.

stories.summary: Plant found in France and northern Italy.

Herbaceous perennial of unspecified native origin, widespread in the mountains of southern and central Europe. Its narrow, undivided leaves accompany flower heads with bright purple inner flowers and azure-blue or deep-mauve outer flowers.

Spring-blooming annual plant native to Mediterranean and temperate Europe, the Caucasus, Western Asia and northwestern Africa. It has been introduced and naturalised in North America, and the charity Plantlife lists it among 101 high conservation priorities in the UK.
An annual or biennial herb native to Central and western Europe. Its white petals are no longer than the sepals and are shallowly split, and it flowers from March to May.

A low annual herb native to Europe, northern Africa and southwestern Asia, it grows in patches on sandy ground and thin soils over rock. Its dull-green growth quickly yellows with age, and its small white petals are shorter than the papery-edged sepals.
Low, spreading perennial herb native to alpine central and southern Italy. Its densely hairy, silvery-grey foliage forms creeping carpets beneath star-shaped white flowers.

A shrub native to tropical parts of North and South America, orange cestrum bears orange or occasionally yellow flowers throughout the year. The flowers release a citrus-like scent at night, and the fruits are white berries.
An evergreen flowering shrub native to central Mexico. It has sometimes-purple, slightly hairy young twigs and dense clusters of hairy red flowers, followed by red berries with white interiors.
Thorny deciduous or semi-evergreen shrub native to eastern Asia. Its flowers are usually red but may be pink, white or green, and its fragrant, hard fruit resembles a quince.

A subtropical palm native to Belize, Guatemala, Honduras and southeastern Mexico, reed palm grows in moist woodlands and forests, often on limestone outcrops. Commonly kept as a houseplant, it has divided evergreen leaves, yellow flower clusters and small round black fruits.
A plant native to the Irano-Turanian region, it is an ancient introduced weed in Europe and now occurs in temperate crop-growing regions across most of the world.
An annual herb of unstated native origin, grey goosefoot is self-supporting, associated with freshwater habitats and has simple, broad leaves.
A flowering plant with no stated native origin, it is widely cultivated for the bitter-leaved vegetables known as endive and escarole. It is often confused with common chicory.
stories.edibilityNote: Widely cultivated for its bitter leaves as the vegetables endive and escarole.

stories.summary: Evergreen tree native to tropical Southeast Asia. Its aromatic bark is sold as cinnamon, while its leaves can season preserved foods and canned meat.
stories.edibilityNote: The bark is sold as cinnamon, and the leaves are used as a spice for preserved food and canned meat.

stories.summary: A herbaceous biennial, or often perennial, native to Europe. It begins as a dense rosette, then develops a tall, spiny stem topped with branching clusters of usually dark-purple flowers.

A tree native to southern Florida, the Caribbean, Guyana, Suriname and Venezuela, spiny fiddlewood bears small white flowers throughout the year in hanging clusters. Its rounded fruits ripen from red to black, and its leaf stalks are orange.

Flowering sedge native to temperate Europe and Asia, growing in mineral-rich boggy ground and beside lakes. Its hard, serrated leaves can cause deep cuts, though they were historically harvested for thatched roofs.

A deciduous woody climber that develops long, branched stems with sparse hairs. Its solitary, nodding violet bell-shaped flowers and dark brown hairy fruits appear from June to August. It favours acidic woodland habitats, especially pinewoods, scrub and thickets.

A climbing shrub native to Europe and western Asia. Its grooved stems, scented greenish-white flowers and clusters of fruit with long silky appendages create its characteristic old man's beard appearance; in Italy, the sprouts are harvested for omelettes.
stories.edibilityNote: In Italy, the sprouts are harvested for omelettes.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to Taiwan, Vietnam and most of mainland China. It bears rounded clusters of fragrant rose, crimson or pink flowers in late summer, while its crushed leaves smell unpleasant. Its rapid suckering growth can form spreading colonies.
A tropical shrub native to Indonesia and Papuasia. It has square-shaped leaves and large, bright red, heart-shaped flowers and is grown as an ornamental.

Evergreen tropical and subtropical tree native from the Caribbean and Florida through southern Mexico and Central America to northern South America. It begins life on rocks or trees and can overtop and strangle host trees with aerial roots. Its leaves retain scratched writing, while its fleshy light-green fruit is toxic.
stories.edibilityNote: The fleshy, light-green fruit is toxic.

stories.summary: An herbaceous plant native across the Paleotropics, from tropical and southern Africa through southern and eastern Asia to Pacific islands. Usually annual but sometimes perennial in the tropics, it creeps along the ground and roots where its stems touch soil. According to one source, its young leaf tips are cooked and eaten in New Guinea.
stories.edibilityNote: According to one published source, young leaf tips are cooked and eaten in New Guinea.

stories.summary: Flowering plant whose native origin is not given in the supplied information. It is introduced in mainland Portugal.

Annual upright herb grown widely in tropical regions. Its bark provides jute fibre, while its leaves and young fruits are eaten as vegetables, dried leaves make tea or thicken soup, and the seeds are also edible.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and young fruits are vegetables, dried leaves are used for tea and thickening soup, and seeds are edible.

stories.summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native from southern Texas to central Mexico, anacahuita bears white funnel-shaped flowers throughout the year and yellow-green, olive-like fruits. The fresh fruits are sweet but slightly toxic and can cause dizziness; jellies made from them are reportedly safe to eat.
stories.edibilityNote: Fresh fruits are slightly toxic and may cause dizziness, but fruit jellies are reportedly safe to eat.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to Europe and Africa, strapwort grows along shingly European pool margins with fluctuating water levels and occupies varied habitats in Africa. It has been introduced to Australia and North America.

A grass native to Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, and widely naturalized in North America. It is rare in the United Kingdom and has narrow leaves with small flower clusters bearing shiny, lance-shaped bracts and hairy flower bases.

An evergreen tree endemic to New Zealand, karaka is mainly coastal, though it also grows inland in the North Island. It has thick, leathery green leaves and oval yellow-orange fruit. Māori ate the uncooked fruit flesh and the highly poisonous seeds only after lengthy detoxification.
stories.edibilityNote: Māori ate the fruit flesh uncooked; the highly poisonous seeds required lengthy detoxification before consumption.

stories.summary: An annual native to Latin America and the West Indies, king's salad bears purple, pink or white flower rays. Its soft, pungent leaves fold as night falls. In Indonesia and Malaysia, the leaves are eaten as a traditional raw salad called ulam.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are eaten raw as ulam in Indonesian and Malaysian cuisine; in Brunei they were usually served with chilli paste.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to parts of the southwestern United States and most of Mexico, from Chihuahua to Oaxaca. Its deeply divided leaves have narrow segments, and its white, pink or violet flowers may show mixed colours within one population. Barbed fruits lodge in fur or clothing.

Fast-growing evergreen low shrub native to central and southern China. Its creeping branches root where they touch the ground; glossy leaves turn purple in autumn, and bright red berries persist well into winter.
Perennial herb native to Europe and Asia Minor. A single plant can bear numerous small flower heads, each packed with yellow ray flowers and lacking central disc flowers.

A European flowering herb widespread across much of Europe and Siberia, stinking hawksbeard may be annual, biennial or perennial. A plant can bear several flower heads packed with yellow ray florets and no central disc florets.

A medium-sized flowering tree native to the Americas, it bears simple leaves either alternately or in clusters on short shoots. Its large fruit is commonly dried and hollowed to make cups, bowls, water containers and musical instruments.

A herbaceous plant native to South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, it grows from large bulbs and thrives in wet places. Its spring and summer flowers are funnel-shaped and sickly-sweet scented, usually pink with a deep pink or red stripe but sometimes white or red.

An erect herb native to southern and central Europe, the Black Sea basin, and southwestern and Central Asia. It is covered with stiff hairs, usually bears four broad leaves at each node, and has tiny pale-yellow flowers.
A thin-stemmed herbaceous vine indigenous to Africa and naturalized widely in the New World. Its oval to oblong fruits have hairs, spines or wart-like bumps and are eaten raw, cooked or pickled.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten raw, cooked as a vegetable or pickled; it is also used in Brazilian stew.

stories.summary: An upright herb native to South America, with rough, reddish glandular hairs on its sparsely branched stems. Its simple green leaves grow in opposite pairs and are paler underneath.
Small evergreen shrub native to Mexico, Guatemala and Honduras. It has fine, narrow, dark green leaves and purple, lavender or white flowers.
A hardy annual flowering plant native to Asia, Chinese forget-me-not has hairy leaves and sprays of sky-blue flowers in late summer. It is also grown as an ornamental.

Perennial herb native to North America, the Great Plains flatsedge grows in sunny, open places such as prairies, fields and roadsides. It spreads through underground stems and has triangular stalks topped by densely clustered, roughly spherical spikes.

A tender aquatic perennial native to Africa, papyrus forms tall, reed-like stands in shallow water, flooded swamps and lake margins. Its triangular green stems end in dense, feather-duster clusters of fine green rays, and it was historically used to make papyrus paper and boats. The pith of young shoots was eaten cooked or raw.
stories.edibilityNote: The pith of young shoots was historically eaten both cooked and raw.

stories.summary: A sedge native to eastern Africa, from Somalia to South Africa's Cape Provinces, and to Madagascar and Mauritius. It has been introduced to Florida, where it is considered invasive.

Flowering sedge native primarily to the Southeastern United States, extending from Martha’s Vineyard, Massachusetts, south to Tamaulipas, Mexico.
